instruction: What is the relationship between the use of levothyroxine and the improvement of symptoms in a patient diagnosed with subclinical hypothyroidism with hyperprolactinemia? (related to the task of Relation Extraction)
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient Name]
Medical Record Number: [MRN]
Date of Service: [Date of Service]

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a 48-year-old female from Honduras who presented to the clinic with chief complaints of breast tenderness and galactorrhea for the past two to three weeks. She had no history of tobacco, marijuana, alcohol, illicit drugs, or over the counter medicines. Physical examination revealed non-tender, diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland. On palpation, breast examination illustrated bilateral tenderness and milky yellowish discharge. Patient doesn't complain of headache or vision changes.

MEDICAL HISTORY:
The patient had a past medical history of hypertension and latent tuberculosis. Additionally, she had been treated for sciatica. She denied having any history of thyroid disease or hyperprolactinemia.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient underwent laboratory investigations and imaging studies, including a urine pregnancy test, mammogram, and MRI brain. The results of these investigations confirmed subclinical hypothyroidism with hyperprolactinemia. She was prescribed levothyroxine 50 mcg daily and three months later, there were significant improvements in her symptoms. Her repeat blood testing showed normal thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) level of 1.4 mIU/ml and normal serum prolactin level of 13.44 ng/ml.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
At the time of discharge, the patient was free from concerning symptoms and was relieved of breast tenderness and galactorrhea. She was able to tolerate her new medications well and was instructed to continue taking levothyroxine as prescribed by the clinician.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient was advised to keep all follow-up appointments with her healthcare provider and to monitor her symptoms. She was also instructed to contact her provider if any new symptoms arise or if there are any concerns regarding her medications.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will follow up with her healthcare provider in three months for repeat blood tests and to discuss any further treatment or management options.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
Levothyroxine 50 mcg daily.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Subclinical hypothyroidism with hyperprolactinemia.

SIGNED BY: 
[Attending Physician Name] MD
output: The use of levothyroxine 50 mcg daily was prescribed to the patient diagnosed with subclinical hypothyroidism with hyperprolactinemia and resulted in significant improvement of symptoms, according to the repeat blood testing.

instruction: What was the relationship between the patient's antibiotic regimen and the timing of her left nephrectomy, according to the discharge summary and using relation extraction?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Admission: The patient, a gravida 2 para 2, was admitted for left-sided abdominal and flank pain on postpartum day 0 (PPD0). She had a history of complete left nephrectomy due to multidrug resistant Klebsiella urosepsis and left pyelonephritis in the earlier postpartum period and was diagnosed with superimposed preeclampsia at 37 weeks' gestation.

Diagnostic Tests: During her admission, the patient underwent a variety of diagnostic tests and procedures, including a urine culture, chest and abdominal/pelvic CT scans, a left kidney ultrasound, and blood cultures.

Treatment: The patient was initially given PO ciprofloxacin and subsequently switched to PO levofloxacin on PPD3. However, when her symptoms worsened, she was transferred to the intensive care unit on PPD4 and started on IV piperacillin/tazobactam 3.375 grams every 6 hours. Her antibiotic regimen was adjusted to IV meropenem 500 mg every 6 hours on PPD5, and she underwent an open left nephrectomy on PPD10.

Discharge: Following her surgery and a 14-day course of IV ertapenem 1 gram daily, the patient's symptoms resolved, and her creatinine levels returned to normal. She was discharged on PPD13 and advised to follow up with her healthcare provider.
output: According to the discharge summary, the patient's antibiotic regimen was adjusted to IV meropenem 500 mg every 6 hours on PPD5, which was before her left nephrectomy on PPD10. However, the summary does not provide explicit information about the relationship between the regimen and the timing of the surgery.

instruction: What was the impact of omalizumab therapy on the disease severity and quality of life of the patient with normocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis?
input:
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 57-year-old female, presented with wheals, arthralgias, and a severe burning sensation on the skin. The skin lesions appeared as urticarial plaques predominantly on the trunk and proximal extremities. The patient reported relapsing and remitting symptoms for approximately 6 months prior to presenting at our office. After a thorough evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with normocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.

The patient was initially treated with a short course of oral corticosteroids, first and second-generation antihistamines, and hydroxychloroquine. However, despite initial treatment, the symptoms did not improve, and the disease worsened during physical examination.

Urticaria Activity Score 7 (UAS7) and Chronic Urticaria Quality of Life Questionnaire (CU-Q2oL) were assessed to evaluate the course of the disease. The patient's UAS7 after the 4-month course of first-line therapy was 19, and the CU-Q2oL showed marked impairment to the patient's quality of life.

Due to the lack of response to first-line treatment and the severity of the disease, treatment with omalizumab was initiated. After three-month therapy, disease severity improved from moderate severity to well controlled. However, due to economic limitations and insurance restrictions, the patient discontinued omalizumab treatment. The patient presented a disease activity and quality of life with a fluctuating pattern that was controlled with additional doses of omalizumab.

While follow-up is still ongoing, the patient is currently asymptomatic without any kind of medications and her disease is well-controlled.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Normocomplementemic Urticarial Vasculitis

Hospital Course Summary:

The 57-year-old female presented to our office with wheals, arthralgias, and a severe burning sensation on the skin. The patient was diagnosed with normocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis and was initially treated with a short course of oral corticosteroids, first and second-generation antihistamines, and hydroxychloroquine. However, due to a lack of response to the initial treatment, omalizumab was initiated. After three-month therapy, disease severity improved from moderate severity to well controlled. Despite discontinuing the treatment due to economic limitations and insurance restrictions, the patient's disease was well controlled with additional doses of omalizumab. The patient is currently asymptomatic and follow-up is ongoing.
output: The omalizumab therapy significantly improved the disease severity from moderate to well-controlled and the quality of life for the patient with normocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis. Despite discontinuing the treatment due to economic limitations and insurance restrictions, the patient's disease remained well controlled with additional doses of omalizumab. However, further follow-up is needed to assess the long-term effects of the treatment.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and treatment for the patient's condition upon readmission to the hospital, three weeks after the initial operation, as described in the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Discharge Date: N/A

Reason for Hospital Admission:
The patient, a 71-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital for right retrosigmoid craniotomy and tumor resection.

Hospital Course:
The patient's operation was uneventful, and she was discharged on dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 3 days. Three weeks later, she was readmitted to the hospital with persistent fever and chills, and occasional headaches for five days.

Diagnostic Assessment:
On admission, her vitals were notable for a fever of 38.5 °C, heart rate of 83 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 158/83 mmHg. A CT scan was ordered, which showed a subgaleal collection overlying the craniotomy site and hypodense areas in the right cerebellum that likely represented postoperative changes. A hypodense extra-axial collection was noted along the right cerebellum. These findings raised concern for postsurgical meningitis, and the patient was started on antibiotics for a presumptive urinary tract infection. However, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, with the development of nuchal rigidity, altered mental status, and seizures in the next 24 hours. A lumbar puncture was performed, which showed significant inflammation in the cerebrospinal fluid. The patient was then taken to the operating room for placement of an external ventricular drain and intrathecal antibiotic administration. A pathology report revealed fungal elements, and further testing confirmed Aspergillus fumigatus as the causative agent.

Treatment:
The patient was started on liposomal amphotericin and voriconazole for the treatment of CNS aspergillosis, which was eventually transitioned to oral voriconazole 250 mg every 12 hours to complete three months of therapy. The patient's mental status improved markedly over the following days, and she was transferred to a rehabilitation facility for physical therapy.

Follow-Up:
The patient was followed up at four months, during which time she was fully alert, and her verbal communication was almost back to baseline. No focal or meningeal signs were noted on examination, and a brain MRI showed complete resolution of leptomeningeal enhancement with no collections.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with CNS aspergillosis.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged to a rehabilitation facility for continued physical therapy.
output: The patient was diagnosed with CNS aspergillosis and was treated with liposomal amphotericin and voriconazole. The treatment was eventually transitioned to oral voriconazole for three months, and the patient's mental status improved markedly over the following days.

instruction: What wound treatment was administered to the patient following the consultation for large full-thickness abdominal skin loss with necrotic slough and MRSA and Acinetobacter infection post-surgical debridement for a gangrenous skin patch, according to the discharge summary?
input:
Electronic Health Record
Discharge Summary
Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient, a 31-year-old male, was admitted to the surgical ICU following a road traffic accident resulting in severe head injury, multiple facial fractures, and brain contusions, as well as bilateral flail rib fractures, lung contusions, and pneumothorax. The patient underwent five laparotomies during the first 10 days of hospitalization for liver injury (segment IV B & V resection) and hepatobiliary anastomosis for bile leak.

On hospital day 60, we were consulted for a large full-thickness abdominal skin loss with necrotic slough and MRSA and Acinetobacter infection post-surgical debridement for a gangrenous skin patch. The patient was deemed a poor surgical candidate, and a decision was made to treat the wound with V.A.C. VERAFLO CLEANSE CHOICE™ Dressing, using 50 cc of MicroSafe solution with a 20-minute dwell time, followed by six hours of negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) at -100 mm Hg. After four days, half of necrotic slough was removed, and almost 90% after the second application. New cultures were collected and appeared negative. The wound was then fixed with a simple V.A.C. for another four days.

Ultimately, the wound was considered ready for skin grafting, but due to the patient's poor surgical candidacy and the development of biliary fistula, it was decided to leave the wound to heal by secondary intention.

Discharge Condition and Disposition:
The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition.

Follow-up Instructions:
The patient was advised to follow up with their primary care physician or any relevant specialists for further care according to existing treatment plans and recommendations.

Primary Care Provider:
N/A

Attending Physician:
[redacted]
output: According to the discharge summary, the patient was treated with V.A.C. VERAFLO CLEANSE CHOICE™ Dressing, using 50 cc of MicroSafe solution with a 20-minute dwell time, followed by negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) at -100 mm Hg for six hours for the large full-thickness abdominal skin loss with necrotic slough and MRSA and Acinetobacter infection post-surgical debridement for a gangrenous skin patch. After four days, half of necrotic slough was removed, and almost 90% after the second application. The wound was then fixed with a simple V.A.C. for another four days.

instruction: What treatments were attempted for a 67-year-old female patient experiencing painful traumatic trigeminal neuropathy in the maxilla following dental implants, and what was the final medication and procedure that provided relief according to the discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The 67-year-old female patient presented to the hospital with complaints of severe pain in the left anterior buccal vestibule and tightened upper lip after multiple dental implants were placed in the maxilla. Painful traumatic trigeminal neuropathy was diagnosed based on clinical and radiological evaluations.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with Tegretol twice a day for 2 weeks, which helped relieve the symptoms, but the tightened pain on the bilateral sides of the nose persisted. The dose was increased for another 2 weeks, followed by another 2 weeks at the same dose. Although the frequency and severity of the pain decreased, side effects such as headache and dizziness occurred.

As a result, the patient was prescribed amitriptyline once a day before bedtime and capsaicin ointment locally applied to the site of the pain. A stent was created in the maxilla and capsaicin ointment was applied to the stent for 20 min, and the stent was to be worn three times a day. However, no improvement was noted, and the pain worsened.

The patient then received Neurontin three times daily and underwent electric acupuncture stimulation therapy (EAST) four times at 2-week intervals, but the burning and throbbing pain in the upper lip and tenderness of the palatal area persisted.

Afterward, medication was changed to Trileptal twice a day by prescribing 300 mg. Though there was a slight improvement, the patient persisted with persistent pain. In the upper part of the mucosa, 250 U of Dysport was injected, and, as a transient side effect, food was spilled due to the unnatural movement of the lips during mealtime, but the pain was significantly reduced. Three months later, the second injection of Dysport 250 U was performed. Thereafter, the pain was alleviated, and treatment was concluded.
output: The patient was treated with Tegretol, amitriptyline, capsaicin ointment, Neurontin, and Trileptal, along with electric acupuncture stimulation therapy and Dysport injections. The final medication and procedure that provided relief for the patient was Dysport injections of 250 U in the upper part of the mucosa, which significantly reduced the pain and concluded the treatment.

instruction: What was the treatment approach for a 24-year-old female patient with sudden bilateral hearing loss and atypical Cogan's syndrome in the provided discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 24-year-old female, presented to the otology clinic with a seven-week history of sudden onset right sided hearing loss and vertigo. One week later, she suffered left sided hearing loss. Initial evaluation by a community otolaryngologist suspected Cogan's syndrome. Subsequent evaluation by otolaryngology, ophthalmology, and rheumatology resulted in a diagnosis of atypical CS. Treatment with prednisone, steroid eye drops, and methotrexate was initiated. The patient's vertigo and imbalance had mostly resolved; however, her hearing did not improve.

Diagnostic Findings:

Initial audiogram and repeat audiogram after prednisone showed profound bilateral hearing loss with 0% speech discrimination bilaterally. MRI scan revealed enhancement of the otic capsule bilaterally. At the time of her scan, there was no loss of fluid signal from the cochlea on FIESTA sequencing. Autoimmune serology labs were normal.

Treatment:

Given the lack of response to medication and duration of her sudden onset hearing loss of 7 weeks, simultaneous cochlear implantation was performed. At surgery, the patient was found to have significant ossification of the scala tympani on both ears. A full electrode insertion was completed on each side after a significant basal turn drill-out was performed (Advanced Bionics HiRes Ultra device with mid-scala electrode, Valencia, CA). Postoperative cyclosporine drops were prescribed for both eyes.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient presented with sudden bilateral hearing loss and was diagnosed with atypical Cogan's syndrome. After unsuccessful medical treatment, simultaneous cochlear implantation was performed. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and the implant has shown improvement in performance. The patient is currently using cyclosporine drops in both eyes and following with rheumatology on a maintenance dose of methotrexate.
output: The treatment approach for the 24-year-old female patient with sudden bilateral hearing loss and atypical Cogan's syndrome in the provided discharge summary was simultaneous cochlear implantation after unsuccessful medical treatment with prednisone, steroid eye drops, and methotrexate. Postoperative cyclosporine drops were prescribed for both eyes, and the patient is following up with rheumatology on a maintenance dose of methotrexate.

instruction: What treatment was administered to the patient for optic neuritis related to vaccination as per the given discharge summary?
input:
HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient, a 27-year-old Hispanic man, was admitted with a 5-day history of headache, pain with ocular movements, and intermittent blurred vision after receiving a DTaP-IPV vaccination. The patient was diagnosed with optic neuritis related to the vaccination and was started on  intravenously administered Solu-Medrol (methylprednisolone). The patient's headache resolved, and vision improved with less optic nerve hyperemia and swelling. The patient was discharged on a prednisone taper and an orally administered diabetic medication.

HISTORY AND FINDINGS:
On examination, the patient's best corrected vision was 20/100 in the right eye, and 20/70 in the left eye, with restricted Confrontational visual fields in both eyes. Posterior segment examination showed optic nerve swelling and hyperemia in both eyes, and two microaneurysms in the mid periphery of the left eye. Intraocular pressures, pupil examination, ocular alignment, and extraocular movements were normal. The automated Humphrey visual field (HVF) testing demonstrated global depression in both eyes.

LABORATORY AND DIAGNOSTIC DATA:
Serum laboratory testing showed elevated glycated hemoglobin (A1C) at 6.9%, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), but normal liver tests including bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and hepatitis serologies. Tests for infectious and inflammatory etiologies including angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), lysozyme, antinuclear antibody (ANA), cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA), perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA), lupus panel, rapid plasma reagin (RPR), fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS), chest X-ray, and QuantiFERON Gold assay were normal. The lumbar puncture revealed a normal opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid studies were positive for myelin basic protein but negative for oligoclonal bands and neuromyelitis optica autoantibody serology.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
DTaP-IPV vaccination-related optic neuritis.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient was discharged on a prednisone taper and an orally administered diabetic medication. The patient is advised to follow up with an ophthalmologist and a primary care provider.
output: The patient was treated with intravenously administered Solu-Medrol (methylprednisolone) for optic neuritis related to the vaccination, followed by discharge on a prednisone taper and an orally administered diabetic medication.

instruction: What was the preliminary diagnosis and treatment plan for the patient with a large tumor in their lower lip and suspected metastatic submental lymph node, as described in the discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient, a 68-year-old male, was admitted with a large tumor in his lower lip, which had been present for approximately a year and had gradually increased in size. The patient reported no pain or bleeding initially, but over the last few months, the tumor had grown rapidly and become painful. On examination, the tumor was measured at 3 x 4 cm, raised, ulcerous and bleeding, expanding to 1/3 of his external upper lip. Additionally, the submental lymph node was firm and immobile and approximately 2 cm in diameter.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
Ultrasound revealed a suspected metastatic submental lymph node, and MRI Scan demonstrated a lesion in the lower lip. Fine needle aspiration results of the lymph node were consistent with metastatic squamous cell carcinoma, and the biopsy of the tumor confirmed SCC. The preliminary diagnosis was cT2N1M0 squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip.

The patient underwent surgery to remove the lower lip and 1/3 of the external upper lip. Bilateral cervical lymph node dissection was also performed. A team of head and neck surgeons completed the operation within 4 hours, and the patient was discharged from the hospital 14 days after surgery without any complications.

Follow-up:
The final pathology confirmed a diagnosis of SCC. Follow-up diagnostic tests including full blood count, biochemistry profile, ds-DNA, and ANA were normal and did not indicate any signs of metastasis. The patient was advised to attend regular clinical follow-up appointments for long-term monitoring.

Overall Assessment and Plan:
This 68-year-old male with a history of SLE, smoking, and alcohol use was diagnosed with SCC of the lower lip. Surgery was successful, and the patient was discharged 14 days post-surgery without any complications. Follow-up diagnostic tests were negative for metastasis, and the patient will receive regular follow-up for ongoing monitoring.
output: The preliminary diagnosis for the patient with a large tumor in their lower lip and suspected metastatic submental lymph node was cT2N1M0 squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip. The patient underwent surgery to remove the tumor along with 1/3 of the external upper lip and bilateral cervical lymph node dissection. The final pathology confirmed a diagnosis of SCC, and follow-up tests did not indicate any signs of metastasis. The patient will receive regular follow-up appointments for monitoring.

instruction: What Named Entities related to the diagnosis of neurocysticercosis can be identified using Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with recurrent headache, blurred vision, and progressive memory loss. The initial headache started 5 years before admission, which progressively worsened over time. A year and a half before admission, she developed blurred vision. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hydrocephalus. Repeated lumbar punctures showed increased pressure, elevated protein and pleocytosis. Two months before admission, she developed progressive memory loss. Brain computed tomography (CT) scan showed scattered parenchymal calcified lesions in her brain. Further investigation with MRI revealed the presence of numerous cystic lesions and diffuse T2-weighted hyperintensity in the juxta-ventricular white matter, together with enhancement of the meninges, especially the basal meninges. CSF cytology showed increased eosinophils, and NGS of CSF identified T. solium DNA sequences. Plain x-rays showed scattered “cigar-shaped” calcified lesions in the legs. With this knowledge of her medical condition, she was diagnosed with NCC (basal subarachnoid NCC and parenchymal NCC with calcified cysts).

Hospital Course Summary:
A 53-year-old woman presented with a recurrent headache, blurred vision, and progressive memory loss. She had a history of recurrent grand mal seizures about 20 years ago. During admission, a head CT scan showed scattered parenchymal calcified lesions in the right frontal lobe, right parietal lobe, right thalamus, left temporal lobe, left occipital lobe, and bilateral basal ganglia area. Brain MRI showed hydrocephalus and diffuse T2-weighted hyperintensity in the juxta-ventricular white matter, together with enhancement of the meninges, especially the basal meninges, and multiple cystic lesions in the prepontine cistern, ambient cistern, and suprasellar cistern. After further investigation, CSF cytology revealed increased eosinophils, and NGS of CSF identified T. solium DNA sequences. Plain x-rays showed scattered “cigar-shaped” calcified lesions in the legs.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The diagnosis was NCC (basal subarachnoid NCC and parenchymal NCC with calcified cysts). The patient was treated with albendazole and dexamethasone and underwent an endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) because of severe hydrocephalus. After treatment, her symptoms, neuroimaging and CSF findings improved markedly.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is recommended for follow-up care with her primary care physician for continued monitoring to ensure complete resolution of her symptoms.
output: The Named Entities related to the diagnosis of neurocysticercosis that can be identified using Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary are T. solium, NCC, and albendazole.

instruction: What Named Entities related to the patient's diagnosis and treatment can be recognized through Named Entity Recognition in the given discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient, a 44-year-old Caucasian male, presented with an 8-month history of reflux and heartburn that was relieved by Esomeprazole. Endoscopic evaluation revealed a polypoid-shaped mass measuring 1 cm in size at the gastroesophageal junction, which was resected via the endoscopic mucosal resection technique (EMR). Ultrasonic evaluation revealed a hypoechoic lesion that was confined to the deep mucosa and submucosa with no deeper layer involvement. The nodule was resected successfully, and the patient had an uneventful postoperative course.

In addition, there were prominent mucus glands with chronic inflammation consistent with heterotopic salivary glands, surrounded by prominent adipose tissue and congested vessels in the submucosa.

Follow-Up and Prognosis:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of a 1 cm gastroesophageal junction nodule. The patient was advised to follow up with their primary care physician regularly and to avoid any triggers that may exacerbate reflux and heartburn symptoms. The prognosis is good, and the patient is expected to have a favorable outcome.

instruction: What was the patient's diagnosis and treatment plan for the infantile form of nephrotic cystinosis with preserved kidney function, according to the discharge summary?

At the last examination, the patient had elevated cystine levels in the granulocytes and nephrocalcinosis of both kidneys, and the cysteamine dose was increased.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Infantile form of nephrotic cystinosis with preserved kidney function.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient should continue taking cysteamine as prescribed and attending follow-up appointments with their healthcare provider for monitoring and management of their condition.

Follow-up with a pediatric ophthalmologist is recommended for monitoring of the cystine crystals in the cornea.

The patient should also follow a balanced diet and maintain adequate fluid intake.

If any concerning symptoms develop, the patient should seek medical attention promptly.

instruction: What was the patient's diagnosis and treatment for Myositis Ossificans, and what were the observed outcomes during the follow-up period?
input:
Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Hospital Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Hospital Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital with a painful and rapidly-growing mass over the proximal phalanx of the right ring finger and numbness along the distribution of the radial digital nerve of the finger. Examination showed a firm tender mass measuring 3.5 × 2 cm with an overlying skin erythema. Plain x-rays showed no bony abnormalities or calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an iso-intense lesion on T1-weighted images and T2-weighted images showed high intensity in the center of the lesion and low intensity at the periphery of the lesion. Surgical excision was done under general anesthesia. The mass infiltrated the entire flexor sheath over the proximal phalanx as well as the checkrein ligament of the proximal interphalangeal joint. The common digital artery of the 3rd web space was obliterated by the tumor. Total excision was done and this required excision of the flexor sheath over the proximal phalanx (including the entire A2 pulley), the checkrein ligament and the common digital artery. The digital nerve was preserved. Histology showed the classic 3 histological zones of myositis ossificans: a central cellular / fibroblastic zone, an intermediate zone of osteoid (immature bone) and an outer zone of mature bone. The patient was followed up for one year after surgery with no evidence of recurrence. At final follow up, there was full flexion of the digit, but the proximal interphalangeal joint had an extension lag of 30o. Upon palpation, bowstringing of the flexor tendon was felt over the proximal phalanx. The static two-point discrimination on the radial side of the ring finger improved to 6 mm.

Diagnosis:
Myositis Ossificans

Treatment:
Surgical excision was performed under general anesthesia. Total excision was done and this required excision of the flexor sheath over the proximal phalanx (including the entire A2 pulley), the checkrein ligament and the common digital artery. The digital nerve was preserved.

Follow-up:
The patient was followed up for one year after surgery with no evidence of recurrence. At final follow up, there was full flexion of the digit, but the proximal interphalangeal joint had an extension lag of 30o. Upon palpation, bowstringing of the flexor tendon was felt over the proximal phalanx. The static two-point discrimination on the radial side of the ring finger improved to 6 mm.

Patient Condition at Discharge:
Stable, improved.
output: The patient was diagnosed with Myositis Ossificans and underwent surgical excision under general anesthesia, requiring excision of the flexor sheath over the proximal phalanx, the checkrein ligament, and the common digital artery. The digital nerve was successfully preserved. After one year of follow-up, there was no evidence of recurrence, although the patient experienced some extension lag and bowstringing of the flexor tendon over the proximal phalanx. The static two-point discrimination on the radial side of the ring finger improved to 6mm.

instruction: What is the histological character of phosphoglyceride crystal deposits in PGDD and how can it be differentiated from malignant tumors?
input:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Abdominal wall tumor
Principal Diagnosis: Foreign-body granuloma
Secondary Diagnosis: Elevated inflammatory markers

Hospital Course:
A 57-year-old Japanese man was admitted to the hospital with increasing right lower abdominal pain. On initial examination, an abdominal wall tumor was detected using transabdominal ultrasound. Laboratory results revealed elevated inflammatory markers. Helical computed tomography (CT) revealed a solid mass and magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass that exhibited low intensity. Positron emission tomography–CT revealed fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation.

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy and a malignant tumor was suspected. Intraoperative findings at laparotomy revealed an elastic, hard, milky-whitish mass with a rough surface and capillary growth in the right lower quadrant. The mass was completely removed, and the surgical margin secured. Pathologic examination revealed that these masses were foreign-body granulomas consisting of string-like crystals and a foreign-body giant cell. Immunohistological staining was positive in cells surrounding phosphoglyceride crystals. The patient underwent regular follow-up abdominal ultrasound examination and CT postoperatively. As of 3 years after the procedure, no signs of recurrence have been detected.

Discussion:
PGDD is a rare disease characterized by deposition of phosphoglyceride crystals. It can sometimes form a large mass and be misdiagnosed as a malignant tumor. Little is known about its etiology and pathogenesis. This deposition disease is apparently triggered by injury and subsequent macrophage aggregation, with a histological picture of deposited crystal radiating from the cell membranes of epithelioid cells. No specific markers exist for PGDD, and differentiating this disease from malignant tumors without pathological examination is difficult.

Conclusion:
In conclusion, a foreign-body granuloma was discovered during the patient's exploratory laparotomy. The mass was completely removed, and the surgical margin secured. Regular follow-up has not revealed any findings suspicious of recurrence.
output: The histological character of phosphoglyceride crystal deposits in PGDD consists of deposition of phosphoglyceride crystals that radiate from the cell membranes of epithelioid cells and foreign-body giant cells. PGDD can be difficult to differentiate from malignant tumors without pathological examination as it does not have any specific markers.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and treatment course for a 33-year-old nulliparous woman who was admitted to the hospital for lower abdominal pain and subsequently underwent emergency laparoscopy for a suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy?

We resected the mass from the left ovary and performed a right salpingectomy. After intraperitoneal irrigation with 3 L of saline, we placed drains into the cul-de sac and finished the operation. 

Hospital Course:
Histopathological analysis confirmed the presence of left ovarian pregnancy with chorionic villi within the ovarian tissue, along with a right tubal pregnancy. She was monitored for a few days postoperatively and subsequently discharged with regular follow-up appointments.

Hospital Course:
The patient's postoperative course was uneventful without any complications. She was advised to avoid strenuous activities for a week and instructed to attend regular follow-up appointments. The patient was referred for further counseling to discuss fertility options and possible future pregnancies.

1. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum 
2. Left ovarian pregnancy with chorionic villi incidentally found intraoperatively 
3. Right tubal pregnancy 

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with regular follow-up appointments.

instruction: What Named Entities related to the diagnosis of mixed squamous cell and glandular papilloma of the bronchus without HPV infection can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 17-year-old female who presented with a history of cough and right chest pain over the past two months, along with bloody sputum over the past week. Upon initial assessment, vital signs and physical examinations were within normal limits, and serum laboratory data were unremarkable. Radiological findings, including chest X-ray and contrast-enhanced thoracic computed tomography, indicated an inhomogeneously enhanced nodule as large as 3 cm in diameter in the right lung field, suggestive of malignancy. A bronchoscopy was performed, which revealed a protruding white intra-bronchial tumour at the orifice of the right B8. Haematoxylin and eosin staining of the biopsied specimens obtained from the tumour showed that a thickened stratified squamous epithelium covered the mucosal surface. A second bronchoscopy showed that the protruded tumour had progressed and completely occluded the lumen of the B8. H&E staining of endobronchial biopsied specimens with forceps obtained from the tumour showed fragments of ciliated columnar (glandular) epithelium admixed in the abundant squamous epithelium and parakeratotic debris. Papanicolaou staining of the bronchial washing fluid from the right B8 demonstrated the aggregation of stratified squamous cells with orange-coloured cytoplasm. Repeated bronchoscopy showed no evidence of malignancy or bloody phlegm irrespective of progression of the intra-bronchial tumour on thoracic CT. The intra-tracheal tumour was considered the source of bloody sputum; therefore, the patient underwent right lower lobe lobectomy via Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery. Pathologic examination of the tumour revealed thick squamous and glandular epithelia both of which proliferated in a papillary pattern along with inflamed fibrovascular cores. The former (squamous) was predominant, and neither component demonstrated malignant features. Upon further histological analysis, our case showed a negative result both in polymerase chain reaction for human papillomavirus (HPV) and immunohistochemical staining with p16Ink4a, a surrogate molecular marker of HPV. Finally, she was diagnosed with mixed squamous cell and glandular papilloma of the bronchus without HPV infection.

Hospital Course:
The patient was discharged in good health with instructions for postoperative care. Further follow-up with imaging studies is recommended. She was also advised to maintain follow-up appointments with her primary care physician.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Mixed squamous cell and glandular papilloma of the bronchus without HPV infection.

Disposition:
Discharged in good health.

instruction: What was the complication arising from ureteroscopy performed on the patient and its treatment? (related to relation extraction)

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 45-year-old female, presented with severe right flank pain and a past medical history of right ureteral calculi secondary to right calyceal diverticulum. Computed tomography revealed a right renal stone in her ureteropelvic junction. Therefore, the patient underwent ureteroscopy with a semirigid 6/7.5 Fr ureteroscope to remove the stone. The procedure lasted 38 minutes with a ureteroscopic duration of 25 minutes. However, the ureteral stone or the calyceal diverticulum could not be located. No ureteral stent was placed after the operation. The patient experienced severe right flank pain and became febrile 15 hours later. A follow-up computed tomography showed perinephric extravasation of urine and bleeding inside the diverticulum confirming the rupture of the calyceal diverticulum secondary to ureteroscopy. The patient was treated with ceftriaxone 2 g per day with additional oral antibiotics (tebipenem pivoxil 300 mg per day) based on the urine culture testing positive for E.coli with extended spectrum beta lactamase. By postoperative day 14, the patient was asymptomatic, and the computed tomography performed in postoperative month 3 confirmed the complete resolution of extravasation.
output: The complication arising from the ureteroscopy is the rupture of the patient's right calyceal diverticulum, resulting in perinephric extravasation of urine and bleeding. The patient was treated with antibiotics, including ceftriaxone and tebipenem pivoxil, and the extravasation completely resolved on a follow-up CT scan in postoperative month 3.

Discharge Summary:

Patient name: [Redacted]
Age: 61
Gender: Male

Hospital: [Redacted]
Service: Otolaryngology

Chief Complaint:
Progressive asymmetric hearing loss and limited communication ability.

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred for hearing rehabilitation with cochlear implant on the left side due to progressive asymmetric hearing loss and limited communication ability. Word recognition score on the left side was 20% with hearing aid and 50% on the right side with FM system testing at 65 dB SPL.

A contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI) revealed an intra- and extracanalicular vestibular schwannoma (VS) or acoustic neuroma. Possible treatment options included tumor removal via a retrosigmoid approach or stereotactic radiotherapy as first-line therapy. The patient underwent tumor removal via a retrosigmoid approach. Vestibulocochlear and facial nerves were preserved as their functionality was monitored with electrophysiologic monitoring (neuromonitoring). There was a small residual intracanalicular VS six months postoperatively. Subsequently, the patient underwent stereotactic radiotherapy before cochlear implantation with 13 Gy (70% Isodose; Dmax 18.6 Gy) delivered in a single session.

Six weeks later, the cochlear implant was placed more posterior than usual to minimize artifacts in postoperative MRI scans. Six months after cochlear implantation, the first postoperative MRI was performed using a 1.5 Tesla MR with medium bandwidth. One month after implantation, aided word recognition score (WRS) with cochlear implant on the left side (and masking of the right side) was 45% with FM testing at 65 dB SPL and six months later, 60%. Binaural hearing with cochlear implant on the left side and hearing aid on the right side resulted in an aided WRS of 90% with FM testing after two years.

Hearing in noise was measured with the aided Oldenburg Sentence test (OLSA). One year postoperatively, the test revealed scores of −1.1 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for the left side with cochlear implant (with masking of the right ear) and −3 dB with cochlear implant and hearing aid on the right side, indicating an improvement of hearing in noise with cochlear implant.

Impression:

The patient underwent vestibular schwannoma resection via a retrosigmoid approach with preserved vestibulocochlear and facial nerves. He subsequently underwent a stereotactic radiotherapy before cochlear implantation with good hearing outcomes. The patient demonstrated significant improvement in word recognition score, binaural hearing, and hearing in noise after cochlear implantation. 

Plan:

Continue follow-up with audiology to monitor hearing outcomes. Consider MRI surveillance to evaluate recurrent/suspicious growth of vestibular schwannoma. Provide annual hearing and vestibular function assessments.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Hospital Admission Dates: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Metastatic breast carcinoma to the left external auditory canal (EAC)

Course of Hospitalization:

The patient, a 53-year-old female, was admitted to our hospital with a history of swelling in her left EAC for 2 weeks and gradually worsening hearing loss. The patient had been diagnosed with invasive ductal breast carcinoma 4 years prior, which was initially treated with a radical mastectomy and followed by chemoradiotherapy. In the follow-up period, the patient had developed bone and lung metastases and relevant treatment was administered.

On physical examination, a soft tissue mass was observed that completely obstructed the left EAC. No neurologic symptoms were observed. A CT scan of the temporal bone was performed, which revealed that the left EAC had been completely obstructed by a soft tissue density mass. Despite the fact that the mass was located in both bony and cartilaginous EAC, no bony or cartilaginous invasion was observed. MRI showed a well-defined and fusiform soft tissue mass that filled the left EAC and was located in both the bony and cartilaginous EAC. Following the administration of the gadolinium-based contrast agent, homogeneous enhancement was seen. DWI showed slightly hyperintense signal on isotropic trace image and the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map revealed slightly restricted diffusion in the mass. There was a small, non-enhancing hemorrhagic fluid collection present between the mass and the tympanic membrane. Middle and internal ear structures were normal on both MRI and temporal CT images. Based on the patient's history and imaging results, the diagnosis of metastatic breast carcinoma to the left EAC was made.

The patient underwent surgical operation by the ENT surgeon and the mass was subtotally removed. Histopathologic examination of specimens revealed metastatic carcinoma that had the same histopathologic features as the primary breast carcinoma. Histopathological findings of the excised lesion showed microscopically a infiltrative carcinoma compatible with a breast origin based on immunohistochemical study results that were positive for Estrogen Receptor (ER), Cytokeratin 7, and E-cadherin but negative for C-Erb-b2 and Progesterone receptor (PR). The tumor was composed of atypical cells with large nuclei and prominent nucleoli in a solid pattern. There was no ductal or tubular structure. The positivity of both ER and E-Cadherin also supported ductal type when compared to lobular carcinoma of the breast.

The patient was discharged with appropriate referrals for further treatment follow-up. The patient's condition was stable upon discharge.

Hospital course summary complete.

A 10 French by 7 cm stent was placed in the common bile duct and there was adequate bile flow. A follow-up ERCP was performed 8 weeks later and showed no biliary dilation or obstruction.

The patient was referred to a tertiary center for further management. She underwent EGD and ERCP with stent placement with no evidence of further bleeding. Her alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin returned to their baseline prior to the liver biopsy. She did not have any recurrence or relapse of her symptoms. There were no further signs of bleeding and her hemoglobin returned to baseline.

The patient is advised to follow up with the gastroenterologist to monitor the steatohepatitis and pancreatitis, and to continue a healthy diet and lifestyle to manage her comorbidities, including type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and internal hemorrhoids. Follow-up with the gastroenterologist for monitoring and further management of the steatohepatitis and pancreatitis.

The patient recovered well and was discharged in stable condition with instructions to follow up with the treating physician.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and treatment plan for severe hypertriglyceridemia in the setting of cGVHD described in the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 50
Sex: Male

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with severe fatigue, aching upper abdominal pain, headache, and nausea. He had a history of myelodysplastic syndrome, which had developed into acute myeloid leukemia and had undergone nonmyeloablative allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. He was diagnosed with chronic GVHD (cGVHD) involving the eyes, skin, liver, and buccal mucosa, which was being managed with prednisone on a taper, sirolimus, and extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP). The patient developed a systemic infection with Mycobacterium abscessus (M. abscessus), following which he was switched to ruxolitinib, along with sirolimus and prednisone.

The patient's blood sample showed high levels of lipids, with triglycerides more than 4000 (ref. range <150 mg/dL), following which he was admitted to the hospital. He was started on an insulin drip with a goal to reduce triglyceride levels, and medications, such as sirolimus and lisinopril, were held for further evaluation. The patient's abdominal pain improved slightly, and therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) was planned to promptly reduce the triglyceride level and prevent any further complications of marked hypertriglyceridemia. Ruxolitinib was stopped at that time.

TPE was performed on hospital day 3, following which the patient's triglyceride level decreased from 2983 (on hospital arrival) to 1305 and 407 on hospital day 4. The patient noted relief of his abdominal discomfort with improved triglyceride levels. He was instructed to follow a low-fat and low-carbohydrate diet.

The patient's triglyceride levels remained high (446-881 mg/dL) for the week following discharge, but trended down to the 200s within two weeks of discharge (211-277 mg/dL) and remained within normal or minimally elevated ranges (94-270 mg/dL) for the following year. After stopping ruxolitinib, the patient's GVHD was managed with prednisone, ibrutinib, topical tacrolimus, dexamethasone oral solution, pancreatic enzymes, and artificial tears. 

Diagnosis:

Severe hypertriglyceridemia in the setting of cGVHD

Treatment:

Insulin drip, therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), and diet modification

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to follow a low-fat and low-carbohydrate diet and must have frequent lipid level monitoring. The patient should immediately report any abdominal discomfort to his physician. instruction: What entities related to the patient's medical conditions can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Large lobulated multicompartmental supra-sellar mass centered within the hypothalamus/optic chiasm.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a two-year-old female with a six-week history of macrocephaly and truncal and peripheral ataxia, was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. An urgent brain MRI demonstrated the presence of a large lobulated multicompartmental supra-sellar mass centered within the hypothalamus/optic chiasm, with extension into the surrounding structures and mass effect on the midbrain and third ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus.

The patient underwent an endoscopic biopsy and septostomy, along with a right-sided ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt to manage her hydrocephalus. The pathology of the lesion confirmed the diagnosis of a low-grade glioma that was BRAF-V600E negative on immunohistochemistry but positive on next-generation sequencing. She was started on chemotherapy with vincristine and carboplatin but had rapid tumor progression with worsening hydrocephalus six weeks into chemotherapy.

This progression caused the patient to develop further complications, including progressive right-sided hemiparesis, bitemporal hemianopia, central hypothyroidism, and feeding difficulties requiring a gastrostomy tube and placement of a second VP shunt.

After extensive discussions and mutual expert consensus, her chemotherapy was stopped, and she was started on the novel targeted agent dabrafenib. By three months of starting dabrafenib, the size of her tumor decreased by more than 70%, with continued decline until plateauing after two years of therapy.

Prior to dabrafenib, the patient had marked motor and speech impairments but is now able to perform all age-appropriate developmental skills independently. She no longer requires tube feeding and has been growing well. Her bitemporal hemianopia has improved markedly. Her visual acuity is the only symptom that has not shown significant recovery, as she continues to have low but stable visual acuity bilaterally.

The patient was enrolled in the ORCYD biomarker study to test her plasma and CSF for the presence of the BRAF-V600E mutation and to correlate the assay results with the MRI changes observed while on dabrafenib therapy. However, the BRAF-V600E mutation was not detected in any of the samples from either plasma or CSF.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with plans to continue on dabrafenib as long as the patient is tolerating the therapy well with no recurrence or progression of the tumor.

Discharge Medications:

None.

Follow-up:

The patient will follow up with her oncologist for regular check-ups and monitoring. Future imaging studies will be performed as needed to evaluate the progression of the tumor.
output: Using Named Entity Recognition, entities related to the patient's medical conditions that can be identified in this discharge summary include the patient's name, gender, date of admission, date of discharge, admitting diagnosis (large lobulated multicompartmental supra-sellar mass), brain structures affected by the mass (hypothalamus/optic chiasm, midbrain, third ventricle), treatment procedures (endoscopic biopsy, septostomy, ventriculoperitoneal shunt), chemotherapy medications (vincristine, carboplatin), targeted therapy medication (dabrafenib), and biomarker study (ORCYD). It is unanswerable through the given information whether the patient has any underlying medical conditions or comorbidities aside from the brain mass.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and surgical treatment for the mid-ureteral stricture detected in a two-year-old girl admitted with hydronephrosis and abdominal pain concerns as described in the discharge summary?
input:

A mid-ureteral stricture with a length of 1 cm was diagnosed during the RGP, and subsequently, the patient underwent a laparoscopic excision of the stricture segment and ureteroureterostomy. The pathological report showed predominant severe chronic inflammation with foreign body giant cell infiltration of the ureteral wall with a severely stenosed lumen. Right RGP was performed at the time of stent removal with smooth passage of contrast media up to the pelvicalyceal system. An ultrasound examination performed 30 months postoperatively revealed SFU grade 1 hydronephrosis.

Summary:
The patient underwent laparoscopic excision of the stricture segment and ureteroureterostomy for the diagnosis of a mid-ureteral stricture, which was confirmed on right RGP. The pathological report showed chronic inflammation with a severely stenosed lumen. An ultrasound examination performed 30 months postoperatively revealed SFU grade 1 hydronephrosis.
output: The diagnosis of the mid-ureteral stricture was confirmed during right RGP, and the patient underwent laparoscopic excision of the stricture segment and ureteroureterostomy. The pathological report showed severe chronic inflammation with a stenosed lumen. The treatment for the mid-ureteral stricture was laparoscopic excision of the stricture segment and ureteroureterostomy. The ultrasound examination performed 30 months postoperatively revealed SFU grade 1 hydronephrosis.

She has been referred to outpatient psychiatric care for continued evaluation and management. The patient was discharged in a stable condition with recommendations to follow a healthy lifestyle and adhere to the medical regimen prescribed.
output: The patient's presenting symptom of psychosis, in the form of auditory hallucinations, was most likely related to her new acute right occipital lobe infarct with hemorrhagic transformation and not due to a pharmacologic etiology or history of mood disorders. The hallucinations resolved without requiring antipsychotic medications on day two of hospitalization. However, the patient's long-standing medical history of cerebral infarcts and low ejection fraction will require ongoing cardiac and neurological management. Follow-up imaging studies will be necessary as deemed necessary.

instruction: What is the relationship extracted through relation extraction between the non-surgical and surgical endodontic retreatments and the recurring pain and pus discharge in the patient's diagnosed chronic apical periodontitis?
input:
Patient Information:
Name: [Patient Name]
Age: 20
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
The patient was admitted to the Department of Operative Dentistry at Dow Dental College with complaints of pain in a previously treated left maxillary lateral incisor. The patient experienced pain on percussion, but showed no discharging sinus and had normal mobility. She exhibited an unusual cervical depression mesially and a 5 mm isolated probing defect on the palatal aspect with an associated shallow palatogingival groove. Cold test revealed the lateral incisor was non-vital, while the adjacent central incisor and canine were vital. Radiographically, a poorly obturated canal was present with a periapical radiolucency and an untreated accessory root with a patent canal. A diagnosis of previous inadequate treatment and chronic apical periodontitis secondary to an untreated canal was made, and non-surgical endodontic retreatment was planned.

Hospitalization:
The patient underwent non-surgical endodontic retreatment using calcium hydroxide and ProTaper rotary NiTi instruments. Subsequently, both canals were dried, and sodium hypochlorite was used to remove dressing. Canals were obturated with warm vertical technique using an obturation device and resin-based sealer. The access cavity was restored with a flowable composite resin.

Discharge:
The patient returned after a month for a recall visit and complained of recurring pain and pus discharge. It was decided to perform surgical retreatment, and a full thickness mucoperiosteal flap was raised. A defect in buccal plate was visible around the apex of the accessory root, and the periapical lesion was easily removed due to no attachment to either root. The bony window was filled with an irradiated allograft and covered with a resorbable collagen membrane. Sling suturing technique with 3.0 silk sutures was used for primary closure. The stitches were removed after a week. On a 2-year follow-up, the patient reported complete absence of symptoms and reduced periodontal probing depth on palatal aspect. Radiographic signs of complete healing but with mild discoloration of the clinical crown were observed, which were treated with a walking bleach technique using sodium perborate powder.

Summary:
The patient was admitted with complaints of pain from a previously treated left maxillary lateral incisor and a diagnosis of previous inadequate treatment and chronic apical periodontitis secondary to an untreated canal was made. Non-surgical endodontic retreatment was performed, followed by surgical retreatment due to recurring pain and pus discharge. The patient was treated with a full thickness mucoperiosteal flap and no root end resection was performed, due to easy removal of periapical lesion. On a 2-year follow-up, the patient showed complete absence of symptoms and reduced periodontal probing depth on palatal aspect. Treatment for mild discoloration of clinical crown was also performed.
output: The patient underwent non-surgical endodontic retreatment, but complained of recurring pain and pus discharge upon returning after a month, which led to surgical retreatment. The relationship extracted is that the non-surgical retreatment was insufficient in treating the chronic apical periodontitis, hence the need for surgical retreatment.

instruction: What treatments were administered to a 9-year-old girl with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and severe asthma who was readmitted to the hospital with cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral wheeze after initial antibiotic therapy and specific asthma treatment?
input:

The patient had a history of childhood asthma and was previously treated with inhaled corticosteroids. After 72 hours of antibiotic therapy for possible pneumonia and specific treatment for asthma, the patient's symptoms improved. However, four days later, the patient was readmitted with cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral wheeze. The patient was treated with Intravenous infusion (IV) of methylprednisolone, IV fluconazole, and a high dose of oral prednisolone for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The patient also received high doses of itraconazole for ABPA and fluticasone plus salmeterol inhaler spray for severe asthma. Oxygen supplementation was given, and a chest tube was inserted due to a decrease in breathing sounds and severe respiratory distress. A follow-up showed a significant improvement in the patient's general condition, and the dose of prednisolone was reduced by 25% every four weeks until stopped.

- Oxygen supplementation 
- Chest tube inserted due to decreased breathing sounds and severe respiratory distress

- Significant improvement in general condition
output: The treatments administered to the 9-year-old girl with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and severe asthma who was readmitted to the hospital with cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral wheeze after initial antibiotic therapy and specific asthma treatment were IV methylprednisolone, IV fluconazole, high doses of oral prednisolone for ABPA, high doses of itraconazole for ABPA, and fluticasone plus salmeterol inhaler spray for severe asthma. instruction: What is the presumed diagnosis of the patient based on the radiological evidence of optic neuritis, limbic, and cortical encephalitis, subcortical, and pontine myelitis, and leptomeningitis? (related to Relation Extraction)
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 42-year-old female with a recent history of bilateral progressive blurring of vision, which had been ongoing for approximately 8 days upon admission. She presented to the hospital with no redness, photophobia, headache, nausea, vomiting, or head trauma. Sluggish pupillary light reflexes were present, and a right relative afferent pupillary defect was detected as well as bilateral red color desaturation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed radiological evidence of bilateral optic neuritis (ON), limbic and cortical encephalitis, subcortical and pontine myelitis, and leptomeningitis. The ultimate diagnosis was a presumptive diagnosis of autoimmune limbic encephalitis. The patient was started on high-dose pulsed steroid therapy 3 days after admission for 72 hours, followed by switching to oral steroids with gradual tapering. She was tapered off oral steroids by March 2016, and she was found to have stable visual acuity (VA) at her last follow-up in July 2016. She is currently being followed with annual PET-CT imaging for tumor surveillance as well as annual serological surveillance.

Hospital Course - Admission:
On March 26, 2013, the patient presented to the hospital with bilateral progressive blurring of vision, which had been ongoing for approximately 8 days. She had no redness or photophobia, nor did she have pain at rest or upon eye movement. Furthermore, she had no recent flulike illness, upper respiratory tract symptoms, fever, chills, or rigor. Physical examination revealed a relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed radiological evidence of bilateral optic neuritis (ON), limbic and cortical encephalitis, subcortical and pontine myelitis, and leptomeningitis.

Hospital Course - Treatment:
The patient was started on high-dose pulsed steroid therapy 3 days after admission for 72 hours, followed by switching to oral steroids with gradual tapering according to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial protocol. In September 2013, due to relapse, the patient was restarted on intravenous methylprednisolone, followed by maintenance therapy with oral prednisolone with the aim of tapering the steroid over time. She was also started on azathioprine.

Hospital Course - Improvement:
VA improved back to 0.7 bilaterally after initiation of immunosuppressant therapy. Limb power returned to full strength by November 2013. Throughout the next 2 years, the patient had slow improvement of VA back to 0.7 bilaterally and color vision recovering bilaterally. She was tapered off oral steroids by March 2016.

Hospital Course - Follow-up:
The patient is currently being followed with annual PET-CT imaging for tumor surveillance as well as annual serological surveillance. Her last follow-up in July 2016 revealed stable visual acuity.
output: The presumptive diagnosis of the patient based on the radiological evidence of optic neuritis, limbic, and cortical encephalitis, subcortical, and pontine myelitis, and leptomeningitis is autoimmune limbic encephalitis.

instruction: What was the patient diagnosed with and what treatment was provided for incomplete intestinal obstruction caused by psyllium husk ingestion?
input:
Subjective:
The patient, a 21-year-old man, presented complaining of lower abdominal pain and constipation for five days. He had no history of chronic medical illness or abdominal operations. The patient ingested psyllium husks as herbal medicine for weight control and health promotion before the onset of constipation. The patient did not consume adequate fluids due to religious fasting during the consumption of the husks.

Objective:
Upon examination, the patient had a mildly distended abdomen. X-ray of the abdomen was normal. The patient was initially diagnosed with constipation and was discharged with a laxative, Psyllium (ispaghula husk) sachets 7 g twice daily. Two days later, he returned with increased abdominal distension without passing any stools, but passing flatus. The patient's vital signs were normal, and his abdomen was markedly distended, but soft and lax. The repeated abdominal x-ray showed a huge fecal loading filling the entire colon with no gas fluid levels. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen with oral contrast confirmed marked dilation of the entire colon, particularly in the sigmoid colon, which was hugely distended and filled with gas and fecal matter.

Assessment:
The patient was diagnosed with incomplete intestinal obstruction due to psyllium husk ingestion causing fecal impaction.

Plan:
The patient received repeated enemas, which helped to relieve the intestinal obstruction. The patient was discharged home two days later without any operative intervention.

Summary:
The 21-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with constipation and abdominal pain, possibly caused by his ingestion of psyllium husks. The patient was initially diagnosed with constipation and discharged with laxatives. However, the patient returned to the Emergency Department with increased abdominal distension and an inability to pass stools. The CT scan confirmed fecal impaction and incomplete intestinal obstruction. The patient received enemas, which relieved the obstruction, and he was discharged without any operative intervention.
output: The patient was diagnosed with incomplete intestinal obstruction caused by psyllium husk ingestion. The treatment provided was repeated enemas, which relieved the obstruction, and the patient was discharged without any operative intervention.

instruction: What Named Entities related to the patient's diagnosis of heterozygotic MKD can be identified using Named Entity Recognition in the given discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient, a twelve-year-old female, presented with recurrent episodes of fever, fatigue, and arthralgia/myalgia of the lower limbs. These symptoms began at the age of three months and occurred once or twice monthly. Various investigations were negative, and it was noted that the patient had a history of Stevens–Johnson syndrome and an appendectomy. At the age of 8, the patient was diagnosed with heterozygotic MKD and was prescribed the anti-TNFα agent etanercept. The patient continued to experience attacks twice a month lasting 3 days, missing 100 days per year of school despite etanercept treatment, and her inflammatory markers remained significantly raised between attacks. Anakinra was discontinued due to an adverse reaction. 
After a six-week washout period, the patient began treatment with intravenous tocilizumab and responded positively with normalization of CRP and ESR, improved energy levels, and decreased pain and oral ulceration. The patient was switched to weekly subcutaneous tocilizumab for ease of administration, and her clinical response has been sustained for more than 24 months. 
The patient had several short-lived flares lasting 1-3 days, but overall expressed a preference for the subcutaneous route, as it was associated with an improved quality of life despite the breakthrough fever attacks. No adverse events were reported. 

Discharge Summary:
This twelve-year-old female presented with recurrent fever, fatigue, and arthralgia/myalgia of the lower limbs beginning at a young age. After further investigation, she was diagnosed with heterozygotic MKD and was prescribed etanercept with limited success. However, the patient responded positively to treatment with intravenous tocilizumab with normalization of CRP and ESR, improved energy levels, decreased pain and oral ulceration. After initial treatment, the patient was switched to subcutaneous tocilizumab to improve her quality of life associated with hospital visits. Her clinical response has been sustained for more than two years. During the course of treatment, several minor flares were documented. The patient expressed a preference for subcutaneous tocilizumab despite these flares. No adverse events were reported.

The patient was also on long-term immunosuppressive therapy for a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the nose. The long-term antimycobacterial medications were not stopped during the admission. The patient's wishes were taken into consideration, and treatment was withdrawn, which led to the patient’s unfortunate death shortly after.

The 81-year-old female patient presented with increasing dysphagia, shortness of breath, and stridor. Her medical history includes radiotherapy to the mediastinum for Hodgkin's lymphoma, radiation-induced interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, and a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the nose. She was diagnosed with Haemophilus influenzae and Mycobacterium kansasii previously and was advised triple therapy for this. The patient was taken to theatre for debulking due to an initial diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma with a differential diagnosis of mycobacterial disease. Later histology report stated that the patient had an inflammatory pseudotumour secondary to the mycobacteria infection. Despite surgical debulking and being started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and steroids, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, following which the treatment was withdrawn. instruction: What was the patient's diagnosis and treatment for low-grade superficial urothelial papillary carcinoma according to the discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The 69-year-old male presented with a macrocytic anemia in 2008 and was diagnosed with myelodysplasia of refractory anemia. Monthly transfusions of red cells were required to maintain the hemoglobin level above 8.0 gr/dl. In October 2013, the patient had painless macroscopic hematuria and was found to have five bladder tumors during a cystoscopy. The patient underwent a TUR-B (transurethral resection bladder tumor) and was later found to have a low-grade superficial urothelial papillary carcinoma without evidence of bladder wall infiltration. The patient received intravesical BCG, weekly for six weeks, then two-weekly for four doses, and then monthly for one year, which effectively treated the bladder tumors but the patient became transfusion dependent once again since February 2017. 

Summary of Medical History:
In 2008, a 69-year-old male presented with a macrocytic anemia and was diagnosed with myelodysplasia of refractory anemia. He required monthly transfusions of red cells to maintain the hemoglobin level above 8.0 gr/dl. In 2013, he was found to have five bladder tumors and underwent a TUR-B. The patient received intravesical BCG, which effectively treated the bladder tumors but he became transfusion dependent once again since February 2017. 

Diagnostic Findings:
A bone marrow biopsy was consistent with refractory anemia and blasts <5%. Repeat bone marrow biopsy after red cell and platelet transfusions revealed a hypercellular bone marrow, with dysplastic features, including micromegakaryocytes and blasts <5%. Cytogenetic study revealed a normal karyotype. A CT scan of the urinary system revealed a lobulated lesion in the region of the left ureteral meatus with a diameter of 16 mm. Pathological analysis revealed a low-grade superficial urothelial papillary carcinoma without evidence of bladder wall infiltration. 

Treatment:
The patient underwent monthly transfusions of red cells to maintain the hemoglobin level above 8.0 gr/dl. For the bladder tumors, the patient underwent a TUR-B, and later received intravesical BCG treatment, which cured the bladder tumors. 

Follow-up and Prognosis:
The patient remained transfusion dependent and received intravesical BCG once a month for one year. The patient's hemoglobin and platelet counts increased and achieved normal levels while receiving BCG, but he became transfusion dependent once again since February 2017. Repeat bone marrow biopsy showed a hypocellular bone marrow, with between 30% and 50% of the intertrabecular spaces being occupied by hematopoietic tissue. There was a significant decrease in the erythroid precursors and megakaryocytes, but no evidence of fibrosis or infiltration of the bone marrow with a CD34 count of less than 5%.
output: According to the discharge summary, the patient received intravesical BCG therapy for low-grade superficial urothelial papillary carcinoma, which effectively treated the bladder tumors.

The patient underwent plasma exchange therapy for hypertriglyceridemia as recommended by the nephrology service provided.

The patient was stabilized in the intensive care unit over the course of 24 hours and was transferred to the general medical floor on an insulin drip. His diet was cautiously advanced in the setting of acute pancreatitis. His blood sugars continued to remain well controlled between 120mg/dl and 200mg/dl while his insulin regimen was optimized according to his oral intake.

Patient Discharge:
The patient was discharged on an insulin regimen with the recommendation to stop all oral glycemic agents. He was advised to continue monitoring his blood sugar levels and to follow up with his primary care physician as needed.

Diagnosis:
The patient's diagnosis was acute pancreatitis secondary to elevated triglycerides and diabetic ketoacidosis induced by dapagliflozin.

The patient presented with acute pancreatitis secondary to elevated triglycerides and a history of two previous episodes of pancreatitis. Hospital Course:
The case report presented detailed information on the medical histories of several patients with Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) insufficiency, including their diagnosis and treatment of Hodgkin lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Patient B.II.3, L.II.2, JJ.II.2, MM.II.1, K.II.1, UU.III.3, and FF.II.1 were diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma or DLBCL at different ages and underwent various treatments such as chemotherapy, bone marrow transplantation, radiotherapy, and immune therapy. Their medical histories showed some common features, including recurrent infections, cytopenia, and immunodeficiency. These patients were also found to have mutations in CTLA-4, a negative regulator of T-cell activation.

Patient B.II.3, L.II.2, JJ.II.2, MM.II.1, K.II.1, UU.III.3, and FF.II.1 received treatments according to the current standards of care for their Hodgkin lymphoma or DLBCL condition. Patient B.II.3 was treated with high dose corticosteroids, rituximab, and etoposide, among other medications, which was followed by bone marrow transplantation. Patient L.II.2 underwent chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation, while patient JJ.II.2 was treated with six cycles of AVD chemotherapy protocol. Patient MM.II.1 underwent four cycles of ABVD chemotherapy protocol. Patient K.II.1 was treated with rituximab and R-CHOP 21, and received therapy for CMV-viremia. Patient UU.III.3 underwent chemotherapy, local radiotherapy, and radio-immune-therapy with ibritumomab-tiuxetan. Patient FF.II.1 was unsuccessfully treated with R-hyper-CVAD and R-ICE, and received rituximab and selinixor followed by another therapy attempt with DA-R-EPOCH protocol.

The response to the treatments varied by patient, but patient B.II.3, L.II.2, JJ.II.2, MM.II.1, and K.II.1 each achieved complete remission, while patient UU.III.3 and FF.II.1 ultimately progressed and deceased. Patient MM.II.1 also had intermittent gastrointestinal irritations and relapses of a past encephalomyelitis during his remission.

In summary, these cases provide insight into the long-term management of Hodgkin lymphoma and DLBCL in patients with CTLA-4 insufficiency.
