instruction: What clinical and electrophysiological findings led to the diagnosis of enhanced S-cone syndrome in the 13-year-old female patient mentioned in the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary

Patient Name: N/A (case report)

Date of Admission: N/A (case report)

Date of Discharge: N/A (case report)

Admitting Physician: N/A (case report)

Departing Physician: N/A (case report)


Hospital Course:

The patient is a 13-year-old Caucasian female who was admitted with a diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa. She underwent a full clinical examination which included visual acuity, ophthalmoscopic evaluation, structural OCT, and photopic and scotopic ERG. The autofluorescence of both eyes showed a hyperautofluorescent halo around the fovea covering 360°, which corresponded to impending photoreceptor loss. ERG showed non-recordable rod response, and reduced maximal and cone responses with a decreased b-wave to a-wave ratio. Specialized ERG recordings of responses mediated prevalently by short-wavelength-sensitive cones (S-cones) and ML-wavelength sensitive cones (ML-cones) were obtained from both eyes. S-cone-mediated ERGs were recorded in response to a blue (420 nm) stimulus of 30 degrees flickered at 4 Hz and presented on a steady yellow background. ML-cone-mediated ERGs were obtained in response to a red (580 nm) stimulus of 30 degrees flickering at 4 Hz and presented on a steady blue (420 nm) background. Blue and red stimuli were photopically matched. In this particular patient, S-cone ERG was of larger amplitude compared to ML cone. 

Based on clinical and electrophysiological findings, the diagnosis of enhanced S-cone syndrome (ESCS) was made. She was evaluated every 6 months for a year, and changes in retinal structure were monitored by performing additional swept source OCTs. 

Genetic analysis showed two variants in NR2E3: a missense variation c.1118T>C, which leads to substitution of leucine with proline in amino acid position 373, and c.349+5G>C, which involves a gene sequence near a splicing site.

Overall, the patient was observed to have visual impairment, macular schisis (involving both the outer and inner nuclear layers), and vascular involvement. OCT-A scans of the superficial plexus showed minimal involvement, while the deep plexus revealed a marked remodeling of this vascular layer.

The patient's visual acuity fluctuated over time, with improvement observed in her right eye 1 month after examination, followed by deterioration in both eyes 3 months after examination. 

Given the patient's diagnosis and ongoing observation, she will continue to receive regular eye exams to monitor for any changes in her condition. 

Discharge Diagnosis:
Enhanced S-cone Syndrome (ESCS)

Disposition:
Outpatient
output: Based on the clinical examination, ophthalmoscopic evaluation, structural OCT, and photopic and scotopic ERG, the patient was diagnosed with enhanced S-cone syndrome (ESCS). Specialized ERG recordings of responses mediated prevalently by short-wavelength-sensitive cones (S-cones) and ML-wavelength sensitive cones (ML-cones) showed that the S-cone ERG was of larger amplitude compared to ML cone. Genetic analysis also showed two variants in NR2E3, which supports the diagnosis of ESCS.

input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 56-year-old Japanese woman

Medical History: Rheumatoid arthritis, Bell’s palsy, granulomatous uveitis, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, mediastinal lymph node swelling, sarcoidosis

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with right-sided Bell’s palsy due to dysfunction of the facial nerve (VII) in October 2013, which improved following oral administration of prednisolone. Subsequently, she was admitted to a general hospital due to bilateral floaters in March 2014, and was diagnosed as having sarcoidosis following skin and transbronchial lung biopsies. She developed dysphagia due to dysfunction of the vagus nerve (X) in February 2015, which improved following treatment with prednisolone. However, in November 2015, she experienced recurrence of nerve VII palsy, despite continued treatment with prednisolone. In December 2015, brain parenchyma lesions were identified in an MRI. In January 2016, she experienced recurrence of nerve X palsy, following which she was treated again with prednisolone. In May 2016, she exhibited increased intraocular pressure (IOP) in her right eye and was referred to our hospital for treatment.

Clinical Findings:

At the initial visit, no inflammation in the anterior chamber was observed, although massive, diffuse vitreous opacities were observed in both eyes. Retinal periphlebitis and macular edema were detected using fluorescence angiography. The right eye IOP was 40 mmHg and the left eye IOP was 14 mmHg. The patient underwent trabeculectomy of her right eye in July 2016, which resulted in a decrease in the right eye IOP to 10 mmHg. No postoperative inflammation was observed.

Treatment and Management:

Following the trabeculectomy, the patient continued to receive 20 mg of prednisolone/day, and has experienced no worsening of brain parenchyma lesions or recurrence of cranial nerve palsy to date.

Follow-up Recommendations:

The patient should continue to receive regular follow-up ophthalmological examinations to monitor for any recurrence of vitreous opacities, periphlebitis or macular edema. In addition, regular imaging of the brain parenchyma should be performed to monitor for any changes in the brain lesions. Lastly, regular monitoring of the patient’s IOP is recommended to ensure that it remains within normal limits.
output: The prescribed medication prednisolone was used to treat the patient's nerve palsy and brain parenchyma lesions, which are likely associated with her history of sarcoidosis. Prednisolone is a corticosteroid that can reduce inflammation and suppress the immune system, which can help improve symptoms of sarcoidosis and prevent recurrence of nerve palsy and brain lesions. However, regular monitoring and follow-up examinations are necessary to ensure proper management of the patient's condition.

instruction: What was the treatment given to the patient with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and how did it affect the patient's symptoms, CT findings, and PR3-ANCA level?

A CT scan revealed an aneurysm of the infrarenal aorta, with a diameter of 34 mm, inflammation of surrounding adipose tissue, nodular lesions of the bilateral lungs and left maxillary sinusitis. A thoracoscopic lung biopsy demonstrated granulation tissue with necrosis and multinucleated giant cells.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with intravenous semipulse dose of methylprednisolone, followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (55 mg) per day and intravenous administration of cyclophosphamide (700 mg/body once per month).

Outcome:

All of the patient's symptoms and CT findings rapidly improved, and the PR3-ANCA level promptly decreased to the normal range. The diameter of the aneurysm changed from 34 mm to 21 mm after treatment. On tapering doses of steroids, the patient is currently in remission, and the inflammation and PR3-ANCA elevation have completely resolved. There has been no disease recurrence for 4 years after initiation of therapy.

Follow-up:

The patient will require lifelong monitoring due to the risk of disease recurrence.

instruction: What was the ultimate diagnosis of the patient after further evaluation and testing, including ultrasound and CT, for recurrent epididymitis symptoms? (Related to the task of relation extraction)
input:
Hospital Course:
23-year-old male from Cameroon presented with acute-onset, right-sided scrotal pain, and swelling while in the US for military training. He was diagnosed with acute epididymitis and treated with ceftriaxone and doxycycline. His symptoms improved, only to recur 6 weeks later, prompting a repeat ultrasound that revealed persistent epididymitis. Repeat urinalysis (no culture) and gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT were negative. He was then given an empiric 30-day course of ciprofloxacin, which improved the pain, but the swelling persisted. Five months after his initial evaluation, he returned with another recurrence of symptoms. Physical exam again revealed prominent right-sided scrotal swelling and tenderness. An ultrasound demonstrated right-sided epididymitis with possible necrosis, increasing complexity of the associated hydrocele, and new concerns for a focal scrotal abscess. This was further evaluated with a contrasted computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which revealed a complex right-sided scrotal fluid collection in addition to an enlarged and heterogeneous prostate, an enlarged juxtaesophageal lymph node, and right lung apical nodular scarring.
Discharge Summary:
23-year-old male from Cameroon presented with acute-onset, right-sided scrotal pain and swelling. He was diagnosed with acute epididymitis and treated with medication that provided relief of symptoms. However, the symptoms recurred, which prompted further evaluation and testing, including ultrasound and CT. Ultimately, the patient was diagnosed with tuberculosis and started on a three-drug regimen. The patient had an episode of drug-induced liver injury that resolved with cessation of the causative medication and was transitioned to an alternate regimen. On treatment day 15, the patient's sputum smears converted to negative. After resolution of his drug-induced liver injury, the patient was discharged and recommended to continue his treatment in Cameroon on an all-oral regimen. After recovery from eye complications, LAmB was administered at SKKRC. On the follow-up of 6 months, the patient's skin qPCR for LD-DNA was negative, and there was no further ophthalmic complaint.

The patient was diagnosed with PKDL and Marginal Keratitis.

PKDL and Marginal Keratitis

The patient is advised to follow up with the attending physician. The patient should avoid any medications without prescription, and instructions should be strictly followed. In case of any complication, the physician should be immediately notified.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 60-year-old left-handed female, presented with progressive behavioral changes, speech disturbance, and episodic memory impairment which were initially characterized by prominent apathy, reduced social interaction, sweet tooth, disinhibition, and new obsessions, followed by reduced speech output and use of stereotypic phrases. Two years after onset, the patient developed difficulty remembering recent events and conversations and got lost in familiar places. She later developed dyscalculia and had occasional visual hallucinations of family members. Her condition rapidly worsened four years after onset and she was admitted to a nursing home with impaired spatial awareness, prosopagnosia, wandering, and incontinence. She later developed an asymmetrical extrapyramidal syndrome with dystonic limb movements, worse on the right. The patient died aged 68 with a final clinical diagnosis of behavioral variant FTD.

Medical History:
The patient’s medical history included progressive right-sided facial hemi-atrophy, diagnosed 15 years prior to onset of cognitive symptoms, with no cause identified. Two years after onset of cognitive symptoms she developed a persistent cough and peripheral eosinophilia, pericardial thickening, and an anterior pericardial effusion. The cause of these symptoms was not identified despite thorough investigation but was felt to be autoimmune in origin. There were no vascular risk factors, no prior smoking history, and consistently normal blood pressure. The patient's mother had developed acute psychosis with delusions and odd behavior aged 65, followed by progressive cognitive decline and admission to a mental health unit for 20 years with an eventual diagnosis of dementia. There was no other family history of dementia or neurological or vascular disease.

Investigations:
A volumetric 1.5 T MRI brain was performed 2.6 years before the patient died. The MRI showed bilateral but asymmetric frontal, temporal, and parietal atrophy, worse on the left, and significant bilateral periventricular WMH, worst in the frontal lobes and on the left side. Cerebrospinal fluid analyses were normal or negative. A wide variety of blood tests were normal, except for peripheral eosinophilia of 1.11 and rheumatoid particle agglutination test (1/80 titer). DNA analysis identified a heterozygous GRN Q130fs mutation but no other FTD-associated mutations.

Conclusion:
In conclusion, the patient presented with progressive behavioral changes, speech disturbance, and episodic memory impairment characterized by prominent apathy, reduced social interaction, sweet tooth, disinhibition, and new obsessions, followed by reduced speech output and use of stereotypic phrases. The final clinical diagnosis was behavioral variant FTD. The patient had a medical history of progressive right-sided facial hemi-atrophy, persistent cough, and peripheral eosinophilia, pericardial thickening, and an anterior pericardial effusion which was felt to be autoimmune in origin. MRI showed bilateral but asymmetric frontal, temporal, and parietal atrophy, worse on the left, and significant bilateral periventricular WMH, worst in the frontal lobes and on the left side. DNA analysis identified a heterozygous GRN Q130fs mutation but no other FTD-associated mutations.

The patient was admitted with purulent cough and progressive dyspnea of a few months’ duration. Physical examination indicated coarse crackles from the right lung and slight wheezes, bilaterally. Chest radiography and computed tomography (CT) showed cavitary lesions and bronchiectasis with a fungus ball in the right upper lobe and mucoid impaction in the bronchi of the right lower lobe. Prednisolone and itraconazole were administered for ABPA. These were later switched to Voriconazole, as the patient’s symptoms and radiographic findings showed no improvement. Although imaging findings revealed improvement of the cavitary lesions and mucoid impaction, the patient still had cough and productive sputum. To control the disease further, lobectomy of the right upper lobe was performed without any complications.

Prednisolone and Voriconazole were discontinued 5 and 7 months after surgery, respectively. Twenty-three months after discontinuation of the medical treatment, the patient complained of gradually worsening cough and dyspnea. CT showed recurrent bronchiectasis and cavities with mucoid impaction in the right lower lobe. Prednisolone was prescribed for relapsed ABPA and was later followed by additional treatment with Voriconazole, which resulted in improvement of symptoms and CT findings.

The addition of Voriconazole resulted in a decrease in the serum total IgE and was discontinued after 20 months as the patient’s condition had become stable. The aspergilloma improved slightly over a 5-year period, and ABPA remained well-controlled with low-dose prednisolone (5 mg/day).

Discharge Diagnosis: ABPA with concomitant aspergilloma

The patient should continue taking low-dose prednisolone (5 mg/day) to maintain ABPA control. The patient should remain vigilant for any worsening of symptoms and report to the hospital immediately if any new or worsening symptoms occur. instruction: What were the leak sites found during the Double Baltazar procedure performed on the patient following complications after a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, as mentioned in the discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to complications after a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. On presentation, he was septic and in distress. An upper GI series and CT scan of the abdomen showed a contained gastric fistula with perigastric fluid collection. The patient was kept NPO, started on parenteral nutrition, intravenous antibiotics and was well-hydrated to control the sepsis. He underwent CT-guided drainage of the collection. One week post-drainage, upper GI series was repeated, which showed a well-drained gastric leak. After 10 days of stabilization, the patient underwent a Baltazar procedure to uncover the gastric tube, which was covered with omental adhesions. Two leak sites were unexpectedly identified along the staple line. The Double Baltazar procedure was performed, and two fistulo-jejunostomies were created using the same jejunal limb, followed by a Jejuno-jejunostomy (Brown anastomosis) to divert the biliary secretions. All quadrants of the abdomen were drained.
 
Hospital Course:
The patient was initially septic and required surgical intervention due to complications after a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. The patient was monitored closely and treated with parenteral nutrition, intravenous antibiotics, and fluids. Drainage of the perigastric fluid collection was performed, and the patient showed improvement in their condition. A Baltazar procedure was performed after 10 days of stabilization. During the procedure, two fistula sites were found along the staple line. The Double Baltazar procedure along with Jejuno-jejunostomy (Brown anastomosis) was performed to divert the biliary secretions, and all quadrants of the abdomen were drained. After the procedure, the patient remained stable and was monitored until discharge. 

Summary:
The patient presented with complications following a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy and required surgical intervention. The Double Baltazar procedure with Jejuno-jejunostomy was performed due to two leak sites found during the surgery. The patient remained stable and was discharged following close monitoring.
output: Two leak sites were found along the staple line during the Double Baltazar procedure performed on the patient following complications after a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, as mentioned in the discharge summary.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to our institution on [Redacted] with a 1-week history of increasing breathlessness and intermittent chest tightness. He was diagnosed and treated as acute coronary syndrome. During the course of his hospitalization, he developed second-degree atrioventricular block (Mobitz Type 2) and underwent successful percutaneous intervention with two drug-eluting stents to a significant stenosis in the circumflex artery. He subsequently underwent implantation of a dual-chamber pacemaker. The patient returned to the hospital within two months with worsening breathlessness and chest discomfort. The final diagnosis was high-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma of B-cell type that involved the myocardium, pericardium, and superior mediastinum, with infiltration into the left atrium. He was treated with i.v. dexamethasone and rasburicase, which led to a significant improvement in his overall condition. The patient subsequently underwent mediastinosopic biopsy of the mass, which confirmed the diagnosis. He was then treated with R-GCVP chemotherapy, followed by palliative oral chemotherapy (DECC regimen) consisting of dexamethasone, etoposide, chlorambucil, and lomustine. Despite initial stabilization, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and he passed away peacefully at home.

Clinical Findings:
The patient presented with breathlessness and intermittent chest tightness. On admission, he was found to be bradycardic with a heart rate of 47 beats per minute; clinical examination was otherwise unremarkable. His blood test showed an elevated cardiac troponin-T level of 224 ng ml−1. His chest X-ray was unremarkable, but transthoracic echocardiogram revealed mild hypertrophy of the ventricles with hypokinesis in the lateral wall. During readmission, transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed marked hypertrophy of both ventricles with granular speckled appearance suspicious of infiltrative disease. In addition, the left atrium was lined with an echogenic speckled mass encroaching on the mitral valve leaflets. CT scan of his thorax confirmed bilateral pleural effusion and an extensive abnormal soft tissue infiltrating the pericardium, much of the myocardium and the inferior portion of the left atrium, extending up to the aortic arch into the superior mediastinum. Blood tests showed mild microcytic anaemia.

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated for acute coronary syndrome, with successful percutaneous intervention with two drug-eluting stents. He subsequently underwent implantation of a dual-chamber pacemaker. Upon readmission, he was treated with i.v. dexamethasone and rasburicase, followed by R-GCVP chemotherapy, which led to remission echocardiographically and radiologically, but he could not tolerate intensification of treatment. Palliative oral chemotherapy (DECC regimen) was initiated but the patient's condition continued to deteriorate.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient passed away peacefully at home.

Instructions at Discharge:
The patient passed away peacefully at home.

The echocardiogram confirmed marked hypertrophy of both ventricles with granular speckled appearance suspicious of infiltrative disease, and CT scan confirmed extensive abnormal soft tissue infiltrating the pericardium, myocardium, and left atrium, extending up to the aortic arch into the superior mediastinum.

instruction: What named entities related to the patient's medical condition, diagnostic work-up, and treatment can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in the given discharge summary, specifically regarding the diagnosis of Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity (NCGS) and Celiac Disease (CD)?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 43-year old woman

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our outpatient clinic due to gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain and bloating, diarrhea, and gastro-esophageal reflux. She also exhibited extra-intestinal manifestations including weakness, headache, limb numbness, skin rash, fibromyalgia-like symptoms and anemia after ingestion of gluten and wheat products. Further diagnostic work-up ruled out celiac disease (CD) and wheat allergy but revealed positivity for HLA-DR7 and -DQ2 haplotype. The patient was diagnosed with Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity (NCGS) after a double-blind placebo-controlled cross-over trial. It was advised to follow a strict gluten-free diet (GFD) and the patient demonstrated symptomatic improvement and normalization of laboratory data.

Family History:

The patient had two asymptomatic children, a 12-year-old girl and a 9-year-old boy. CD antibody screening revealed positivity for tissue transglutaminase antibodies (tTGA) of IgA class and anti-endomysial antibody (EMA) in the girl and a low titer of tTGA in the boy. Genetic testing showed that both siblings inherited the HLA-DR3 and -DQ2 haplotype. Duodenal biopsy in the girl showed active CD with subtotal villous flattening and in the boy, it revealed potential CD with the presence of normal villi but increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs).

Final Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity (NCGS), and her children were diagnosed with CD.

Discharge Plan:

The 43-year-old patient was advised to continue following a strict gluten-free diet (GFD). The 12-year-old girl was started on a GFD due to the diagnosis of active CD, while the 9-year-old boy was advised to follow a gluten containing diet, as suggested for asymptomatic potential CD. Both children were monitored for the development of any clinical symptoms or laboratory abnormalities. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to monitor the patient and her children's progress.
output: The named entities related to the patient's medical condition, diagnostic work-up and treatment for Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity (NCGS) and Celiac Disease (CD) include gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, and gastro-esophageal reflux, weakness, headache, limb numbness, skin rash, fibromyalgia-like symptoms, anemia, positivity for HLA-DR7 and -DQ2 haplotype, double-blind placebo-controlled cross-over trial, and a strict gluten-free diet (GFD). The patient was diagnosed with NCGS and advised to continue following a strict GFD. The patient's 12-year-old daughter was diagnosed with active CD and started on a GFD, while her 9-year-old son was advised to follow a gluten-containing diet as he had asymptomatic potential CD.

A 21-year-old female patient with a history of multiple intractable cutaneous abscesses and cysts was admitted to the Allergy-Immunology Clinic for evaluation. She had a past medical history significant for hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and anxiety. The patient had more than fifteen hospitalizations for pneumonias with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, sinusitis, mastoiditis, and oral candidiasis since childhood. The patient denied any history of atopic dermatitis, other types of eczema, or food allergy. Evaluation for cystic fibrosis and hypogammaglobulinemia at the time had been negative. Family history was pertinent for her paternal grandmother with recurrent pneumonias and her biological brother had a history of recurrent skin boils.
Important physical findings included coarse facial feature, deep set eyes, broad nasal bridge, high arched palate, and multiple scattered healed scars on skin with some remnant cold abscesses. Pulmonary and cardiovascular exam were unremarkable. Laboratory investigations revealed a normal complete blood count with no eosinophilia. IgE level was elevated, with erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 64 mm/hr and C-reactive protein of 1.56 mg/dl. IgG, IgM, and IgA levels were within the normal limit. Total complement (CH50) levels were normal, and testing for chronic granulomatous disease was unrevealing. Due to history, physical findings, and these initial labs, Hyper-IgE Syndrome was suspected. A calculated HIES score was >40 required for diagnosis. Mutation analysis of STAT3 gene was sent, and a novel pathogenic mutation was detected, C.1388 T>A (pVal463Glu) at DNA-binding domain of STAT3 gene.
Penicillin allergy testing and TMP-SMX oral challenge were performed in the clinic. With a normal response, she was started on prophylaxis with TMP-SMX (800mg-160mg) once daily for the prevention of infections. Patient was advised to follow up for clinical response and monitoring tolerance to treatment. She was asked to have regular dental exam, chest imaging, bone density scan, and pulmonary function testing. She was also advised to have genetic counseling. Genetic testing for her biological brother was offered.

The patient was admitted with a diagnosis of ipilimumab-related acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) after receiving two doses of ipilimumab 10 mg/kg IV for stage IIIB superficial spreading melanoma. The patient developed parasthesias in the distal lower extremities bilaterally that subsequently ascended to involve proximal lower extremities, then upper extremities along with weakness and loss of deep tendon reflexes. MRI brain and whole spine revealed abnormal enhancement involving the bilateral 5th, 7th and 8th cranial nerves, cauda equina nerve roots as well as the conus surface and peripheral nerves at the thoracolumbar junction. CSF studies were negative for malignant cells but showed lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated CSF protein. Methylprednisolone 1.5 mg/kg twice daily was initiated with rapid improvement in motor symptoms in hands and lower extremities after 2 days. Steroids were gradually tapered over a 12-week period with gradual recovery. The patient was also treated for concomitant adrenal insufficiency with physiologic doses of hydrocortisone. 

Outcome:
The patient's weakness resolved completely, with the exception of minimal parasthesias in upper extremities and lower extremities in a glove-and-stocking distribution. Approximately 4 months after initial ipilimumab therapy, the patient developed hypothyroidism for which he was treated with levothyroxine 125mcg daily. Systemic imaging studies remain negative for recurrent disease. 

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow-up regularly with his primary care physician and oncologist. Further evaluation for other potential side effects of ipilimumab therapy should also be undertaken during follow-up visits.

instruction: What genetic changes were identified in the lung metastasis, and which candidate drugs were identified to target the mutations found?
input:
Discharge Summary: 

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Hospital ID: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Diagnosis: Lung metastasis resembling low-grade right ureteral orifice bladder tumor

Hospital Course: 

Patient presented to the hospital with signs and symptoms of lung metastasis that resembled the low-grade right ureteral orifice bladder tumor. The patient had a 40 pack-year smoking history and had previously undergone transurethral resection of the bladder tumor and ureteroscopic resection of the right ureter. The patient also underwent hand-assisted laparoscopic nephroureterectomy for upper urinary tract tumor removal. Following the surgery, the patient underwent six rounds of bacillus Calmette-Guérin treatment in an adjuvant setting, followed by maintenance treatment for three years.

After careful examination, the patient's mutations present in the tumors were analyzed to identify genetic changes that could point towards a therapeutic target for any future recurrence or metastasis. Variants shared by the primary bladder tumor and the lung metastasis include mutations in the KMT2D and RXRA genes. Mutations unique to the lung metastasis included a clinically actionable, activating mutation in mTOR (C1483F). 

A mutational signature for the patient was developed, which resembled published mutational Signature 1A/B and Signature 5. Using the Drug Gene Interaction Database, candidate drugs targeting 12 of the 100 genes with SNVs in the lung tumor were identified, including the RXRA agonist bexarotene and mTOR inhibitors like everolimus. 

Primary culture of the lung metastasis was established in the laboratory, and the cells were treated with mTOR inhibitor everolimus at two concentrations (10 and 50 nM). The treatment showed a marked inhibition of mTOR activity and downstream signaling via two of its effectors, p70 S6K and 4E-BP1, at both concentrations. AKT activity increased with everolimus treatment, possibly indicating a mechanism of resistance to the mTOR inhibitor. 

On discharge, the patient was advised to follow up with their oncologist regarding further treatment options and therapy. Further genetic testing was recommended, along with regular lung function and cancer screenings due to the patient's history of tobacco smoking. The patient was discharged in stable condition and was advised to attend all follow-up appointments as scheduled.
output: The identified mutations in the lung metastasis included mutations in the KMT2D and RXRA genes shared by the primary bladder tumor and a clinically actionable activating mutation in mTOR (C1483F) unique to the lung metastasis. Candidate drugs targeting 12 of the 100 genes with SNVs in the lung tumor were identified, including the RXRA agonist bexarotene and mTOR inhibitors like everolimus, using the Drug Gene Interaction Database. Furthermore, primary culture of the lung metastasis was established in the laboratory, and the cells were treated with mTOR inhibitor everolimus at two concentrations showing a marked inhibition of mTOR activity and downstream signaling via two of its effectors, p70 S6K and 4E-BP1, at both concentrations, with AKT activity increasing with everolimus treatment, possibly indicating a mechanism of resistance to the mTOR inhibitor.

instruction: What medication switch was made for the patient's Crohn's Disease treatment, and what was the result of this change?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital due to abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhea and weight loss. Physical examination demonstrated moderate abdominal tenderness with an abdominal mass in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory findings revealed a significantly elevated CRP level. Colonoscopy showed ulcerations localized at the Bauhin’s valve and histological examination of obtained mucosal biopsies were suggestive for active Crohn’s Disease (CD). MR enteroclysis was performed due to inability to intubate the terminal ileum and indicated a predominant inflammatory, short-segment stenosis of the terminal ileum. Medical treatment was switched from prednisolone and azathioprine to adalimumab. 

Course of Treatment:
Twelve weeks after induction of adalimumab therapy, clinical remission was achieved and CRP level returned to normal. Another four months later, the patient presented with severe pain in the mandibular area. A biopsy of the oral lesions was obtained and revealed ulcerative stomatitis with noncaseating granulomas consistent with oral CD. Intensification of immunosuppressive therapy was initiated by shortening the adalimumab administration interval to weekly administration. A follow-up examination after 10 weeks confirmed complete healing of the oral CD lesion. During a follow-up period of 12 months, no signs of active CD became evident under continued therapy. 

Summary:
This 34-year-old man with a 15-year history of Crohn’s Disease (CD) was admitted to our hospital due to abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhea, and weight loss. The patient underwent MR enteroclysis and was found to have a predominant inflammatory, short-segment stenosis of the terminal ileum. After unsuccessful treatment with prednisolone and azathioprine, the patient was switched to adalimumab and achieved clinical remission after 12 weeks. Although the patient maintained clinical remission and low laboratory inflammation markers, the patient later presented with ulcerative lesions of the buccal-side mucosa of the right mandible consistent with oral CD. Intensification of immunosuppressive therapy was initiated by shortening the adalimumab administration interval to weekly administration. A follow-up examination confirmed complete healing of the oral CD lesion. The patient remained in remission for a 12 month follow-up period under continued therapy.
output: The patient's Crohn's Disease treatment was switched from prednisolone and azathioprine to adalimumab, and the result was clinical remission achieved after 12 weeks.

instruction: What was the relation between the patient's administration of crizotinib and the development of ground-glass opacities and consolidations in both lungs?
input:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A

ADMISSION DATE: January 2018
DISCHARGE DATE: N/A

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 47-year-old female of Chinese ethnicity, was admitted in January 2018 due to persistent cough and breathlessness. A chest CT scan revealed multiple abnormalities in both lungs, including a large mass on the upper right lobe. Nodular thickening of the interlobular septa and fissures, along with bilateral pleural effusions and lymphadenopathy, were also observed. After testing, the patient was diagnosed with advanced lung adenocarcinoma with extensive dissemination in the chest. A next-generation sequencing conducted on malignant pleural effusion (MPE) identified a SDC4-ROS1 fusion gene, and the patient was orally administered crizotinib, after which the symptoms improved significantly.
 
However, on the tenth day of medication, the patient had a low-grade fever and slight aggravation of dyspnoea, and a chest CT re-scan revealed multiple new-onset ground-glass opacities and consolidations throughout both lungs. The patient was then treated with cefoperazone/sulbactam to exclude the possibility of infection. A re-examination of blood tumour markers, and characteristics of hydrothorax, combined with percutaneous lung biopsy, showed acute lung injury and the pathological stage was assumed to be a transition from exudation to organization. Accordingly, MP pulse therapy (0.5 g once per day) was immediately substituted for the original crizotinib treatment and applied for three days. 

However, due to progressive deterioration leading to respiratory failure, the patient was tracheally intubated and mechanically ventilated. All necessary and additional treatment procedures were conducted to prevent ILD. The patient died 20 days after the first administration of crizotinib. Upon approval of the family, a next-generation sequencing analysis of a lung biopsy sample was performed, which revealed a de novo exon 19 deletion mutation in EGFR, not detected in MPE before treatment with crizotinib. On the other hand, the frequency of ROS1 rearrangement decreased after crizotinib treatment. 

Discharge Diagnosis:
Crizotinib-induced ILD leading to respiratory failure.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
N/A

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
N/A

FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENTS:
N/A

FOLLOW-UP CARE:

instruction: What was the patient's diagnosis and treatment plan for multiple thrombotic events associated with antithrombin deficiency (ATD) according to the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The 14-year-old male adolescent was admitted to the emergency department due to subfebrile temperatures and localized pain in his right popliteal fossa. Prior to these symptoms, the patient had been immobilized following a minor sports injury. The patient's medical history revealed an asymptomatic antithrombin deficiency (ATD) diagnosed 8 years ago and a maternal history of ATD. No other hereditary thrombophilic disorders were detected. The patient's blood analysis indicated elevated levels of D-dimers and C-reactive protein (CrP), and reduced antithrombin activity. The vascular ultrasound confirmed thrombosis of the right lower extremity. The patient received continuous infusion of unfractionated heparin followed by direct thrombin inhibition by argatroban. Empirical antibiotic treatment was initiated.

The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) results showed complete deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the right lower extremity, and extended thromboses of the left lower extremity and thrombosis of both iliac vessels. It also revealed occlusion of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with prominent venous lumbar collaterals suggestive of IVC associated with ATD. Catheter-directed local thrombolysis using recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) was initiated in both extremities. Anticoagulative therapy was switched from argatroban to vitamin K antagonist phenprocoumon. The patient was discharged on day eight after hospital admission.

A follow-up examination showed extended re-thrombosis of both pelvic axes and the right lower extremity, leading to a second hospital admission and re-induction of therapy. Recanalization of the right lower extremity and pelvic axis was subsequently achieved, but the left pelvic vessels remained thrombotic. The patient's oral anticoagulation was intensified to prevent re-thrombosis. Regular follow-up examinations at the outpatient clinic did not give evidence for any new thrombotic events to date.

The patient was discharged on day seven after admission. The left iliac vessels remain thrombotic, but the IVC was successfully recanalized using balloon dilation and subsequent stenting. The patient’s mother was also found to have recanalized IVC upon angiography intervention.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the right lower extremity, left lower extremity, both iliac vessels, and inferior vena cava (IVC) associated with antithrombin deficiency (ATD).

2. Recanalized IVC and thrombotic left iliac vessels.

3. IVCA.

Recommendations:

1. Oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon should be continued lifelong to prevent thrombosis due to the combination of extended multilocal thromboses with underlying ATD.

2. Follow-up examinations should be done regularly at the outpatient clinic.

3. The patient and their family should be counseled on the importance of continued medical management for ATD.

4. More interventions should be done for thrombotic lesions found in pelvic vessels. 

Signed, 

[Doctor's Name] 

[Specialty]
output: The patient was diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the right lower extremity, left lower extremity, both iliac vessels, and inferior vena cava (IVC) associated with antithrombin deficiency (ATD). The treatment plan involved catheter-directed local thrombolysis using recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA), followed by anticoagulative therapy with vitamin K antagonist phenprocoumon. To prevent re-thrombosis, oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon should be continued lifelong and regular follow-up examinations should be done at the outpatient clinic. The patient and their family should be counseled on the importance of continued medical management for ATD. While interventions were done for thrombotic lesions in the right lower extremity and pelvic axis, the left iliac vessels remained thrombotic and required further interventions. Therefore, more interventions should be considered for thrombotic lesions found in the pelvic vessels.

instruction: What was the primary source of the tumor found in the patient's abdomen, and what procedures were performed to diagnose it?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
The patient is a 40-year-old female who presented with epigastric pain and weight loss. She has a history of RYGB surgery performed 13 years ago for morbid obesity and was recently diagnosed with bilateral metastatic signet cell carcinoma to the ovaries.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with symptoms of epigastric pain and weight loss. CT imaging of the abdomen was unable to reveal the primary source of the tumor. Upper and lower GI endoscopies were performed but were unrevealing for malignancy with the upper endoscopy failing to examine the excluded stomach due to the limited length of the scope. The excluded stomach was subsequently approached using ADBE via the afferent limb of the Roux-en-Y bypass. Biopsies were negative for H. pylori infection and revealed invasive signet cell gastric adenocarcinoma that likely had metastasized to the ovaries. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Stage IV gastric cancer with a large infiltrative ulcerated circumferential mass found in the prepyloric region and antrum of the stomach. Molecular analysis showed a human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative tumor.

Treatment:
The patient is currently undergoing chemotherapy with fluoropyrimidine, plus oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) for Stage IV gastric cancer.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was discharged with instructions for follow-up care with their oncologist. Instructions were given for managing symptoms related to the chemotherapy. The patient was also advised to undergo genetic counseling and testing due to the significant family history of gastric cancer in her maternal aunt.

Summary:
The patient presented with symptoms of epigastric pain and weight loss and was diagnosed with Stage IV gastric cancer with underlying signet cell gastric adenocarcinoma. The patient is currently undergoing chemotherapy with FOLFOX and has been advised to undergo genetic counseling and testing. Follow-up care is recommended with their oncologist.
output: The primary source of the tumor found in the patient's abdomen was identified as invasive signet cell gastric adenocarcinoma, which was located in the excluded stomach. To diagnose it, ADBE was used via the afferent limb of the Roux-en-Y bypass, and biopsies were taken. Upper and lower GI endoscopies were performed, but they were unable to examine the excluded stomach due to the limited length of the scope.

The patient is scheduled for follow-up appointments as needed.

instruction: What was the detected microorganism and its antibiotic susceptibility pattern in a patient diagnosed with Post-Operative Endophthalmitis according to the given discharge summary through relation extraction?

The patient presented with redness, pain and decreased vision in the right eye one day after cataract surgery done elsewhere. AC appears well-formed while the rest of the anterior segment details were not clear.

Diagnosis:
Post-Operative Endophthalmitis due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Treatment:
Anterior chamber wash, intravitreal imipenum, intravitreal ceftazidime, intravitreal dexamethasone, oral ciprofolxacin, oral prednisolone, and intravitreal triamcinolone.

Follow-up:
The patient's corneal lesions were stable and the eye appeared stable. Further follow-up and management will be arranged upon discharge. The patient was advised to maintain good hygiene and follow up with an ophthalmologist for regular check-ups.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and treatment for the patient's left flank mass according to the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [insert date]     Discharge Date: [insert date]

Patient Name: [insert patient name]     Age: 39 years     Gender: Female     Medical Record Number: [insert number]

Hospital Course Summary:

This 39-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of worsening left flank pain, intermittent visible hematuria, and a fullness in the left flank. The patient also reported constitutional symptoms such as loss of appetite and significant weight loss. The patient has been treated five times by her local general practitioner for recurrent urinary tract infections. The physical examination revealed an ill-defined left flank mass with pain on palpation. Laboratory work showed normocytic, normochromic anemia. 

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan images revealed a large, heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue mass arising from the lower pole of the left kidney, which measured about 108 × 106 × 105 mm. The collecting system and the ureter were poorly visualized. The mass displaced the left renal artery superiorly, and the left renal vein was not well demonstrated. The inferior vena cava appeared patent. No bladder lesions were identified on cystoscopy. A tentative diagnosis of RCC, cT3aN0M0 was made, and the patient underwent hand-assisted laparoscopic radical nephrectomy. Intraoperatively, a large, left lower pole renal mass was identified and a bulky, dilated proximal ureter was found. So, a decision was made to proceed with radical nephrectomy as well as ureterectomy. The ureter was mobilized caudally and divided at the level of the pelvic brim. A lymph node dissection was not performed.

The patient had an uneventful postoperative course and was discharged 4 days postsurgery.

Macroscopically, the cut surface of the bisected kidney showed a large, solid, unicentric, well-circumscribed tumor in the inferior pole of the left kidney with hemorrhage and necrosis. There was extensive involvement of the pelvicalyceal system and associated hydronephrosis. The renal sinus demonstrated the presence of a tumor thrombus within the opened ureter. The renal vein was uninvolved. The tumor capsule was intact, and Gerota's fascia was uninvolved. The margins, including the distal ureteric margin, were uninvolved by the tumor. The overall morphological features and immunophenotype were in keeping with an eosinophilic variant of clear cell RCC (ccRCC). The nuclear features corresponded with World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology grade 3. There was extensive coagulative tumor necrosis, but no evidence of sarcomatoid differentiation or lymphovascular invasion.

In summary, this patient presented with worsening left flank pain, intermittent visible hematuria, and a fullness in the left flank. She underwent hand-assisted laparoscopic radical nephrectomy and ureterectomy. The final pathology report revealed an eosinophilic variant of clear cell RCC with a World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology grade 3. The patient had an uneventful postoperative course and was discharged 4 days postsurgery.
output: According to the discharge summary, the patient was diagnosed with an eosinophilic variant of clear cell RCC with a World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology grade 3 and underwent hand-assisted laparoscopic radical nephrectomy and ureterectomy.

instruction: What features of the patient's clinical presentation and diagnostic testing suggest encephalomyelitis in the context of Chikungunya virus infection? (related to Relation Extraction)
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Date of admission: 

Date of discharge: 

Admission diagnosis: Acute fever, malaise, generalized rash, and multiple joint pains with history of diabetes mellitus II, hypothyroidism, and ocular myasthenia gravis. 

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted with symptoms of acute fever, malaise, generalized rash, and multiple joint pains with a history of diabetes mellitus II, hypothyroidism, and ocular myasthenia gravis. On admission, the patient presented with acute sensorimotor quadriparesis and urinary retention, which was followed by altered sensorium.

The patient had no history of headache, vomiting, seizure, dimness of vision, double vision, dysphagia, change in voice, and neck/back pain. However, the patient had previously received methyl prednisolone injection pulse therapy 1g each for 5 days before presenting to our institute, which showed a partial response with improved level of consciousness.

Diagnostic testing, including complete blood count, random blood sugar, renal and liver function tests, and serum electrolytes were within normal limits except for slightly raised WBC to 14500/µL, CRP 16, and CPK total 84. Serum CHIKV IgM detection by ELISA came positive. Serum chikungunya real-time PCR was performed, which showed positive results. The patient's RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit, and one-step RT-PCR was performed using the access quick RT-PCR kit.

Diagnostic testing was also performed to assess the patient's neurological symptoms, including EEG and electrophysiology study, which showed generalized bilaterally symmetrical diffuse theta-delta slowing suggest diffuse encephalopathy and distal symmetrical sensory motor axonal polyneuropathy more in the lower limbs than the upper limbs.

CSF routine analysis showed protein 96mg/dL, glucose 60mg/dL, and total cells 140 with lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative Gram and ZN stain. ANA (antinuclear antibody) was detected by immunofluorescence with a dilution of 1: 100 and 1: 200, a homogeneous pattern, and +1 intensity. ANA profile by immunoDOT was negative, and anti-aquaporin-4 Ab was negative.

Imaging studies showed multiple tiny altered signal intensity foci with restricted diffusion seen in subcortical and periventricular white matter of bilateral (B/L) cerebral hemispheres, corpus callosum, and B/L corona radiata consistent with features of encephalomyelitis.

IV immunoglobulin (IgG) treatment of 140 grams was administered to the patient, and the supportive treatment was provided for the patient's comorbidities. 

The patient had a stable hemodynamic condition and was discharged with power 5/5 in both UL and 3/5 in both LL. The patient was advised supportive treatment and neurorehabilitation in form of active physiotherapy. 

Follow-up imaging studies were not conducted during the patient's hospitalization. 

Discharge diagnosis: Chikungunya virus infection with features of encephalomyelitis. 

Discharge instructions: Supportive treatment and neurorehabilitation in form of active physiotherapy under a physician's guidance. Follow-up appointment advised with a physician for monitoring the patient's recovery.
output: The patient's diagnostic testing showed positive results for CHIKV IgM and chikungunya real-time PCR, indicating Chikungunya virus infection. The diagnostic tests also showed features of encephalomyelitis, including diffuse theta-delta slowing on EEG and electrophysiology study, distal symmetrical sensory motor axonal polyneuropathy in the lower limbs, lymphocytic pleocytosis in the CSF, and multiple altered signal intensity foci in subcortical and periventricular white matter of bilateral cerebral hemispheres, corpus callosum, and corona radiata on imaging studies.

Upon admission, her blood pressure was 101/60 mmHg, heart rate was 106 beats per minute, and body temperature was 39.5 °C. A physical examination revealed no major abnormalities. The patient's laboratory tests showed an elevated white blood cell count, hypoproteinemia, and hypokalemia. She was diagnosed with infective endocarditis due to E. coli in accordance with the modified Duke criteria.

The patient was treated with combined antibiotics including sulbactam/ampicillin (SBT/ABPC) and gentamycin. Her general condition improved over the course of her hospitalization. Her temperature normalized on day 5, and her white blood cell count returned to a normal level. Blood culture analysis after antibiotic treatment revealed no bacterial growth. Echocardiography on day 14 showed a decrease in the size of the vegetations, and transthoracic echocardiography on day 35 revealed complete resolution of the vegetations.

On day 20, the patient developed severe lumbago, and an MRI of the lumbar spine revealed purulent spondylitis lesions in the L1 and L2 lumbar vertebrae. The patient's clinical course was good thereafter, and her lumbago improved with intravenous meropenem treatment. Oral levofloxacin was administered for 2 months after discharge. Both upper endoscopy and colonoscopy performed 3 months after discharge showed no abnormalities.

The patient was discharged from our hospital on day 56 after her CRP level decreased to 0.34 mg/dL. She had stopped drinking alcohol for 12 months and remained well during that time.

Final Diagnosis and Disposition:
The patient was diagnosed with infective endocarditis due to E. coli. She was discharged from our hospital after her symptoms improved with antibiotic treatment, and she continued with oral levofloxacin for two months.

instruction: What clinical Named Entities can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary related to the diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up care of acute porphyria?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Patient is a 33-year-old male, who presented with intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, and numbness of bilateral lower limb extremities. He was conservatively managed in a surgical unit as partial intestinal obstruction and was awaiting diagnostic laparoscopy. The patient was transferred to a medical ward for further management due to new-onset systemic hypertension and confusion.

Past medical and surgical history revealed similar neurovisceral attacks requiring five acute hospital admissions over 2 years, which ended up in questionable diagnoses. The sixth acute attack raised the suspicion of an acute porphyria. In all presentations, findings from ultra sound scans and diagnostic laparoscopy did not support a diagnosis of intra-abdominal pathology.

On examination, the patient was thin-built and pale. The laboratory investigations showed severe hyponatremia, serum osmolality abnormalities, anemia, and left ventricular hypertrophy. A urine sample collected during the acute attack was sent for biochemical analyses, which showed a positive Watson and Schwartz test for urinary porphobilinogen (PBG) and elevated urine total porphyrin level.

He was managed symptomatically as heme arginate is not available in Sri Lanka. Carbohydrate loading with intravenous dextrose and oral carbohydrates were the only feasible option. Response to treatment could not be assessed due to unavailability of quantitative tests to measure urinary aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and PBG in Sri Lanka. The patient was educated regarding precipitating factors of acute porphyria and a diagnostic card with information regarding medications to avoid was provided to the patient.

Patient was discharged from the ward after symptoms gradually improved over 6 days to a degree that he can be managed as an outpatient. Follow up of the patient over 1 year following diagnosis revealed that patient suffered from two mild attacks. Pre-symptomatic relatives who inherited the HMBS mutation were also advised to avoid trigger factors of acute attacks such as certain medications, fasting, alcohol, and hormones. The brother of the proband was counseled regarding the risk of his children inheriting the HMBS mutation and recommended targeted mutation analyses for both children.
output:
Based on Named Entity Recognition, the clinical Named Entities that can be identified from the given discharge summary related to the diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up care of acute porphyria are as follows:

- Diagnosis: partial intestinal obstruction, new-onset systemic hypertension, acute porphyria, severe hyponatremia, left ventricular hypertrophy, positive Watson and Schwartz test for urinary porphobilinogen (PBG), elevated urine total porphyrin level, anemia
- Treatment: managed symptomatically with carbohydrate loading with intravenous dextrose and oral carbohydrates
- Follow-up Care: patient suffered from two mild attacks over 1 year following diagnosis, pre-symptomatic relatives who inherited the HMBS mutation were advised to avoid trigger factors of acute attacks

It is unanswerable whether the patient had any underlying genetic mutations associated with acute porphyria since the discharge summary did not have this information.

instruction: What was the patient diagnosed with due to malaria and what brain abnormalities were detected on the MRI? (related to Relation Extraction)
input:

The 55-year-old Japanese male patient with a persistent high fever and parasitemia was admitted on day 2 of his illness. PCR confirmed P. falciparum. Upon presentation, he had cerebellar ataxia symptoms and expressive aphasia, which persisted even after the parasites were undetectable by a blood test. Hematological investigations showed elevated bilirubin, transaminase, lactate dehydrogenase, creatine kinase, creatinine, and C-reactive protein levels. A serum test revealed hyponatremia. CT scan of the brain was unremarkable. He was started on artemether/lumefantrine at home, but upon admission, a new course of this medication was restarted. MRI of the brain showed a high-signal lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum. On day 10, the platelet count was recovered, and the cerebrospinal fluid showed slightly increased total cell count and normal protein and glucose levels. Renal function recovered by day 7, and hyponatremia improved by day 21. Neurological symptoms started to improve by day 12. Brain MRI on day 16 showed complete regression of the splenic lesion.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 55-year-old Japanese man with P. falciparum was admitted to our hospital with a persistent high fever and cerebellar ataxia symptoms. He was started on artemether/lumefantrine at home, but upon admission, another course of the medication was initiated. MRI of the brain showed a splenial lesion, which was resolved on the follow-up brain MRI on day 16. Hyponatremia and renal functions were normalized by day 21. The patient was diagnosed with mild encephalitis/encephalopathy with a reversible splenial lesion (MERS) due to malaria.
output: The patient was diagnosed with mild encephalitis/encephalopathy with a reversible splenial lesion (MERS) due to malaria, and the MRI of the brain showed a high-signal lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum.

The associated periradicular bone defect was properly addressed, and the patient was recalled for follow-up appointments where healing and bone formation were observed.

Clinical History:
The patient is a 65-year-old male with a medical history of hypertension, cholelithiasis, and panic disorder. He presented with a two-year history of recurrent episodes of flushing, diaphoresis, systolic blood pressure surges up to 200 mmHg, loss of vision, headaches, palpitations, and tremors. The patient was diagnosed with a large right adrenal pheochromocytoma.

Hospital Course:
The patient was started on a high-salt diet, terazosin, and metoprolol. He was admitted one day prior to surgery with a well-controlled blood pressure of 112/70 mmHg. In the operating room, shortly after intubation and Foley catheter insertion and prior to surgical incision, the patient's blood pressure rose to 350/180 mmHg without improvement despite intravenous phentolamine boluses. Given the inability to control the patient's labile blood pressure, a decision was made to abort the operation and transfer the patient to the intensive care unit while remaining intubated. In the ICU, the patient required massive doses of intravenous phentolamine, nitroprusside, and nicardipine as well as intravenous hydration. Interestingly, his blood pressure oscillated between 60/34 and 350/186 mmHg within a matter of 2-3 minutes in a cyclical pattern. A nasogastric tube was inserted, and the patient was started on phenoxybenzamine per tube. After 72 hours in ICU, he was weaned off intravenous antihypertensives and sedatives and extubated.

Upon transfer back to the surgical ward, the patient underwent successful open right adrenalectomy three weeks later. He was hypotensive intraoperatively, requiring vasopressors. Pathology confirmed an 8 cm right adrenal pheochromocytoma without angioinvasion, extra-adrenal extension, or necrosis.

One month postoperatively, the patient was seen in the Endocrinology clinic and reported feeling overall well with no documented hypertension. He stopped all antihypertensive medications and had no palpitations, diaphoresis, flushing, headaches, or other symptoms of catecholamine excess. instruction: What was the treatment plan and long-term outcome for a patient who underwent PTK+CXL after developing corneal ectasia following SMILE for myopia?
input:
Hospital Course:
The 19-year-old male patient underwent SMILE for myopia in both eyes in June 2013. A history of eye rubbing and allergic conjunctivitis was noted, but there was no prior health concern of pellucid marginal corneal degeneration or family history of keratoconus or high myopia. Preoperative characteristics and parameters suggested no abnormalities. After the procedure, the patient exhibited no complications and was discharged.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
At 1-month post-operation, UDVA was 20/20 in both eyes and corneal topography revealed corneal ectasia. The concerning posterior elevations were detected in both eyes, and respective TCTs were 433 mm and 429 mm in the right and left eyes. After 7.5 months, topography showed more posterior elevation. At 14 months following SMILE, UDVA had decreased to 20/32 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left, with eye rubbing and intermittent allergic conjunctivitis still noted. The patient was treated with simultaneous PTK and CXL (PTK+CXL) for both eyes.

Procedure:
Before CXL, the central 9.0-mm diameter epithelium with a 50 μm depth was removed using EX500 by Wavelight Technologies. PTK+CXL procedure was based on the original CXL procedure, as described by Wollensak et al. Riboflavin solution (0.1%) was administered topically every 2 min for 30 min total, during which the cornea was exposed to ultraviolet A light (370 nm, 3.0 mW/cm2) for 30 min at a distance of 5 cm. Antibiotic eye drops were administrated 4 times-daily for 1 week, and fluorometholone eye drops 0.1% were administrated 4 times-daily for 4 weeks. The patient did not experience any intraoperative or postoperative complications. 

Follow-Up:
Keratometry values, TCT, spherical equivalent, and UDVA were monitored at 6, 12, 24, and 36 months after PTK+CXL. At 36-months, maximum corneal keratometry (Kmax) and mean corneal keratometry (Kmean) in the right eye were decreased by 2.6 D and 1.5 D, respectively, while in the left eye, the corresponding reductions were 4.0 D and 1.6 D. TCT had decreased from 432 μm to 412 μm in the right eye but had remained stable in the left eye. Spherical equivalent improved significantly over time, from − 4.25 D to − 2.75 D in the right eye and from − 5.25 D to − 3.5 D in the left eye at 36 months. Furthermore, the UDVA increased over time, allowing the patient to not require glasses or enhancement.
output: The patient who developed corneal ectasia following SMILE for myopia underwent PTK+CXL in both eyes. The PTK+CXL procedure involved removing the central 9.0-mm diameter epithelium with a 50 μm depth and administering riboflavin solution topically while exposing the cornea to ultraviolet A light. At 36-months post-procedure, the patient experienced a significant improvement in maximum and mean corneal keratometry, spherical equivalent, and UDVA, allowing the patient to not require glasses or enhancement. However, TCT had decreased in the right eye but remained stable in the left eye.

Further follow-up care and neurorehabilitation were recommended for the patient to optimize his functional outcome.

instruction: What was the working diagnosis and subsequent surgical procedure performed for the patient's transient ischemic attack (TIA) according to the provided discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:

This 32-year-old, previously healthy, African American man presented to the emergency department 45 minutes after the acute onset of left facial droop and right-sided weakness. A thorough history confirmed an episode 1-week prior, during which he developed sudden onset of dizziness associated with nausea and vomiting that resolved within hours. He denied any past medical or surgical history and was taking no medications. In the emergency room, his vital signs were within normal limits. His physical examination was significant for a left facial droop and right hemiparesis.

Investigations:

A chest X-ray was normal, and an electrocardiogram showed a normal sinus rhythm. A head computed tomography (CT) scan was negative for signs of intracranial hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of his brain demonstrated a right basal ganglia infarct and an old left cerebral infarct. A carotid ultrasound was negative. TTE demonstrated a 1 cm by 1 cm mass on the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve with moderate mitral regurgitation. TTE also revealed a questionable mass on the left coronary cusp of the aortic valve. These findings were confirmed with TEE, which verified no sign of endocarditis and no atrial septal defect. A complete hypercoagulable workup was negative.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

Stroke protocol was initiated, and he was subsequently started on tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) therapy. Stroke protocol continued with the working diagnosis of cerebrovascular accident secondary to emboli from the mitral valve mass. Within 24 hours, he regained function of the right side of his body and had complete resolution of symptoms. He was diagnosed as having transient ischemic attack (TIA) and discussion was undertaken regarding surgical excision of his mitral valve mass.

Procedure:

A median sternotomy was performed, and cardiopulmonary bypass was employed via aortic and bicaval cannulation with full anticoagulation. His aorta was cross-clamped, and his heart arrested with retrograde cardioplegia. A left atriotomy was made, and the mass was easily identified on the posterior mitral valve leaflet adjacent to the mitral valve annulus. The mass was excised, and a frozen section confirmed globular myxoma cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm consistent with myxoma. The valve leaflet was reconstructed with an autologous pericardium patch, and the annulus was supported using a running DeVega-type suture. His left atrium and aorta were closed. His aorta was unclamped, and after aggressive venting and de-airing maneuvers, his heart returned to normal sinus rhythm with successful weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass. Anticoagulation was reversed with protamine, and his chest was closed after placement of drains and pacing wires. At the conclusion of the operation, TEE confirmed appropriate mitral valve function and normal aortic valve with no evidence of a mass and no regurgitation at either location.

Outcome:

The patient had a successful recovery after the procedure with complete resolution of symptoms. His TIA was resolved, and he was discharged with follow-up appointments to monitor his mitral valve function.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Transient ischemic attack (TIA) secondary to mitral valve myxoma.
output: The working diagnosis for the patient's transient ischemic attack (TIA) was cerebrovascular accident secondary to emboli from mitral valve myxoma. The subsequent surgical procedure performed was the excision of the mitral valve mass and reconstruction of the valve leaflet using an autologous pericardium patch, as confirmed by TEE at the conclusion of the operation.

instruction: What Gram-negative organisms were isolated from the patient's sputum samples and how were they treated based on the susceptibility patterns of the isolates?
input:

The patient was admitted to University Malaya Medical Centre with the chief complaints of recurrent pneumonia, poor growth and steatorrhoea since childhood. The patient received multiple courses of antibiotics, including intravenous ceftazidime, gentamicin, vancomycin, oral rifampicin, sodium fusidate, azithromycin, nebulised gentamicin, and other CF-related medications. The antibiotics were then changed to intravenous meropenem, doxycycline, amikacin and oral clarithromycin to treat both Burkholderia cepacia and the suspected nontuberculous mycobacterium. The patient was also treated for various other infections over the years, including melioidosis.

The patient had several admissions for intravenous antibiotics against Burkholderia pseudomallei, which grew repeatedly in his sputum sample. Despite best efforts, the patient ultimately passed away from end-stage respiratory failure.

The patient had multiple infective exacerbations over the years, with sputum samples growing different Gram-negative organisms, including Burkholderia cepacia, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Burkholderia pseudomallei. The patient’s history of visiting endemic areas for melioidosis may have contributed to the subsequent growth of Burkholderia pseudomallei in his sputum samples. Despite best efforts, the patient passed away from end-stage respiratory failure.

instruction: What was the relationship between the left iliac vein and the leiomyosarcoma, and how was it treated in this 51-year-old Japanese man?
input:
Hospital Course:

A 51-year-old Japanese man was referred to our hospital for abnormal ultrasound findings. His past history included diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and fatty liver. Physical examination showed nothing of note, and laboratory findings were within normal range. A contrast computed tomography scan revealed a mass closely adjoining the left external iliac vein, which was diagnosed to be a leiomyosarcoma, probably derived from the left external iliac vein.

Treatment:

Before surgery, the patient's vascular surgeons discussed how to deal with the left iliac vein. The patient was engaged in physical labor and did not want to take an anticoagulant after surgery. So, combined resection of the left iliac vein with the tumor was conducted. The extirpation of the tumor was successful, and complete tumor resection was achieved.

Pathology:

Pathological examination revealed that the tumor was a well-defined, gross, firm mass of 60 mm at the greatest diameter, mostly composed of interlacing fascicles of spindle cells with a mild to moderate degree of cellular pleomorphism. It was considered to be a low-grade leiomyosarcoma. Immunostaining for α-SMA was positive, and positive ratio of MIB-1 was low at 5-10%.

Recovery:

Immediately after surgery, the patient developed left leg pain and swelling. However, the painful swelling of his left thigh improved one week later and ultimately disappeared by about 3 months after surgery. The patient has remained free from recurrence at 30 months after surgery.

Conclusion:

The diagnosis is venous leiomyosarcoma originating from a branch vessel of the left external iliac vein. The combined resection of the left iliac vein with the tumor was successful, with the patient showing no signs of recurrence 30 months after surgery.
output: The leiomyosarcoma in the 51-year-old Japanese man originated from the left external iliac vein and was treated with combined resection of the left iliac vein with the tumor.

The patient was admitted to the Endocrinological section of the Pediatric Unit due to short stature. The patient exhibited unusual facial features that included hypertelorism, low-set ears, a low posterior hairline, down-slanting palpebral fissures, pectus excavatum, and ogival palate. The patient's family history included paternal familiarity for psychotic crises in his adolescence and mother with thrombophilia and history of five pregnancies with three spontaneous abortions and two parts.

The peak growth hormone (GH) value in a clonidine stimulation test was within a normal range, while the IGF-1 level was within normal limits. In addition, a microduplication involving the SHOX gene was identified. GH treatment (0.2 mg/kg/wk) was prescribed, and after 18 months, there was improvement in the patient's height, weight, and growth velocity.

At discharge, the patient's height was 109.8 cm, weight was 18 kg, growth velocity was 7 cm/year, arm span:height ratio was 96%, and sitting height:height ratio was 56%. Follow-up appointments have been scheduled every 6 months.

Noonan Syndrome (NS) with mesomelic short stature and mild cognitive impairment.

Improved height and growth velocity with GH treatment.

Follow-up appointments scheduled with primary care pediatrician every 6 months.

The patient improved clinically with medical management, and a repeat ERCP 9 weeks after the procedure showed no extravasation of contrast from the pancreatic tail. The pancreatic duct stent was downsized to 5Fr. Repeat ERCP 15 weeks after the index procedure showed no extravasation of contrast or stenosis, and the pancreatic duct stent was removed. instruction: What is the significance of detecting Colpodella spp. DNA in both the CSF of a patient with tick bite history and ticks from the same region according to the given discharge summary? (related to the task of Relation Extraction)
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient, a 55-year-old female, was admitted to Mudanjiang Forestry Central Hospital with symptoms including dizziness, gait disturbance, and headache. Upon admission, the patient displayed a body temperature of 39.5 °C, blood pressure of 125/70 mm Hg, pulse rate of 60 beats/min, and respiration of 18 breaths/min. The neurological examination revealed moderate nuchal rigidity. Routine blood tests indicated an inflammatory response, with elevated neutrophil—granulocyte proportion and CRPs. An engorged adult tick had been removed from the patient two weeks before admission. Eleven days after tick removal, she had visited a local clinic with persistent high fever up to 42.0 °C and received supportive treatment with compound paracetamol tablets for two days with no clinical improvement. The routine test for the antibody of Borellia spp. and TBEV in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was negative for TBEV but positive for IgG antibody against Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato (sl) at titer of 1:256 in the serum, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of Lyme disease. During her 10-day admission, the patient was administered doxycycline (100 mg/twice daily).

Diagnostic Tests:
Laboratory tests of blood showed 53.1 U/L for alanine aminotransferase, 54.3 U/L for aspartate transaminase, and 78.0 U/L for gamma-glutamyl transferase in the blood that was collected on the day of admission, with 0.15 g/L protein detected in urine. CSF tests revealed 0.4 g/L of protein, 4.28 mmol/L of glucose, and 125.3 mmol/L of chloride chloridate, with no white blood cell (WBC) or red blood cell (RBC) in the CSF, collected at four days after hospitalization, and presented visually crystal clear and faint yellow. 

Hospital Course and Treatment:
During her 10-day admission, the patient was administered doxycycline (100 mg/twice daily) for treatment of Lyme disease. On April 15, 2015, almost two years after initial infection, no Colpodella spp. HLJ strain was detected, indicating no chronic or relapsing infection.

Follow-up:
In addition, the hospital conducted a screening for Colpodella spp. in 474 Ixodes persulcatus ticks collected in woodlands around the patient’s living area in the Mudanjiang area in 2015 with the same PCR assay, followed by direct sequencing, and subsequently found two I. persulcatus ticks positive for Colpodella spp. The detection of Colpodella spp. DNA in both the CSF of a patient with tick bite history along with isolation in ticks from the same region warrants deeper investigations.
output: Detecting Colpodella spp. DNA in both the CSF of a patient with tick bite history and ticks from the same region suggests that further investigation is warranted to determine if this organism may be involved in the pathogenesis of Lyme disease and whether it plays a role in the persistence of symptoms even after antibiotic treatment. However, the given information does not provide any conclusive evidence or causal relationship regarding Colpodella spp. and Lyme disease, and further studies are needed to determine this possibility with certainty.
