instruction: What was the pre-operative diagnosis and treatment for the patient, a 70-year-old female, with upper abdominal pain mentioned in the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: N/A
DOB: N/A
Gender: Female

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient, a 70-year-old female, was admitted to our hospital due to upper abdominal pain. Upon physical examination, left hypochondriac pain and tenderness in the upper abdomen were noted. The laboratory examinations revealed elevated inflammatory markers and biliary enzymes. The levels of tumor markers were also elevated. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed a markedly dilated main pancreatic duct (MPD) 55 mm in length in the whole pancreas, and the whole pancreatic parenchyma was thinning with atrophy. Additionally, gastropancreatic fistula and splenopancreatic fistula were detected, suggesting penetration of the pancreatic tumor. Upon examination by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, four gastropancreatic fistulas were identified on the posterior wall of the gastric body and mucus discharged from the gastropancreatic fistulas. On the basis of the findings, the patient was pre-operatively diagnosed with non-invasive intraductal papillary-mucinous cancer (IPMC) of the pancreas. 

The patient underwent total pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and distal gastrectomy combined with resection of the fistulas. Considering the malignant potential based on the main ductal type with > 10 mm MPD dilatation, lymphadenectomy was also performed. Macroscopic examination of the resected specimen indicated swelling of the whole pancreas. When the resected specimen was divided, mucus swelled out, and then most of the cut surface of the whole pancreas was occupied by the dilated MPD and the mucus accompanied by atrophy of the pancreatic parenchyma. The gastropancreatic fistula and splenopancreatic fistula were macroscopically identified. In the spleen, bleeding and infarction were detected in addition to the mucus penetration. Microscopic examination of the resected specimen revealed cancer cells in the epithelium of the MPD in part of the tumor. There was no sign of infiltration on the cancer cells, and the remaining part of the MPD epithelium was adenoma. At the gastropancreatic fistula and splenopancreatic fistula, no cancer cells were detected, only mucus and inflammatory cells. 

The patient did not experience any postoperative complications. The patient has remained disease-free without evidence of recurrence for 15 months.

SUMMARY:

A 70-year-old female with upper abdominal pain was pre-operatively diagnosed with non-invasive intraductal papillary-mucinous cancer (IPMC) of the pancreas. The patient underwent total pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and distal gastrectomy combined with resection of the fistulas. Mechanical penetration was identified as the underlying mechanism in the development of the fistulas. The patient did not experience any postoperative complications and has remained disease-free without evidence of recurrence for 15 months.
output: The pre-operative diagnosis for the 70-year-old female with upper abdominal pain was non-invasive intraductal papillary-mucinous cancer (IPMC) of the pancreas. The patient underwent total pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and distal gastrectomy combined with resection of the fistulas. The patient did not experience any postoperative complications and has remained disease-free without evidence of recurrence for 15 months.

instruction: What was the nature of the lesion found in the patient at the T3 level according to the discharge summary, and how was it successfully treated?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [DATE] Discharge Date: [DATE]

This is a summary of the hospital course for [PATIENT NAME], a 75-year-old male who presented with chronic numbness in his lower extremities due to peripheral neuropathy. Over time, the patient’s symptoms progressed, leading to urinary retention and diagnosis of an intramedullary lesion at the T3 level. The lesion was suspected to represent a neoplastic mass, and a positron emission tomography (PET) CT was performed.

Due to the patient’s advanced age and comorbidities, the nature of the lesion was not immediately clear, and cardiothoracic surgery was consulted to replace the pacemaker with an MRI-compatible alternative to enable further investigation. A subsequent MRI demonstrated that the lesion was actually a dorsal, extramedullary dural-based tumor causing significant canal stenosis and cord compression at T3.

Although the patient's age and comorbidities raised concerns about the surgical approach, it was deemed necessary to proceed with a T2-T4 laminectomy with resection of the meningioma. The operation was a success, with a repeat MR with gadolinium at three months follow-up showing complete resection with no evidence of recurrence.

The patient remained clinically improved two years post-resection, with no reported complications. A discharge plan was put in place, and the patient was recommended for physical therapy to aid recovery.
output: According to the discharge summary, the lesion found in the patient at the T3 level was a dorsal, extramedullary dural-based tumor causing significant canal stenosis and cord compression. The patient underwent a T2-T4 laminectomy with resection of the meningioma which was successful, as confirmed by a repeat MR with gadolinium at three months follow-up showing complete resection with no evidence of recurrence.

instruction: What Named Entities can be recognized through the task of "Named Entity Recognition" related to the patient's diagnosis and treatment history in the given discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary

Patient: 67-year-old male with thymoma

Admission Date: Summer 2016
Discharge Date: N/A (deceased)

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with ascites and leg oedema. He had a history of thymoma, which was diagnosed in 1992. He underwent an extended thymectomy and received radiotherapy. He had two recurrent episodes, one in 1996 and the second in 2004. After the second recurrence, he did not receive any chemotherapy or radiotherapy. The CT scan at our hospital revealed a left peritoneal mass, peritoneal dissemination with massive ascites, and multiple bone metastases. Biopsy of the left peritoneal mass confirmed a recurrent type B1 thymoma.
As a first-line therapy, the patient received carboplatin and paclitaxel, but he developed severe pneumonia and febrile neutropenia. He was treated with antibiotics and recovered. A second-line therapy of everolimus was given, but it was stopped after one month due to thrombocytopenia. Paclitaxel was administered as a third-line therapy, but the patient's abdomen gradually enlarged and the pleural effusion on the right side increased. Thoracentesis was performed, which resulted in the removal of 800 mL of fluid. However, the patient developed acute dyspnoea and had to undergo immediate tube thoracostomy, which removed 10 L of sanguineous fluid. The patient's general condition gradually deteriorated, and he passed away 12 days later.
Autopsy examination revealed one hole on the right diaphragm, which did not match the position by thoracentesis, and several metastases on the diaphragm.

Impression:
The patient had a history of thymoma and experienced two recurrent episodes. He received several lines of therapies, but his condition gradually deteriorated. The autopsy examination revealed a hole on the right diaphragm, which was not related to thoracentesis.

Recommendations:
N/A (deceased)
output: The Named Entities related to the patient's diagnosis and treatment history in the discharge summary include thymoma, ascites, leg oedema, carboplatin, paclitaxel, everolimus, pneumonia, febrile neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, peritoneal mass, peritoneal dissemination, bone metastases, pleural effusion, thoracentesis, tube thoracostomy, dyspnoea, and diaphragm metastases. However, there is no Named Entity related to the cause of the hole on the right diaphragm.

instruction: What was the treatment for the patient with tetanus and BB accompanied by T1LR, and how effective was it in reducing symptoms and achieving a stable condition at discharge?
input:
Discharge Summary
Patient Name: Not Provided
Medical Record Number: Not Provided
Admission Date: Not Provided
Discharge Date: Not Provided

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of erythematous plaques and pain over the left upper limb and foreign object sensation in the throat when swallowing. She was diagnosed with tetanus and BB accompanied by T1LR. The patient had a 6-year history of leprosy and was treated with MDT resulting in a clinical cure in 2012. Initially, T1LR was suspected, followed by treatment with oral methylprednisolone. However, the patient's symptoms worsened, with neck muscle tension and difficulty in opening her mouth, and the erythematous plaques had spread over most of her left upper limb.

On physical examination, the patient displayed shortness of breath and facial expressions indicating trismus and difficulty speaking. The patient's abdominal muscles were too stiff for palpation of the liver and spleen. There was persistent stiffness in the neck and limbs, together with opisthotonus, and occasional paroxysmal spasms. The patient's bilateral ulnar nerves and right common peroneal nerve were thickened and exhibited tenderness. The patient exhibited right foot drop, atrophy of the extensor of the right lower leg, and an ulcer on the right foot.

Treatment:
The patient was administered 100,000 IU tetanus antitoxin in a 500-ml 5% glucose-saline intravenous infusion daily, 200,000 U penicillin in an intramuscular injection four times a day, and 200 mg of hydrocortisone in a 250-ml 5% glucose intravenous infusion daily. Additionally, 10 mg/day of diazepam and 50 mg/day of phenergan were given by intramuscular injection. The patient was hospitalized in a dark, quiet room to reduce light stimulation and prevent spasms. In addition, a dental pad was placed in the oral cavity to prevent the patient from biting her tongue. The ulcer on her right foot was debrided every day, followed by rinsing with 3% hydrogen peroxide and injection of 20,000 IU tetanus antitoxin around the wound. The paroxysmal spasticity and intensity of the spasms started to decrease after 5 days.

Outcome:
Twelve days later, the patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition. She was followed up in our outpatient department and treated with MDT and oral prednisone to prevent T1LR for 4 months. The erythematous plaques and neuropathic pain eventually subsided.

She had a history of leprosy and was diagnosed with tetanus and BB accompanied by T1LR. The patient received appropriate treatment and was discharged after 12 days of hospitalization. She was followed up in our outpatient department and was treated with MDT and oral prednisone to prevent T1LR for 4 months. The patient was discharged in stable condition.
output: The patient with tetanus and BB accompanied by T1LR was treated with tetanus antitoxin, penicillin, hydrocortisone, diazepam, and phenergan. The patient was hospitalized in a dark, quiet room to reduce light stimulation and prevent spasms, and a dental pad was placed in the oral cavity to prevent the patient from biting her tongue. The ulcer on her right foot was debrided every day, followed by rinsing with 3% hydrogen peroxide and injection of 20,000 IU tetanus antitoxin around the wound. The treatment was effective in reducing symptoms, and the patient was discharged in stable condition after 12 days of hospitalization. The patient was then followed up in the outpatient department and treated with MDT and oral prednisone to prevent T1LR for 4 months.

instruction: What was the patient's diagnosis and treatment for the condition identified as melorheostosis in the hospital course section of the given discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [Date]

Patient: 20-year-old Danish female

Medical History:
- Constant pain in the right proximal thigh for 8 years
- Menarche at age 13
- No family history of sclerosing bone diseases
- Polycystic ovaries with normal androgen status
- Leg length discrepancy
- Previous consultation with a rheumatologist for hip joint pain
- Mild traffic accident six months prior to referral

Summary of Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with constant pain in the right proximal thigh that had persisted for 8 years, which had been moderately relieved during physical activity and by cold baths. Mild pain relief was achieved with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, paracetamol and weak opioid agonists. The patient had a gynecological examination that revealed a mild degree of polycystic ovaries with normal androgen status. An X-ray showed significant cortical thickening in the right femoral diaphysis that partially obliterated the medullary cavity. MR and PET-CT scans revealed uneven surface of the sclerotic bone. A bone biopsy was performed and showed thickened bone springs with preserved lamellar structure and slightly accentuated cement lines. After ruling out several other diagnoses, melorheostosis was diagnosed as the most plausible diagnosis. The first line of treatment with zoledronic acid 5mg was given, with the second and third injections being less effective than the first. Denosumab was then chosen as the second line of treatment to control a hypermetabolic state. Pain relief was achieved after the first injection; however, there was a slight increase in pain after 6 weeks. Therefore, the interval between injections was shortened and remained constant up to the latest follow-up in February 2018. There were no adverse effects reported during the entire treatment period. After the first three doses given 8 weeks apart, there was pain remission for 8 months, where the patient did not take any orally administered analgesics. At the latest follow-up, the patient complained of a slight increase in pain, which was occasionally treated with paracetamol and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. A Tc99-bone scan and CT scan were performed in February 2017 and in February 2018, respectively, and the pathologically increased activity and cortical thickening were stationary.

- Melorheostosis was diagnosed as the most plausible diagnosis
- Zoledronic acid 5mg was given, with the second and third injections being less effective than the first
- Denosumab was chosen as the second line of treatment to control a hypermetabolic state
- Pain relief was achieved after the first injection; however, there was a slight increase in pain after 6 weeks
- Interval between injections was shortened and remained constant up to the latest follow-up in February 2018

- Tc99-bone scan and CT scan performed in February 2017 and in February 2018, respectively, and the pathologically increased activity and cortical thickening were stationary.

instruction: What is the relationship between the patient's diagnosed condition of diffuse parenchymal pulmonary amyloidosis accompanied by multiple myeloma and the results of the serum free light chain analysis, serum protein electrophoresis, 24-h urine test, and bone marrow examination? (related to the task of Relation Extraction)
input:
Patient Identifier: [Patient Name]
Gender: Female
Age: 58

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to a 2-year history of non-productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. She had a history of renal insufficiency and persistent proteinuria, without any extra-renal involvement. She was diagnosed with IgA nephropathy for 15 years and had received immunosuppressive therapy for 6 years.

Physical Examination:
On examination, the patient was afebrile with stable vital signs. Auscultation detected slight coarse crackles at the bilateral bases while the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Diagnostic Tests:
Her hemoglobin was 95 g/L but renal function and calcium level were normal. The patient was negative for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. Serum free light chain analysis showed measuring lambda light chain of 2.59 g/L. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed low IgG, IgA, and IgM levels, with reported monoclonal lambda light chain peak with the monoclonal protein. A 24-h urine contained 5521 mg of protein. High-resolution chest CT revealed disclosed ground-glass opacities (GGOs) with interlobular septal thickening in bilateral lungs. Chest and abdominal CT shows soft tissue infiltration of the subcutaneous fat layer with asymmetric bulging of the chest and abdominal wall. Pulmonary function tests revealed a moderately restrictive ventilation disorder, with a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 1.76 L and severe reduction of diffusion capacity (DLCO SB). Cardiac biomarkers including B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and cardiac troponin-T were normal. Echocardiography showed normal left ventricular ejection fraction of 61% and there were no features of cardiac amyloidosis. A VATLB showed marked thickening of the alveolar wall deposition of amorphous eosinophilic amyloid at the bronchial mucosa, pulmonary vessel wall, and interstitium. Congo red staining displayed apple-green birefringence in polarized light. The bone marrow examination showed 11.5% plasma cells with lambda light chain restriction.

Diagnosis:
Diffuse parenchymal pulmonary amyloidosis accompanied by multiple myeloma, lambda light chain type, stage I.

Treatment:
The patient was referred to the hematology department, where she started chemotherapy with bortezomib and dexamethasone. Her symptoms relieved 2 months after the initial presentation. No adverse effects were observed, and the laboratory results were stable.

Discharge Condition:
The patient is in a stable condition and ready for discharge.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will receive regular follow-up care, including close monitoring of renal function, proteinuria, and pulmonary function. She will receive ongoing chemotherapy and management of her underlying conditions, including IgA nephropathy and multiple myeloma, involving immunosuppressive therapy. She is advised to seek immediate medical attention if she experiences any worsening of her symptoms.
output: The patient's diagnosis of diffuse parenchymal pulmonary amyloidosis accompanied by multiple myeloma with lambda light chain type stage I can be explained by the results of the serum free light chain analysis, serum protein electrophoresis, 24-h urine test, and bone marrow examination. Specifically, the serum free light chain analysis showed elevated lambda light chain levels, and the serum protein electrophoresis revealed a monoclonal lambda light chain peak with the monoclonal protein. The 24-h urine test found a significant amount of protein, and the bone marrow examination showed lambda light chain restriction with 11.5% plasma cells. These results are indicative of multiple myeloma and the presence of amyloidosis.

instruction: What was the clinical course and treatment plan for a 32-year-old female patient with an unknown Gram-negative bacterium infection who was admitted with a history of lymphoblastic leukemia, allogeneic bone marrow transplant, and cervical cancer?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 32-year-old female from Mexico City
Diagnosis: Unknown Gram-negative bacterium infection

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to National Medical Centre on 20 November with general discomfort and a history of lymphoblastic leukemia, allogeneic bone marrow transplant, and cervical cancer. Upon admission, the patient presented with shooting cephalea, night sweats, asthenia, adynamia, dyspnoea and an unknown origin fever (39°C). The patient was also experiencing transvaginal bleeding. A clinical report showed leukocyte count, neutrophils, hemoglobin, haematocrit, and platelet count. A blood transfusion was administered, and the patient was treated with imipenem and ciprofloxacin for 16 days with no improvement. A chest X-ray was performed, but no infection was detected. A gram-negative bacterium was isolated from the central catheter, but the Vitek 2® system was not able to identify it. The patient was treated with amikacin, ceftazidime, caspofungin, and normal human immunoglobulin. While no further bacteria were isolated, the patient still presented with a fever (39°C) and fatigue. After 20 days of hospitalization, two haemocultures from a peripheral vein were performed, and a gram-negative bacterium was identified. A broad-range PCR reaction was performed, indicating a phylogenetic relationship with Ochrobactrum anthropi. The patient was treated with amikacin and ciprofloxacin for 31 days, and the fever disappeared. The patient was discharged three months later, asymptomatic.

Medication on Discharge:
None

Instructions on Discharge:
None

Follow-Up on Discharge:
The patient was advised to return for a check-up if symptoms reappeared.
output: The healthcare professional should advise the 32-year-old female patient, who was discharged after being treated for an unknown Gram-negative bacterium infection, to return to the hospital for a check-up if symptoms reappear.

instruction: What Named Entities related to the patient's glomus tumor diagnosis and surgical excision can be identified using Named Entity Recognition in the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 60-year-old Moroccan man with a 3-year history of a progressively asymptomatic nodule of his right index finger.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with a voluminous, purplish, painless soft tumor on the first phalanx of the right index finger, compressing the nail plate. Neurological examination did not reveal any signs of paresthesia or hypoesthesia. The differential diagnosis included angifibroma, pyogenic granuloma-like Kaposi sarcoma, epidermized pyogenic granuloma, superficial acral fibromyxoma, and glomus tumor. Radiographic and MRI studies suggested glomus tumor.

The patient underwent surgical excision with a direct approach, respecting the principles of cutaneous incisions and avoiding nerve fiber pathways. The mass was well circumscribed and removed. Histopathological examination showed round to ovoid cells traversed by narrow vascular clefts lined with regular flattened endothelial cells. The absence of mitotic activity and presence of tumoral smooth muscle actin confirmed the diagnosis of glomus tumor.

At follow-up visits, no further radiological investigations were requested, and no recurrence was noted. The finger healed completely within 6 months, and the nail regained its normal appearance in 10 months.

Summary:

The patient presented with a painless soft tumor on the first phalanx of the right index finger, which was diagnosed as a glomus tumor. Surgical excision was performed, and the patient had a smooth recovery without any complications. At follow-up visits, no further radiological investigations were requested, and no recurrence was noted. The finger healed completely within 6 months, and the nail regained its normal appearance in 10 months.
output: Using Named Entity Recognition (NER) in the discharge summary, named entities related to the patient's glomus tumor diagnosis and surgical excision that can be identified are "glomus tumor," "surgical excision," and "histopathological examination."

instruction: What diagnostic tests confirmed the patient's ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome and where was the mass lesion located according to abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scanning?
input:
Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Confidential
Admission Date: XX/XX/XXXX
Discharge Date: XX/XX/XXXX

History of Presenting Illness:
The patient, a 27-year-old woman, was admitted with a one-month history of facial edema, weight loss, and acne. She had previously sought medical attention at a local hospital for facial redness and edema caused by eating a mango, and was treated with dexamethasone for five days. The patient gradually developed severe facial edema, beard, central deposition of fat with slim extremities and atrophic muscles, and no pretibial edema over the course of one month. 

Medical History:
The patient had a history of a 5.5-cm mass located in the right posterior lobe of the liver detected by ultrasound in a routine physical examination 16 months ago at a local hospital. However, the patient did not experience any symptoms at that time.

Physical Examination:
Upon hospitalization, the patient was found to have “moon face” and severe facial edema, beard, central deposition of fat with slim extremities and atrophic muscles, and no pretibial edema. The skin was diffused with acne, and both armpits had hyperpigmentation.

Diagnostic Findings:
Laboratory tests revealed that the patient had marked hypokalemia, which did not normalize with oral and intravenous potassium supplementation until spironolactone was added. A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test confirmed diabetes mellitus. Endocrinological investigation identified severe hypercortisolism with loss of circadian rhythm, and plasma ACTH level was elevated to 1157 pg/mL, confirming ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome. MRI and contrasted MRI revealed no pituitary adenoma. Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scanning revealed that the mass lesion was located in the right adrenal gland and not in the right hepatic posterior lobe. PET/CT showed moderate fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in the mass.

Treatment:
Adrenal tumorectomy was performed, and no hypertensive crisis occurred during surgery. A 6.5-cm black mass was found arising from the medial branch of the right adrenal gland. Hematoxylin-eosin staining of the tumor revealed that most of the cells were chromaffin-like cells. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor showed positive staining for chromogranin A (CgA) and CD56, with a Ki67 labeling index of approximately 16% for chromaffin-like cells. ACTH levels decreased from 715 to 14.3 pg/ml one day after surgery, and serum cortisol levels decreased from more than 50 to 10.4 μg/dl. The patient's signs and symptoms of Cushing’s syndrome gradually disappeared within two months, and the hydrocortisone supplementation was discontinued seven weeks postoperatively. CT revealed that the left adrenal gland was almost reduced to the normal size three months later.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition and is currently under regular follow-up.

Follow-Up:
The patient is currently well nine months after surgery and will continue to be followed up regularly.
output: The patient's ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome was confirmed by elevated plasma ACTH levels of 1157 pg/mL. The mass lesion was located in the right adrenal gland according to abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scanning.

On admission, she was somnolent, moderately dehydrated, with right hemiparesis and right hemihypoesthesia. The warmth of right limbs was decreased, but the pulse on peripheral arteries was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed symmetrical changes in postero-lateral thalami and medial occipital lobes, as well as some smaller areas noted in the region of splenium of corpus callosum and within deep structures of the left cerebral hemisphere.

During her hospitalization, a series of tests towards the diagnosis of metabolic, autoimmune, and rheumatoid diseases, or coagulopathies was performed, with no positive response. After 7 days, her condition worsened. She became non-responsive with anisocoria R > L, right-sided central facial palsy, bilateral hemiparesis R > L, and positive bilateral Babinski sign. MRI scan revealed a new large hyperintense area in the pons and some smaller areas in the cerebellum, and 3D-TOF angiography showed an embolic mass within the basilar artery (BA) at the level of left AICA and partial occlusion of P2a segments of both posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs).

Physical examination revealed a loss of right radial pulse, and Doppler-US showed normal flow values in the arteries of right arm and forearm but the complete occlusion of right SA due to an embolic mass at the origin of right vertebral artery (VA). The VA was partially occluded but had a torticuous canal of patency in its initial segment. Chest X-Ray revealed the presence of cervical ribs bilaterally, and CT-angiography of subclavian arteries in two typical arm positions was done. It showed the occlusion of right SA with a developed suprascapular arterial anastomosis supplying the brachial artery. The scans also revealed bony anomalies in the region of superior thoracic aperture: cervical ribs and bifid 1st rib on the right, which fixed the diagnosis of right-sided aTOS, confirmed subsequently in catheter angiography a few days after.

The surgeon decided to postpone surgical excision of the cervical rib until the end of skeletal growth. She was placed on anticoagulant therapy with low molecular weight heparin combined with warfarin. After a few days, her neurological status improved—she was in good logical contact, responsive with scattered speech. After rehabilitation sessions, she started to sit and walk without support. She was discharged with right-sided weakness and intention tremor.

instruction: What is the relationship extracted between the patient's Mantle Cell Lymphoma and the observed bilateral bronchiectasis, tracheal and bronchial wall thickening, and lymphadenopathy noted in the CT and PET-CT scans?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 65-year-old male with a history of productive cough and progressive dyspnoea.

Diagnosis: Mantle Cell Lymphoma (MCL)

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a history of productive cough and progressive dyspnoea. On physical examination, the patient had mild fine bibasilar crackles on lung exam without wheezing. The patient was a 40 pack-year smoker. Laboratory values were normal, except for a lower PaO2 of 74.4 mmHg on room air. The patient's serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) level was high (1655 U/mL). Pulmonary function testing revealed severe irreversible obstructive ventilatory dysfunction with normal diffusing capacity of the lung. A CT scan of the chest revealed irregular wall thickening of the trachea and bilateral bronchi, bilateral bronchiectasis, and mediastinal and both hilar lymphadenopathy were noted. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a diffuse irregular surface of the tracheal and bilateral bronchial mucosa and multiple macroscopic submucosal nodules involving the trachea, the distal trachea above the major carina, and throughout the left and right main bronchi. Endobronchial biopsy of the mucosa on the major carina showed a population of small atypical lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei of irregular nuclear contours. These atypical lymphocytes were CD20 positive B-cells co-expressing CD5, blc-2, and Cyclin D1, leading to the diagnosis of MCL. Further PET-CT imaging showed the persistence of FDG-avid lymphadenopathy within the chest, FDG-avid wall thickening of the trachea and bilateral main bronchi, as well as FDG-avid nasopharyngeal soft tissue thickening. Biopsies of the nasopharyngeal mucosa further demonstrated B-cells with the same immunophenotype as the endobronchial biopsy, and 11;14 translocation was confirmed by FISH analysis using a CCND1/IGH probe. Bone marrow biopsy showed an increased lymphocyte percentage of 23%, with 1% of immature lymphocytes, and a positive immunoglobulin rearrangement. Bone marrow flow cytometry demonstrated a surface kappa clonal B-cell population with CD5, CD20, and FMC-7 expression. Taken together, these findings were consistent with an MCL involving the tracheobronchial wall, nasopharyngeal soft tissue, and bone marrow.
  
Clinical Course:
The patient was treated conservatively with supportive care and was referred to a hematologist for further management. The patient and his family were educated on the diagnosis of MCL and the management options available. The patient was advised to stop smoking, and the importance of smoking cessation was discussed. The patient will follow up with the hematologist for further management of his MCL.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged home with palliative care for his MCL. The patient was advised to follow up with the hematologist within a week of discharge. The patient will continue with supportive treatment for his MCL. The patient was educated on the signs and symptoms of MCL progression and was advised to seek medical attention immediately if such signs and symptoms occur. The patient was advised to continue smoking cessation.
output: The observed bilateral bronchiectasis, tracheal and bronchial wall thickening, and lymphadenopathy noted in the CT and PET-CT scans are consistent with an involvement of the tracheobronchial wall by the patient's Mantle Cell Lymphoma. Furthermore, the PET-CT scan also noted FDG-avid nasopharyngeal soft tissue thickening which is further consistent with the diagnosis of MCL involving the nasopharyngeal soft tissue. The bone marrow biopsy also showed the involvement of the bone marrow with MCL.

instruction: What was the intervention performed for the patient with a dissecting fusiform SCA aneurysm in the lateral ponto-mesencephalic segment, and how was it successful in preserving vessel patency?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Hospital Day 1:
A 31-year-old African-American female presented to the emergency department with sudden onset severe headaches, highly suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). A neurological examination revealed no deficits.

Hospital Day 2:
Computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a SAH filling pre-pontine, crural, ambient, and quadrigeminal cisterns more prominently on the left side of the brain, with mild hydrocephalus. A CT-angiography (CTA) showed an enlarged vessel within the left ambient cistern. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) revealed a large and irregular appearance of the left SCA in the ambient cistern. No immediate intervention was undertaken.

Hospital Day 14:
Patient remained stable in the neurosurgical intensive care unit with regular neurological examinations and daily transcranial-doppler (TCD) studies. TCD values showed only moderate vasospasm. The patient did not require any treatment for the mild radiographic hydrocephalus. On Day 14, the patient underwent a repeat DSA which showed a persistent vasospasm in the distal basilar and bilateral posterior cerebral arteries. 3-D reformatting also demonstrated a dissecting fusiform SCA aneurysm in the lateral ponto-mesencephalic segment. No intervention was undertaken at that time.

Hospital Day 21:
The patient underwent a successful endovascular procedure where a low-profile visualized intraluminal support (LVIS Jr.) device was placed, covering the fusiform aneurysm measuring 3-mm wide and 18-mm in length. The intervention aimed to preserve the intraluminal flow with flow diversion from the aneurysm for reduction and eventual obliteration.

Hospital Day 90:
At the 3-month follow-up, the patient remained neurologically stable with no complaints. A CTA showed the SCA patency proximal and distal to the stent without evidence of persistent dilatation or an aneurysm.

Hospital Day 300:
At the 10-month follow-up, a DSA demonstrated the interval healing of the aneurysm with preserved vessel patency as well as mild distortion caused by the stent in the SCA. The patient remained neurologically stable with no complaints.

Final Diagnosis:
Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) due to a dissecting fusiform SCA aneurysm in the lateral ponto-mesencephalic segment.

Interventions/Procedures:
Placement of a low-profile visualized intraluminal support (LVIS Jr.) device covering the fusiform aneurysm.

Condition at Discharge:
Stable and neurologically intact.

Follow-up Instructions:
Catheter angiogram deferred by the patient.

Other Instructions:
None specified.
output: The intervention performed for the patient with a dissecting fusiform SCA aneurysm in the lateral ponto-mesencephalic segment was the placement of a low-profile visualized intraluminal support (LVIS Jr.) device, which was successful in preserving vessel patency with no evidence of persistent dilatation or aneurysm at the 3-month and 10-month follow-up.

Neurological exam revealed a slight upward gaze palsy, and velocity-dependent hypertonia in the upper extremities. Reflexes and sensation were intact.

Lab and Imaging Studies:
White blood cell count was 2.7 × 109, hemoglobin was 134 g/L, and platelets were 196 × 109. The electrolytes and extended electrolytes were within normal limits except for a low sodium level. MRI showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss and mild microangiopathic changes. EEG was abnormal but nonspecific. CSF showed a nucleated cell count within normal limits, normal glucose, and slightly elevated protein. Oligoclonal bands were not detected in the CSF. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with sCJD based on the postmortem autopsy that demonstrated microspongiosis, neuronal loss, and gliosis in the cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged to a palliative care facility where he passed away eight weeks after presentation. 

Follow-up:
None specified.

Discharge Summary

Final Diagnosis: Gastric fundus splenosis with associated hemangioma

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 74-year-old woman with a history of schistosomiasis cirrhosis splenectomy at 29 years old, was admitted to the Gastroenterology Department of our hospital for an asymptomatic gastric mass. CT scans and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy were performed, and the diagnosis of a gastric GIST was confirmed. A multidisciplinary conference was held to discuss the patient's case, and she was considered for a GIST resection under gastroscopy.

During the procedure, the surface of the mucosal, submucosal, muscle layers, and tumor surface were diffusely oozing, and the effect of electrocoagulation and hemostasis was extremely poor. Endoscopic surgery was arrested due to the risk of difficulties in controlling intra-abdominal bleeding on the serosal side. A combination of laparoscopic-gastroscope double-mirror surgery was decided to preserve the stomach, but the tumor location was high and concealed, even under laparoscopic direct vision. Ultimately, a traditional surgical resection was performed, and the tumor was removed. The patient's vital signs were stable, and she was transferred to the intensive care unit and discharged on postoperative day 10.

CT scans revealed pipe stem cirrhosis, a well-demarcated 4-cm solid mass confined to the gastric wall suggestive of a GIST, and a 1-cm low-density lesion with a clear outline in the mass. Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a 3.95 × 2.82-cm slightly low-level echoic homogeneous mass derived from the muscularis propria and a 1 × 1-cm lower level echoic area with a clear boundary in the mass. On macroscopic examination, 3.9 × 2.8 × 2.4-cm dark red masses surrounded by a completely thin capsule were observed in the gastric fundus muscularis propria, along with an approximately 1 × 1-cm nodule appearing as a circumscribed, non-encapsulated, honeycomb-like, and red-purple nodule, which formed with dilated congested vascular space with bleeding.

No medical management regimen to report.

The patient was discharged on postoperative day 10 in stable condition. She was instructed to follow-up with her primary care provider and scheduled for future visits with her gastroenterologist and surgeon to monitor her condition.

The patient was diagnosed with gastric fundus splenosis with an associated hemangioma. She underwent a traditional surgical resection and was discharged in stable condition. Close follow-up with her care team was arranged to monitor her condition going forward.

instruction: What was the modified chemotherapy regimen for the patient with mixed germ cell tumor and why was it changed from the initially planned regimen?
input:
Subjective:
The patient is a 32-year-old male who presented with a painless and gradually enlarging right testicular swelling of 3 months duration.

Objective:
Upon examination, histopathology showed yolk sac tumor (65%), immature teratoma (20%), and seminoma (15%). Baseline CT scan revealed a 1.8cm right para-aortic lymph node with no other metastatic disease. The patient was staged as Stage IIA-S1, Good risk Mixed Germ Cell Tumor (MGCT) depending upon the markers & CT findings.

Assessment:
Chemotherapy was planned within 3 weeks of surgery; however, the patient presented to the ER after 2nd week of orchiectomy with severe chest pain. EKG showed 1.8mm ST segment elevation in leads V1-V3 with elevated Trop-I. Cardiology team was consulted immediately & echocardiogram was performed which showed apical hypokinesis with EF of 49%. His cardiac catheterization was reported to be normal with normal coronaries and without any flow restriction. TCM diagnosis was established based upon Mayo clinic diagnostic criteria.

Plan:
Patient was started on angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and beta-blockers, and his chemotherapy was delayed by 3 weeks. His chemotherapy regimen was modified to EC (Etoposide 100 mg/m2IV Day 1-5 / Carboplatin AUC-5 IV Day 1 only) instead of EP (Etoposide / Cisplatin) due to a risk of Cisplatin induced vasculitis or acute thrombosis. Patient was treated with 4 cycles of EC and achieved complete biochemical and radiological response. After 6 months of his treatment with ACEi and BBs, both were also stopped as he had normal EF (62%) on echocardiogram.

Outcome:
Patient has completed 4.6 years of follow-up according to National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines and remains well without any evidence of relapse.
output: The modified chemotherapy regimen for the patient with mixed germ cell tumor was EC (Etoposide 100 mg/m2 IV Day 1-5 / Carboplatin AUC-5 IV Day 1 only) instead of EP (Etoposide / Cisplatin), due to the risk of Cisplatin induced vasculitis or acute thrombosis.

instruction: What is the history and treatment plan of a 72-year-old male patient who underwent stent removal due to recurrent dysphagia caused by localized esophageal carcinoma and subsequent placement of multiple stents?
input:
Patient Information:
This is a discharge summary for a 72-year-old male patient who was referred to this institution for management and consideration of stent removal due to recurrent dysphagia. The patient had a history of localized esophageal carcinoma and had undergone neoadjuvant chemoradiation and esophagectomy in the past.

Hospital Course:
Upon examination, the patient was found to have a benign-appearing stricture at the site of the anastomosis, which was treated with a series of esophageal dilations and temporary placement of a stent. The stent was later replaced with a 100 mm x 23 mm Wallflex PC-SEMS in an attempt for a permanent solution to the patient's dysphagia. However, the patient developed recurrent symptoms after 3 months, and a CT scan showed evidence of circumferential soft tissue almost occluding the proximal side of the stent. The patient was once again subjected to a stent replacement.

After undergoing cryoablation of the tissue ingrowth with the CryoSpray Ablation, the patient underwent placement of a 125 mm x 23 mm Wallflex FC-SEMS within the previously placed PC-SEMS to promote tissue necrosis and permit subsequent removal of both stents. A rescue FC-SEMS was removed after 2 weeks on repeat endoscopy, with less tissue ingrowth visible on the proximal end and with no stricture evident. An attempt was made to remove the PC-SEMS but was unsuccessful. Another 125 mm x 23 mm Wallflex FC-SEMS was placed within the embedded PC-SEMS. A repeat endoscopy was performed at 6 months with successful retrieval of both the FC-SEMS and PC-SEMS with minimal resistance with the help of rat-tooth forceps under fluoroscopic guidance.

Discharge Condition:
The patient is reported to have been symptom-free and was started on high dose oral proton pump inhibitor with a slow taper to a low daily dose.
output: The 72-year-old male patient with a history of localized esophageal carcinoma underwent neoadjuvant chemoradiation and esophagectomy in the past. The patient was referred to the institution for management of recurrent dysphagia and subsequent stent removal. The patient underwent multiple stent placements, cryoablation of tissue ingrowth, and insertion of a 125 mm x 23 mm Wallflex FC-SEMS within the embedded stents for tissue necrosis, which allowed successful removal of both stents six months later. The patient was symptom-free after discharge and placed on a high dose oral proton pump inhibitor with a slow taper to a low daily dose.

The margins of the fistula were elevated and excised before bladder and uterus were drawn together with fine sutures. The uterus was closed with a 2-0 polyglycolic acid suture, and the bladder with 3-0 suture. A 3-way Foley catheter (20 Fr) was inserted into the bladder while fibrin sealant patch and omental flap interposed between the uterus and bladder. Postoperative care was provided to the patient for 10 days. The patient's operation was uneventful, with no intraoperative and postoperative complications. The total operative time was 150 min, with blood loss less than 100 ml during the first postoperative day.

The patient was admitted for surgical repair of the VUF. The surgery had no complications, and the patient's pain was managed with analgesic regimens. The patient's urine output was well-maintained with a 3-way Foley catheter (20 Fr) inserted into the bladder, which was removed 30 days after the surgery. The patient was discharged in stable condition with a recommendation for follow-up at 3, 6, and 12 months.

instruction: What named entities related to the patient's neurological deterioration can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted due to a 2-day history of mild dysarthria and naming impairment with difficulty finding words and holding a conversation. Furthermore, his family reported at least one-month history of motor awkwardness and gait instability. During the neurological examination, the patient displayed fluent, coherent spontaneous language and had mild dysnomia. He was diagnosed with Parkinsonism.

Further investigations revealed increased signal intensity in the left putamen with diffusion restriction, suggesting lacunar infarction. Parkinsonism was also studied using 123I-ioflupane SPECT, which revealed asymmetrical tracer uptake in the caudate nuclei and a near-complete lack of activity in the putamina, particularly on the left side. 

Progression was poor, and the patient was readmitted to the hospital. An EEG revealed short-interval lateralized interictal epileptiform discharges in the left hemisphere. The patient went into a coma and was admitted to the intensive care unit. An additional MRI revealed progression of the lesions, with a patchy, gyriform hyperintensity predominantly affecting the cortex of the left hemisphere and the right temporoparietal cortex, visible in diffusion sequences only.

A diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was reached based on the patient's rapid neurological deterioration, the presence of myoclonus, and MRI findings. The patient died 5 months after disease onset. Autopsy was not granted.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was admitted with symptoms of mild dysarthria, naming impairment, motor awkwardness, and gait instability. The patient's neurological examination revealed fluent, coherent spontaneous language, mild dysnomia, and clinical symptoms of parkinsonism. Further investigations, including a brain MRI, echocardiogram, Holter monitoring, and Doppler ultrasound of the supra-aortic trunks were performed, which showed no significant abnormalities.

However, the patient's condition deteriorated quickly, and they were readmitted to the hospital. The patient went into a coma and was admitted to the intensive care unit. After further investigations, a diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was reached based on the patient's rapid neurological deterioration, the presence of myoclonus, and MRI findings.

The patient passed away 5 months after the onset of the disease, and autopsy was not granted.
output: Based on the given discharge summary, the named entities related to the patient's neurological deterioration are Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, myoclonus, and the MRI findings showing patchy, gyriform hyperintensity predominantly affecting the cortex of the left hemisphere and the right temporoparietal cortex.

instruction: What was the treatment approach and subsequent therapy provided for the patient suffering from Guillain-Barré syndrome, which ultimately led to the successful weaning off the mechanical ventilation and discharge? (related to Relation Extraction)
input:
Patient Identification:
The patient is a 33-year-old male without comorbidities who was admitted to the hospital reporting fever and paresthesia in the feet upwards.

Admission:
The patient was admitted to the ICU with dyspnea, pneumonia, and complaints of persistent muscular pain. His laboratory tests showed a positive serology for the Zika virus.

Hospital Course:
The patient developed acute respiratory insufficiency type II, which required orotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. He was subsequently diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome from a cerebrospinal fluid sample, which led to his prolonged mechanical ventilation for 25 days. The patient underwent intravenous immunoglobulin administration for 5 days without improvement.

On day 26 of mechanical ventilation, an inspiratory muscle training program was initiated with an electronic isokinetic loading device. The program progressed to 60 efforts daily, and the MIP increased from 11cmH2O to 85cmH2O over several weeks. The IMT program was accompanied by an early mobilization and physical therapy protocol, ultimately leading to successful weaning off the ventilator and discharge.

Discharge:
After 71 days of hospitalization, the patient was discharged.

Summary:
The patient was admitted to the ICU with respiratory insufficiency and was placed on mechanical ventilation due to Guillain-Barré syndrome. The patient underwent intravenous immunoglobulin administration for 5 days. After 26 days of mechanical ventilation, an inspiratory muscle training program was initiated, which led to successful weaning off the ventilator and discharge after 71 days of hospitalization.
output: The treatment approach for the patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome was an inspiratory muscle training program initiated on day 26 of mechanical ventilation, which progressed to 60 efforts daily and accompanied by early mobilization and physical therapy protocol. This led to successful weaning off the ventilator and discharge after 71 days of hospitalization.

input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 41-year-old HIV-1-infected male farmer
Hospital Course:
September 2016 - diagnosed with pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonitis (PJP) and successfully treated with co-trimoxazole and prednisolone.
Current Admission:
Presented with a five-day history of right hypochondriac abdominal pain associated with decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, and icterus. A physical examination was unremarkable except for icterus and hepatomegaly. Fundoscopy did not reveal retinitis. Hepatomegaly with grade I-II intrahepatic biliary dilatation with a focal parenchymal lesion was seen on abdominal ultrasound. An ERCP was performed revealing a stenosis with CBD stricture, consistent with AIDS cholangiopathy. Papillotomy was performed, and a CBD stent was placed for biliary drainage. A bile aspirate was negative for Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium, Cyclospora, and Mycobacterium. Brush cytology of the stricture revealed inflammatory cells and pigment-laden macrophages with no acid-fast organisms. Histopathological examination of ampullary biopsy showed focal ulcerations with superficial mucosal necrosis and acute and chronic inflammation in the mucosa and lamina propria. Submucosal Brunner's glands showed nucleomegaly with eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic cytoplasmic inclusions.
Treatment and Outcome:
The patient had immediate symptomatic relief and did not receive any anti-CMV treatment. Liver enzymes normalised 2 weeks later. The CD4 count improved to 363 cells/μL with HIV viral load of 423 copies/ml after 6 months. Repeat ERCP revealed a normal cholangiogram with no residual stricture in the lower CBD, and cells from ampullary biopsies did not reveal intranuclear/cytoplasmic inclusions. The ART was switched.
Follow-up:
A repeat viral load after 8 months was <50 copies/ml. The patient was discharged in stable condition. Appropriate outpatient follow-up was arranged.

instruction: What diagnostic testing and clinical findings supported the diagnosis of Mycobacterium chimaera infection in the 67-year-old male patient?
input:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: December 26, 2017
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 67-year-old male, presented with shortness of breath on exertion and persistent cough for three weeks. He reported a productive cough with white to yellow sputum. The patient experienced chest tightness and heaviness along with orthopnea, and waking up in the middle of the night due to shortness of breath. Review of systems was negative for palpitations, chills, night sweats, dizziness, recent travel, contact with birds, exposure to tuberculosis, and contact with wild animals. Physical examination findings of a barrel-shaped chest and poor air exchange supported a diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In addition, a chest x-ray exhibited right-sided apical opacity. The patient underwent computed tomography angiography (CTA), which was negative for pulmonary embolism, while patchy reticulonodular opacities consistent with infiltrates were present in the right upper, right middle, right lower, and left upper lobe. These findings led to a diagnosis of cavitary pneumonia, and further workup was conducted to determine the underlying cause. Blood cultures, mycoplasma IgM, HIV-1 and HIV-2 were ordered, and the QuantiFERON®-TB Gold test (QFT-G) was used to check for tuberculosis. Bronchoscopy with biopsies was performed to yield a necrotic black specimen, and testing confirmed the diagnosis of Mycobacterium chimaera infection.

Clinical Findings:
Upon admission, the patient's blood pressure ranged from 95/57 to 125/63 mmHg, a heart rate of 98 beats per minute, respiration rate of 19 breaths per minute, and temperature of 97.3 F. His oxygen saturation was 94% on room air. Pulmonary function tests revealed a Gold 3 category with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV-1) of 41%, forced vital capacity (FVC) of 69%, and an FEV-1/FVC ratio of 47%. Bicarbonate, electrolytes, platelets, and transaminases were within normal limits.

Hospital Course and Treatment:
The infectious disease team was consulted and provided expertise and recommendations for a complete workup. The patient was optimized on his respiratory regimen and treatments were initiated according to the diagnosis. Communication and coordination with the infectious disease team was conducted throughout the patient’s hospital stay.

Discharge instructions and follow-up care:
The patient was counseled on his diagnosis, treatments, and the need for ongoing follow-up appointments for his COPD. He was also instructed to adhere to treatments prescribed by the infectious disease team. The patient was scheduled for a chest computed tomography (CT) in three months to assess disease resolution and any need for treatment adjustments. 

Summary:
The patient presented with symptoms of shortness of breath and persistent cough. Upon diagnosis, he was discovered to have Mycobacterium chimaera and received appropriate treatments from the infectious disease team. The patient was counseled on his diagnosis, treatments, and the need for ongoing follow-up appointments for his COPD. Communication was maintained between the various healthcare providers throughout the patient's hospital stay. The patient was discharged with instructions for follow-up care including scheduling a chest CT in three months to assess disease resolution and any need for treatment adjustments.
output: The diagnosis of Mycobacterium chimaera infection was supported by the bronchoscopy with biopsies that yielded a necrotic black specimen, which was confirmed by testing. Additionally, blood cultures, mycoplasma IgM, HIV-1 and HIV-2 testing, and QuantiFERON®-TB Gold test (QFT-G) were negative. Clinical findings included pulmonary function tests revealing a Gold 3 category with an FEV-1 of 41%, FVC of 69%, and an FEV-1/FVC ratio of 47%, along with right-sided apical opacity on chest x-ray and patchy reticulonodular opacities consistent with infiltrates present in the right upper, right middle, right lower, and left upper lobe on computed tomography angiography (CTA).

On ocular examination, visual acuity was 6/5 in both eyes, and she had a temporal subconjunctival hemorrhage as the only ocular finding. The left eye worm she had seen earlier was no longer present.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and management plan for a 3-year-old boy admitted with severe respiratory distress and a large mediastinal mass compressing the neck vessels and airway?

Management: Corticosteroids were started because of respiratory distress and superior vena cava syndrome. After three days, the patient became stable enough to be discharged. The patient is to be followed up in the outpatient clinic for ongoing management of his condition.

Condition on Discharge: The patient was discharged in a stable condition, and arrangements were made for outpatient management.
output: The diagnosis for the 3-year-old boy with severe respiratory distress and a large mediastinal mass compressing the neck vessels and airway was in favor of neurofibromatosis, as indicated by an incisional biopsy taken from the neck mass. The patient had a postoperative BCVA of 20/40 with -2.0 cyl 90° on the first day after surgery in the left eye. The patient's bilateral cataracts were successfully treated with surgical interventions. The patient was very pleased with the visual results and improvement in his eyesight. output: The toric IOL AcrySof IQ Toric SN6AT8 was implanted in the left eye with a target refraction of -2.26D.

instruction: What was the eventual diagnosis of the patient's left facial condition, and what treatment protocols were implemented to manage the condition?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 25-year-old female with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus who was urgently referred to plastic surgery for possible necrotizing soft-tissue infection of her left orbitomaxillary region. The patient had been admitted to the hospital seven days prior for a suspected bacterial sinusitis and diabetic ketoacidosis. Following stabilization, the patient was discharged on oral doxycycline. The patient returned to the hospital with two days of worsening left facial pain, left facial droop, profound edema, and grayish discoloration to the skin to the left orbital region.

Physical Exam:
At the time of plastic surgery assessment, all vital signs were within normal limits, with no evidence of fever. Marked left facial edema, erythema, and an area of grayish skin involving the left face and ear were present. Cranial nerve examination demonstrated a left-sided unilateral facial nerve palsy and lack of left trigeminal nerve sensation (V1-2). The left neck was tender, with palpable cervical adenopathy. Laboratory investigations revealed leukocytosis and elevated blood glucose levels.

Diagnostic Results:
The computed tomography scan revealed nonspecific subcutaneous tissue stranding with no subcutaneous gas or localized collections. Maxillary sinusitis was improving, when compared with imaging from her prior admission. Intraoperative cultures for anaerobic and aerobic bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungal organisms all demonstrated no growth. However, numerous repeat cultures were negative, and the eventual diagnosis was made on tissue biopsy, positive for fungal hyphae, and polymerase chain reaction, confirming a diagnosis of orbitomaxillofacial mucormycosis with Rhizopus oryzae approximately 2 weeks after presentation.

Treatment:
The patient underwent 11 debridements for progressing left facial necrosis over the following 6 weeks, with adjunct measure implemented including wound irrigation and dressing with amphotericin B deoxylate, exclusion of the exposed middle ear, and intravenous amphotericin B liposomal injection for systemic rhinomucormycosis coverage. Additionally, hyperbaric oxygen therapy was instituted but discontinued after 3 sessions due to left-sided mandibular pain and patient intolerance.

Outcome:
Vascular thrombosis progressed to involve the entire left external carotid artery and all terminal branches. Final soft-tissue deficit included the left middle ear, large portion of the external ear, temporal bone and facial nerve, parotid gland, mastoid sinus, maxillary sinus, ethmoid sinus, sphenoid sinus, upper eyelid and brow, facial muscles, superior oblique muscle, trochlea, overlying facial muscles, subcutaneous tissue and skin. Reconstruction with an anterolateral thigh flap and skin graft was used to cover the large remaining soft-tissue deficit. The patient stayed in the hospital for an extended period due to acute renal failure, which required hemodialysis, and ongoing volatile glucose control. Finally, after all the treatment protocols, the patient was discharged from the hospital in a stable condition.
output: The eventual diagnosis of the patient's left facial condition was orbitomaxillofacial mucormycosis with Rhizopus oryzae. The patient underwent 11 debridements for progressing left facial necrosis over 6 weeks, with adjunctive measures including wound irrigation and dressing with amphotericin B deoxylate. Intravenous amphotericin B liposomal injection was used for systemic rhinomucormycosis coverage, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy was also initiated but later discontinued due to patient intolerance and left-sided mandibular pain. Reconstruction was done using an anterolateral thigh flap and skin graft to cover the large remaining soft-tissue deficit.

The patient presented with chronic headache with infrequent exacerbations that gradually worsened and associated with vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. During the hospital course, the patient experienced a marked improvement of her headache and was able to perform daily activities normally. After a year of anti-TB medication and follow-up, she did not complain of any worsening of symptoms.

Dural tuberculosis.

Hospital Course:

An 81-year-old female patient was admitted to the Department of Surgery with a chief complaint of right breast erythema and edema, with over two weeks duration and progressive worsening. The patient reported that this condition was associated with an episode of breast trauma, and she denied having any previous breast nodules, nipple drainage, nipple retraction, fever, or constitutional symptoms. The patient was multiparous (three pregnancies and three births) and nursed all children. The patient had multiple medical co-morbidities but had no past history of breast pathology or family history of breast malignancy.

On physical examination, the patient demonstrated mammary asymmetry because the right breast was bigger and tender. The outer quadrants and the periareolar region had inflammatory signs with orange peel skin. There was no palpable mass or nipple changes. The left breast was normal. She had the right upper limb swollen and palpable axillar and supraclavicular lymph nodes.

Ultrasound of the right breast revealed skin thickening and tissue densification, involving principally the external quadrants, and it was identified an irregular hypoechoic mass with 8 cm × 5 cm. Multiple axillary and supraclavicular enlarged lymph nodes were observed. The ultrasound of the left breast and of the left axilla was normal.

The core needle biopsy of an axillary lymph node and of the breast mass identified morphological and immunophenotypic features consistent with diagnosis of primary non-Hodgkin DLBCL.

CT scan of the chest confirmed right breast alterations identified in ultrasound and ipsilateral axillary and supraclavicular lymph nodes enlargement. No other enlarged lymph nodes were observed. CT scans of the brain, abdomen and pelvis were normal. Bone marrow aspiration was negative. Serum lactate dehydrogenase level was normal.

The patient was diagnosed with primary non-Hodgkin DLBCL. The therapy plan included R-CHOP x8. The patient also received radiotherapy (4500 cGY) to the breast and regional lymph nodes with 180 cGY daily fractions.

The patient was monitored closely during treatment and showed no evidence of residual disease after 24 months. The patient was discharged from the hospital with no additional complications.

The patient's condition improved significantly with treatment and is now ready for discharge.

The patient is advised to complete the course of antibiotics as prescribed. Routine monitoring of blood sugar levels and HbA1c is also recommended to manage diabetes mellitus. instruction: What relation extraction can be inferred from the discharge summary regarding the patient's Burkitt's lymphoma diagnosis, involvement of the thyroid gland, and successful treatment with Hyper-CVAD chemotherapy?
input:
Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for evaluation of a growing thyroid mass and was subsequently diagnosed with Burkitt’s lymphoma with involvement of the thyroid gland. The patient was successfully treated with chemotherapy with Hyper-CVAD and had complete resolution of the thyroid mass. The patient remained disease-free at regular follow-up.

History and Physical Examination:

The patient is a 52-year-old woman with a history of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis who presented with a rapidly growing thyroid mass which obstructed her airway. On examination, there was a large, firm thyroid nodule with absence of calcifications. The patient was otherwise in good health.

Diagnostic Studies:

Further investigations revealed a solid hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe of the gland, with significant internal vascularity on thyroid ultrasonography. The FNA cytology showed only atypical lymphoid cells with no thyrocytes and the specimens were considered suggestive of a lymphoproliferative disorder but insufficient to make a diagnosis, such that a CNB was scheduled for the following day. A subsequent CNB showed that normal thyrocytes were virtually all replaced by homogeneous medium-sized lymphocytes with scanty blue cytoplasm, round nuclei, coarse chromatin, and multiple small nucleoli. The CT of chest and abdomen showed the thyroid nodule with left tracheal deviation. Bone marrow biopsy showed almost 100% lymphoid infiltration, consisting of a population of intermediate-sized blast-like cells, with prominent nucleoli, which were replacing all normal cells. These cells expressed CD10, CD20, and were negative for Bcl2, CD34, and TdT.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital’s Haematology Unit and received 3 cycles of Hyper-CVAD chemotherapy which were completed in five months. The therapeutic regimen was successful and the thyroid mass disappeared. The platelets returned to baseline levels. The patient was closely monitored during the entire course of treatment and achieved full remission.

Follow-up and Prognosis:

At 60 months after diagnosis the patient is alive and remains disease-free at regular follow-up. The patient was scheduled to undergo regular follow-up, including laboratory tests and diagnostic imaging to monitor any recurrence or progression of lymphoma. Further management will be tailored to the patient’s ongoing health status and clinical condition.
output: Based on the given discharge summary, it can be inferred that the patient was diagnosed with Burkitt's lymphoma with involvement of the thyroid gland, and was successfully treated with Hyper-CVAD chemotherapy, resulting in complete resolution of the thyroid mass. The patient remained disease-free at regular follow-up, with ongoing monitoring scheduled to detect any possible recurrence or progression of lymphoma.

instruction: What relation can be extracted from the discharge summary regarding the efficacy of radiosurgical thalamotomy using GK on the VIM of the left thalamus in treating the patient's tremors due to FXTAS?
input:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [patient's name]
Medical Record Number: [patient's number]
Age: 73   Sex: Male
Date of admission: [admission date]
Date of Discharge: [Date of discharge]
Discharge Diagnosis: FXTAS

Hospital Course:
A 73-year-old male patient was admitted to the Department of Neurology due to tremors of the head, neck, and upper limbs, along with moderate tremors of the lower limbs. Initial symptoms appeared 20 years prior, primarily as a kinetic tremor of the left upper and lower limbs. During a neurological examination, the patient also presented dysarthria, paresis of the right facial nerve, brisk reflexes on the right side, bilateral dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesis, truncal ataxia, ataxia of lower limbs which was more significant on the left side, and unstable gait. Psychological examination exposed mild cognitive impairment and deficits of executive functions.

An MRI in 2016 revealed bilateral hyperintensity in the cerebellar hemispheres and the MCP. The combination of intention tremor, ataxia, MCP sign, and gait instability of the patient's son and daughter instigated the diagnosis of FXTAS. Use of the Amplide X FMR1 PCR kit for extended molecular examination revealed permutations in the FMR1 gene. The diagnosis of FXTAS with expansion of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene was confirmed.

Radiosurgical thalamotomy using GK on the VIM of the left thalamus was performed due to insufficient effects of pharmacological treatments (primidone and propranolol) to treat the tremors. The Leksell Gamma Knife Perfexion model was used, and a maximum dose of 130 Gy was delivered with a single, fully opened 4-mm collimator. A control examination was done 6 months after GK thalamotomy, which showed improvement observed 4 months after the procedure.

Comparison of tremor intensity before and after the procedure was done using the FTRS and the Tremor Rating Scale. The case presented in this study showed an improvement in both rating scales. The most significant change was observed in the right side corresponding to the lesion. Neurological examination showed that features remained unchanged or insignificantly changed. Psychological examination did not present any relevant changes. Physiotherapist's examination revealed certain changes in the period before and after thalamotomy. Deterioration in certain features of the examination performed by the physiotherapist were associated with the progressive nature of FXTAS.

Follow-up and plan of action:
Patient was discharged on [Date of Discharge] with instructions to follow up with their primary care physician and Neurologist as needed. Instruction given to join rehabilitation therapy for further improvement in the quality of life.
output: The discharge summary suggests that radiosurgical thalamotomy using GK on the VIM of the left thalamus was effective in treating the patient's tremors due to FXTAS, as evidenced by improvement observed on both the FTRS and the Tremor Rating Scale. However, the physiotherapist's examination revealed some deterioration in certain features, likely due to the progressive nature of FXTAS. The plan of action is for the patient to follow up with their primary care physician and Neurologist as needed and join rehabilitation therapy for further improvement in the quality of life.

This 42-year-old male patient was admitted to the emergency room with sudden loss of consciousness for half an hour. He had been experiencing headaches, blurring vision in the left eye, and vomiting for the past month. The patient was drowsy, confused, and irritable. General physical examination was unremarkable, but there was a relative afferent pupillary defect in the left eye. Optic fundus examination showed bilateral papilloedema, while visual assessment showed no perception of light in the left eye and a visual acuity of 6/24 in the right eye. 

CT scan revealed a heterogeneous lesion in the suprasellar region that extended into the left basifrontal region and left orbit, with peripheral tram-track-like calcification. A widened optic canal and thickened, tortuous optic nerve sheath complex was seen, with minimal hydrocephalus. MRI showed a large, ill-defined lesion in the suprasellar region, extending into the left basifrontal region, with significant mass effect on the anterior aspect of the left lateral ventricle and obstructive hydrocephalus. There was also cerebral edema, with the lesion extending into the interpeduncular cistern. 

The patient was taken for emergency surgery and underwent left frontal craniotomy with decompression of the tumor. A sample was taken for histopathology, which revealed anaplastic oligoastrocytoma with multiple necrotic areas and varying consistency with gritty calcification. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt tube was placed for relieving hydrocephalus, and the patient was treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy and chemotherapy with temozolomide.  

Overall, the patient remained hospitalized throughout the hospital course for treatment and observation. The team closely monitored their condition and provided necessary interventions to alleviate symptoms, such as surgical decompression and medication management. The patient was discharged after completing the treatment regimen and recovering well. They were advised to have regular follow-up appointments with the specialists to monitor their condition and make necessary changes to their treatment plan.
output: The observed lesion in the suprasellar region with gritty calcification seen on CT scan was confirmed to be anaplastic oligoastrocytoma with multiple necrotic areas by histopathology.

The patient exhibited pulsus paradoxus, distant heart sounds without murmurs or gallops, marked jugular venous distension, diminished breath sounds at the bases and mild bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. An electrocardiogram showed low voltage, and a chest radiograph indicated an enlarged cardiac silhouette and bilateral moderate pleural effusions. An echocardiogram demonstrated moderate to large pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. 

Management:
Pericardiocentesis was performed, draining 1200 cc of bloody fluid. Follow-up echocardiogram showed resolution of the pericardial effusion. The patient's blood pressure normalized after pericardiocentesis. 

Findings:
Right heart catheterization showed severely elevated right-sided pressures and equalization of right atrial, right ventricular, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with diminished cardiac output. Following pericardial drainage, there was significant improvement in right-sided pressures, with a mean right atrial pressure of 10 mm Hg down from 21 mm Hg.

Further workup was done to identify the etiology of the pericardial effusion, including fluid cytology, culture, lactate dehydrogenase, serum antinuclear antibodies, serum complement, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, anti-double-stranded DNA, and anti-Smith antibody. Analysis of the pericardial fluid showed exudative fluid, and it was negative for malignant cells.

Summary:
The patient's shortness of breath was attributed to a pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. After draining 1200 cc of pericardial fluid, the patient's blood pressure normalized, and right-sided pressures improved significantly. The etiology of the pericardial effusion was not determined. The patient was discharged in stable condition with follow-up appointments scheduled with her primary care physician.

After one hour of monitoring, the patient's upper lip swelling gradually decreased over the following hours. The patient was discharged five days later and prescribed a thrice daily dose of prednisolone (tapered as 20 mg, 10 mg, and 5 mg), along with a twice daily peroral dose of cetirizine for ten days. The patient was advised to notify the hospital immediately if the swelling re-occurred, and to continue taking the nifedipine and hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension management.

Follow-up:
One week from the date of discharge, the patient was reviewed and observed to be symptom-free. On subsequent follow-up after three weeks, a significant resolution of the swelling was observed, and the patient remained symptom-free. The patient was advised to continue any medication as prescribed and to see a physician if any new symptoms occurred.

Summary: 
The patient was diagnosed with enalapril-induced angioedema, was treated and monitored, and was eventually discharged with a peroral prescription. On follow-up examinations, the patient remained symptom-free and was advised to notify the hospital of any new symptoms.
output: The observed edema in the patient's upper lip was caused by enalapril-induced angioedema, which was managed by withholding enalapril, administering dexamethasone, and prescribing prednisolone and cetirizine. The patient's medication was adjusted upon discharge to a thrice daily dose of prednisolone and a twice daily peroral dose of cetirizine for ten days, with follow-up examinations at one and three weeks showing significant resolution of the swelling and the patient remaining symptom-free. The patient, a 21-year-old female with primary ciliary dyskinesia and situs ambiguus, was admitted electively for a diagnostic laparoscopy due to a history of recurrent subacute bowel obstructions. Intraoperatively, extensive jejunal adhesions were found, which required conversion from a laparoscopic to an open procedure. Adhesiolysis and appendicectomy were performed.

Post-Operative Course:
In the early post-operative period, the patient experienced a prolonged ileus with intractable vomiting and high nasogastric tube output. As she was unable to tolerate oral nutrition, it was decided to start her on total parenteral nutrition (TPN), for which a peripherally inserted central venous catheter (PICC) insertion was requested. The PICC was successfully inserted under fluoroscopic guidance using a modified Seldinger technique. TPN was commenced and the patient’s ileus gradually resolved.

Complications:
On the ninth day following PICC insertion, the patient experienced dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. A chest radiograph showed a small right-sided pleural effusion and coiling of the PICC within the SVC. A CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) was requested, which showed large bilateral pleural effusions, moderate-sized pericardial effusion, mediastinal effusion, and pneumomediastinum. Bilateral intercostal chest drains were inserted into the chest to remove accumulated TPN solution, and the PICC was removed. The patient was transferred to a cardiothoracic centre and made a good recovery. She was discharged home a week after the removal of the PICC.
output: Using Named Entity Recognition in the provided discharge summary, the identified Named Entities related to adhesiolysis and appendicectomy are "extensive jejunal adhesions" and "appendicectomy".
