instruction: What was the patient's treatment plan and response to chemotherapy after switching to cladribine and Dasatinib in the given discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient was a 47-year-old female with a history of ulcerative colitis, Sjogren’s syndrome, migraines, and fibromyalgia who presented with a 6 month history of left lower extremity paresthesia followed by a 2 month history of progressive headaches, imbalance, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, and diplopia. She was promptly started on steroids, admitted to the hospital, and underwent a midline suboccipital craniotomy for debulking of a large intracerebellar tumor. Upon entering the cystic cavity, grossly purulent material without hemorrhage was noted, and a subtotal resection was achieved. Final pathology rendered the diagnosis of primary CNS histiocytic sarcoma.
Post-operative MRI showed continued bilateral-enhancement along multiple cranial nerves, concerning for leptomeningeal spread. A staging PET scan was performed two weeks following surgery suggesting diffuse leptomeningeal spread, which was confirmed by spinal MRI. Due to progressive lower back pain, the patient initiated radiation therapy including whole brain radiotherapy followed by a posterior fossa boost and a gross tumor boost. Interval follow up MRI showed a partial response with near-complete resolution of previous leptomeningeal enhancement. Chemotherapy with high CNS penetrating therapeutic agents including high-dose methotrexate, high-dose Ara-C, and thiotepa followed by high-dose chemotherapy with BCNU and thiotepa rescued by autologous stem cell transplantation was initiated, but was poorly tolerated after one cycle due to patient intolerance. The patient was then switched to cladribine, which was better tolerated. However, within two weeks after the completion of this infusion, the patient developed symptoms of malignant meningitis and was started on IV antibiotics.
The patient underwent further radiation therapy targeting C4-C6 and T1-T7 for new lesions consistent with metastatic disease in the untreated cervical spinal cord and thoracic vertebrae, including intramedullary involvement. The patient was then started on Dasatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor with known CNS penetration, but was poorly tolerated because of nausea, diarrhea, and acute pancreatitis and was discontinued after one week. CT images of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed progressive bilateral pulmonary nodules. An MRI of the spine showed persistent but significantly improved leptomeningeal enhancement.
Due to progression of symptoms, worsening systemic disease despite control of CNS disease, and limited systemic options available, the patient chose to enroll in hospice. 

Hospital Course Summary:
47-year-old female with a history of ulcerative colitis, Sjogren’s syndrome, migraines, and fibromyalgia presented with a 6 month history of left lower extremity paresthesia followed by a 2 month history of progressive headaches, imbalance, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, and diplopia. She underwent a midline suboccipital craniotomy for debulking of a large intracerebellar tumor diagnosed as primary CNS histiocytic sarcoma, which had leptomeningeal spread. She initiated radiation therapy and chemotherapy but was poorly tolerated and switched to cladribine and Dasatinib. Due to progression of symptoms, worsening systemic disease despite control of CNS disease, and limited systemic options available, the patient chose to enroll in hospice.
output: The discharge summary states that the patient was poorly tolerated to chemotherapy with high CNS penetrating therapeutic agents, and was switched to cladribine and Dasatinib. However, it is reported that Dasatinib was poorly tolerated and discontinued after one week due to nausea, diarrhea, and acute pancreatitis. There is no information provided in the given discharge summary regarding the patient's response to cladribine after switching from the previous chemotherapeutic agents.

instruction: What Named Entities related to breast cancer and lymph nodes can be recognized through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?

Discharge Summary:

Admitting Diagnosis: Palpable right axillary mass
Discharge Diagnosis: Bilateral breast cancer consisting of occult right breast cancer with axillary metastasis (TxN1M0) and early-stage left breast cancer (T1bN0M0)

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a palpable right axillary mass. A 14-gauge core-needle biopsy revealed the right axillary lymph node as a metastatic carcinoma, possibly from the breast, with positive estrogen receptor (ER) status. Breast MRI showed a 0.6-cm irregular enhancing mass in the left upper inner breast, assessed as breast imaging reporting and data system (BI-RADS) category 4C. Second-look US confirmed the mass as an invasive carcinoma of no special type, same as that of right axillary metastasis. Subsequently, the patient underwent right axillary lymph node dissection and left breast conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy. Histologic findings of cancer cells in all three lymph nodes of the right axilla were fairly different from those of cancer cells in the left breast, indicating that the metastasis to the right axillary lymph node did not originate from the left breast cancer, although both of them showed ER positivity. Metastatic cancer cells in the right axilla were also positive for gross cystic disease fluid protein-15 (GCDFP-15) and GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3), suggesting that the metastasis was derived from the breast. Finally, the patient received four cycles of doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide followed by four cycles of taxane (AC-T) chemotherapy and radiation therapy for each breast and hormone therapy.

Evaluation and Management:
The patient received prompt and appropriate evaluation and management of her right axillary mass, invasive carcinoma of no special type in the left upper inner breast, and macrometastatic lymph nodes in the right axilla. The patient underwent right axillary lymph node dissection and left breast conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy, followed by appropriate treatment based on the final diagnosis.

Hospital Course and Discharge Status:
The patient's postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged in stable condition. No recurrence or metastasis was observed 14 months postoperatively.

Follow-up:
The patient will be followed up regularly with appropriate imaging studies to monitor for any recurrence of the cancer. She will also continue hormonal therapy, as appropriate.

instruction: What was the reason for resuming continuous intravenous fentanyl infusion in the patient and how was the opioid tapered off without causing withdrawal symptoms?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]

Admission Date: [redacted]

Discharge Date: [redacted]

Medical History:

The patient is a 43-year-old male with a medical history significant for hepatocellular carcinoma who underwent liver transplantation from a living donor.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital for severe acute pancreatitis with severe abdominal pain. Continuous intravenous infusion of fentanyl at 1200 μg/day was started to control abdominal pain. The fentanyl dose was increased according to pain intensity, reaching 2400 μg/day (MED 240 mg/day) after 10 days in the hospital. Administration of a pancreatic enzyme inhibitor, antibiotic, and fluid alleviated the pancreatitis and abdominal pain.

The patient subsequently developed nausea/vomiting, elevated blood pressure, and restlessness 12 hours after discontinuation of continuous intravenous fentanyl infusion. Continuous intravenous fentanyl infusion of 240 μg/day was resumed, and these symptoms disappeared.

The patient was then switched to a transdermal fentanyl patch to taper the opioid more slowly. Pancreatitis with abdominal pain recurred transiently one month later, and therefore, continuous intravenous fentanyl infusion was resumed, titrated to 600 μg/day. The dose was gradually decreased daily (600, 300, 240, 180, 120, and 60 μg/day).

Once the pancreatitis had improved, the fentanyl could be discontinued without causing withdrawal symptoms. The discontinuation was finally completed 64 days after the onset of withdrawal symptoms.

Final Diagnosis:

Severe acute pancreatitis with severe abdominal pain secondary to hepatocellular carcinoma and liver transplantation.

Summary:

The patient was admitted to the hospital for severe acute pancreatitis with severe abdominal pain, and continuous intravenous infusion of fentanyl was initiated to control the pain. The patient experienced withdrawal symptoms after discontinuation of the fentanyl infusion, and therefore, a transdermal fentanyl patch was initiated to taper the opioid more slowly. The fentanyl infusion was successfully discontinued without causing withdrawal symptoms 64 days after the onset of withdrawal symptoms. The patient was discharged home in stable condition.
output: The reason for resuming continuous intravenous fentanyl infusion in the patient was due to the development of withdrawal symptoms such as nausea/vomiting, elevated blood pressure, and restlessness. The opioid was tapered off by switching to a transdermal fentanyl patch and gradually decreasing the daily dose from 600 μg/day to 60 μg/day, without causing withdrawal symptoms. The discontinuation was finally achieved 64 days after the onset of withdrawal symptoms.

instruction: What was the cause of the patient's extrahepatic portosystemic connection, and what was the diagnosis given to the patient upon discharge?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 68 years

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the haematology clinic with left-sided above-knee deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which was unprovoked. Her medical history included osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and sciatica. She had undergone a subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis for large bowel obstruction due to colonic diverticular disease 16 years ago. Additionally, she had a history of consuming alcohol in large amounts until 4 years ago when her daily intake increased additionally. She also had asymptomatic mild thrombocytopenia since 2006 and mild liver function derangement. A portovenous phase CT scan showed bulky enlargement of the left thyroid lobe with multiple nodules. There was an incidental finding of an extrahepatic portosystemic connection, with an enlarged vein arising from the portal vein, and ultimately draining into the left renal vein.

Assessment and Treatment:
During her hospital stay, a full assessment including physical examination was conducted to rule out any clinical signs of chronic hepatic disease or cardiac abnormalities. There was no evidence of hyperdynamic circulation or audible murmurs on auscultation. The liver was not palpable, and there was no free fluid in the abdomen. There was, however, a mildly enlarged spleen, about 2 cm below the left costal margin; this was also confirmed on the CT images. To further investigate the cause of her extrahepatic portosystemic connection, a non-invasive liver screen with immunoglobulins, autoimmune and viral hepatitis markers were done, along with a fibroscan and endoscopy to look for portal hypertension and varices. The fibroscan showed a median liver stiffness measurement value, which was within the normal range to exclude liver fibrosis. The platelet count on the most recent pathology test was also normal.

Outcome and Follow-up:
Given the findings, chronic liver disease and portal hypertension were ruled out, and a long-standing congenital anomaly was suspected to be the cause of her shunt. The patient was discharged back to the care of her general practitioner without any further follow-up planned, as she was asymptomatic with Type II Abernethy malformation. She was advised to avoid alcohol and monitor the enlargement of the left thyroid lobe with multiple nodules. Further investigations were not indicated. 

Diagnosis:
Type II Abernethy malformation with an extrahepatic portosystemic communication. Left-sided above-knee deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Plan:
Avoid alcohol intake. Monitor the thyroid lobe enlargement with multiple nodules.
output: The patient's extrahepatic portosystemic connection was most likely caused by a long-standing congenital anomaly, which was diagnosed as Type II Abernethy malformation. The instruction given to the patient was to avoid alcohol intake and monitor the enlargement of the left thyroid lobe with multiple nodules. There was no further follow-up planned as she was asymptomatic.

instruction: What Named Entities can be recognized through Named Entity Recognition related to the task of lymphoma diagnosis in this discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary

Patient: 70-year-old male with fatigue and loss of appetite

Medical History: Diabetes Mellitus (DM), hypertension

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with fatigue and loss of appetite. Laboratory examination showed thrombocytopenia and an elevated concentration of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). DM was poorly controlled. Chest X-ray and computed tomography (CT) showed consolidation and surrounding ground-glass shadows in both lungs, and transbronchial lung biopsy was therefore performed. Histopathological analysis revealed diffuse proliferation of medium-sized lymphoid cells leading to the diagnosis of Extranodal Natural Killer/T-cell Lymphoma (ENKL) with Epstein–Barr virus- (EBV-) encoded small RNA (EBER-ISH).

Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was performed to search for other lesions, revealing abnormal uptake in the stomach in addition to the lung lesions. Gastroscopy showed an ulcerative lesion that was biopsied. Histopathological analysis showed diffuse proliferation of large lymphoid cells infiltrating under the mucosa leading to the diagnosis of Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) (nongerminal center B-cell-like type).

The patient was diagnosed with composite lymphoma comprising ENKL and DLBCL. Chemotherapy was initiated with dexamethasone, etoposide, ifosfamide, and carboplatin (DeVIC) plus rituximab. During the clinical course, bone marrow was strongly suppressed and febrile neutropenia occurred. Piperacillin/tazobactam and granulocyte-colony stimulating factors were used, and platelet transfusions were necessary to address severe thrombocytopenia.

After two courses of chemotherapy, gastrointestinal endoscopy showed shrinkage of the ulcerative lesion and elimination of lymphoid cells in the biopsy. On the other hand, lung lesions did not show any improvement, and the chemotherapy regimen was therefore changed. After one course of chemotherapy with gemcitabine, dexamethasone, and cisplatin (GDP), the disease remained progressive and dyspnea appeared. Best supportive care was initiated, and the patient died 3 months after diagnosis.

Diagnoses:

1. Extranodal Natural Killer/T-cell Lymphoma (ENKL) with Epstein–Barr virus- (EBV-) encoded small RNA (EBER-ISH)
2. Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) (nongerminal center B-cell-like type)

Condition at Discharge: Deceased

Follow-up: None.
output: The Named Entities that can be recognized through Named Entity Recognition related to the task of lymphoma diagnosis in this discharge summary are Extranodal Natural Killer/T-cell Lymphoma (ENKL), Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), dexamethasone, etoposide, ifosfamide, carboplatin, rituximab, gemcitabine, cisplatin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and granulocyte-colony stimulating factors.

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Primary Diagnosis: Recurring bladder tumor with adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) differentiation

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) in 2004 and was diagnosed with a high-grade UC with adenocarcinomatous differentiation (pT2a, G2>G3). Following radical cystectomy, only carcinoma in situ (CIS) was found in the surgical specimen, and no lymph node involvement was detected. In 2010, the patient experienced continuous pain and bleeding from the residual vagina, and a tumor was found on the anterior wall of the residual vagina. A biopsy revealed adenocarcinoma, and tumor resection was performed with partial resection of the sigmoid colon. On pathological examination, adenocarcinoma and SCC were detected, which were mostly present in the superficial layer of the TURBT specimen. Based on these findings, the tumor was diagnosed as a recurring bladder tumor. Local recurrence and pelvic bone metastasis were detected 3 months later, and the patient underwent radiation therapy (52 Gy, 26 fractions). In January 2011, the patient developed ileus and subsequently underwent release surgery. Multiple lung metastases and local recurrence in the pelvis developed in June, and the patient died of disease progression the following month.

Summary:
The patient presented with a recurring bladder tumor with adenocarcinoma and SCC differentiation, which was initially diagnosed in 2004. The tumor recurred in 2010, with local recurrence and pelvic bone metastasis detected three months later. Following radiation therapy, the patient developed ileus in January 2011 and underwent release surgery. Multiple lung metastases and local recurrence in the pelvis were detected in June, and the patient subsequently died of disease progression.
output: The patient's prior high-grade transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) with adenocarcinomatous differentiation in 2004 is related to the diagnosis of recurring bladder tumor with adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) differentiation in 2010, as this diagnosis was based on the detection of these two types of cancer cells in the superficial layer of the TURBT specimen.

The patient, a 54-year-old woman with no previous medical history, was admitted to our Emergency Department with complaints of myalgia in the upper and lower limbs, oedema, and fever of 7 days’ duration. The patient was diagnosed clinically with scrub typhus and rhabdomyolysis, which was treated with intravenous fluid and doxycycline. She was observed to have an eschar in the area of the right shin. The patient was initially suspected of having myocarditis due to the rapid increase in cardiac enzymes levels. Pericardial effusion was noted, and pericardiocentesis was performed as a treatment. The pericardial fluid was classified as an exudate, and real-time PCR targeting the O. tsutsugamushi 16S rRNA gene using a pericardial fluid specimen showed a positive result. On day 10 of hospitalization, the patient was confirmed to have rhabdomyolysis. The patient received diuretics and was on a course of doxycycline for 6 days for scrub typhus infection. Conservative therapy was provided for myocarditis. A follow-up TTE revealed normal left ventricular function with no pericardial effusion. The patient was discharged on day 17 of hospitalization after resolution of her presenting symptoms.

Medical history:
The patient had no previous medical history.

Diagnosis:
The patient was clinically diagnosed with scrub typhus with rhabdomyolysis and myocarditis.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with intravenous fluid and doxycycline for scrub typhus and rhabdomyolysis, pericardiocentesis for pericardial effusion, and conservative therapy for myocarditis.

Lab and Radiology data:
Various laboratory tests showed elevated levels of creatine phosphokinase, CK-MB, and troponin I, while normal levels of creatine and potassium were observed. A follow-up TTE revealed normal left ventricular function with no pericardial effusion. The bone scan showed increased soft tissue uptake in both arms and legs.

Outpatient Plan:
Follow-up with the primary care doctor and possible referral to infectious disease specialist.
output: The patient was diagnosed with scrub typhus with rhabdomyolysis and myocarditis, and was treated with intravenous fluid and doxycycline for scrub typhus and rhabdomyolysis, pericardiocentesis for pericardial effusion, and conservative therapy for myocarditis. The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of left-sided foot drop, low back pain and radicular symptoms. Physical examination revealed a significant weakness in the left leg muscles, particularly the tibialis posterior, extensor hallucis longus, and anterior tibialis muscles. Sensory findings indicated decreased detection in the L5 dermatome. Despite the clinical presentation and imaging not classically correlating, the L2-L3 disc was determined to be the etiology of the patient's L5 radiculopathy. Therefore, a left L2-3 microsurgical discectomy was performed, and there were no complications postoperatively.

At the six-week follow-up, the patient's foot drop was near normal, sensation was intact with minimal paresthesias, and he remained pain-free. At the one-year follow-up, the patient experienced full resolution of his foot drop, regained full function and sensation, and remained pain-free.

instruction: What is the relationship between AIN recurrence and the added medication of 1500 mg of oral mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) to the patient's corticosteroid therapy? (related to Relation Extraction)
input:
Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Enter Date]
Discharge Date: [Enter Date]

Patient: [Patient's Name]
Age: 25
Gender: Male
Diagnosis: Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN)

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with complaints of increased serum creatinine levels and no other symptoms. The physical examination did not show any particular findings. Laboratory tests revealed renal dysfunction with elevated C-reactive protein. Urinary markers for tubular injury were also high. Renal biopsy was performed, which showed marked interstitial lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration indicative of AIN. 

The patient's medication history revealed he had been diagnosed with temporal lobe epilepsy 12 years ago and was using carbamazepine, zonisamide, valproate, and lacosamide. After discontinuing zonisamide and starting oral prednisolone, the patient's serum creatinine levels decreased, and prednisolone dose was tapered monthly. However, serum creatinine levels increased again 10 months later, and 67Ga scintigraphy showed AIN recurrence. 

Valproate and lacosamide were discontinued, and oral prednisolone was restarted. Renal function immediately improved, although minor epilepsy occurrence increased. Prednisolone dose was gradually tapered; however, serum creatinine levels rose again after reaching 1.99 mg/dL. Repeat renal biopsy revealed similar findings as tubulitis with both lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrations. 

A dose of 1500 mg of oral mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) was added to the corticosteroid therapy since the patient had multiple AIN recurrence, and was corticosteroid dependent, which was well tolerated. This allowed for successful prednisolone dose tapering to 5 mg daily, serum creatinine level stabilization, and no AIN recurrence for over 20 months.

Discharge Medications:
- Prednisolone 5 mg daily
- Carbamazepine

Follow-Up:
The patient should see the neurologist regularly for epilepsy treatment and continue following up with the nephrology department for AIN recurrence monitoring. 

Codes:
AIN - 593.89
Temporal lobe epilepsy - 345.5 
Carbamazepine - 250237
Zonisamide - 215410
Valproate - 347217
Lacosamide - 471364
output: The added medication of 1500 mg of oral mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) was effective in allowing for successful prednisolone dose tapering to 5 mg daily, serum creatinine level stabilization, and no AIN recurrence for over 20 months. This suggests that the added medication played a crucial role in preventing AIN recurrence and maintaining the patient's renal function.

instruction: What were the interventions and procedures performed to manage the patient's acute right ventricular graft dysfunction that resulted in cardiogenic shock after orthotopic heart transplantation, as determined through relation extraction?

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to fatigue, dyspnea, weight gain, and increased serum creatinine. After receiving inotropic and diuretic therapy, the patient was listed for heart-kidney transplant and transferred to the intensive care unit. On HD 24, the patient underwent orthotopic heart transplantation, which resulted in cardiogenic shock due to acute right ventricular graft dysfunction. During postoperative care, the patient showed significant improvement in volume, cardiovascular status, and renal function.

The patient tolerated all interventions well and was weaned off mechanical ventilation, vasopressin, and ECMO.

Diagnosis and Outcome:
The patient had biventricular systolic heart failure due to ischemic cardiomyopathy and chronic stage IV kidney disease due to diabetic nephropathy. The patient also had antiphospholipid syndrome, multiple myocardial infarctions, and placement of left ventricular assist device. The patient underwent successful orthotopic heart transplantation and deceased-donor renal transplantation, and showed significant improvement in cardiovascular and renal function. The patient was transferred to the posttransplant care unit for further care.

Follow-up and Discharge Instructions:
The patient was provided with instructions on how to care for the transplanted organs, including medication management and postoperative care, and was advised to follow up with his transplant team regularly. The patient was discharged with stable vital signs and improved cardiovascular and renal function.

instruction: What was the treatment course followed for a 40-year-old man diagnosed with rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis complex isolate, and what antibiotics were used to treat the patient after the diagnosis of treatment failure?

A 40-year-old man presented to Chakib Saad Hospital in February 2016 with a three-month cough, and was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. He was previously living in Balbala (Bouldhouqo) in Djibouti, and reported no travel outside Djibouti, no medical, surgical or tuberculosis histories.

Treatment course:
The patient received first-line antituberculosis drugs, but after three months of treatment returned to the hospital with persistent symptoms. The patient was then diagnosed with rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis complex isolate, and was hospitalized with daily kanamycin, moxifloxacin, prothionamide, clofazimine, isoniazid, ethionamide and pyrazinamide, the doses being adjusted to his weight. Direct microscopic examination of the sputum smear after Ziehl-Neelsen staining exhibited acid-fast bacilli. Direct examination of the sputum was positive and a rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis complex isolate was detected by GeneXpert® MTB/RIF lab test. In September 2016, improved clinical course contrasted with the positivity of sputum cultures in MGIT but the patient was readmitted to the hospital in November 2016 for persisting cough.

Summary:
A 40-year-old man presented at Chakib Saad Hospital in February 2016 with a three-month cough and was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. He received first-line antituberculosis drugs, but was diagnosed with rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis complex isolate three months later. After persistent symptoms and improved clinical course, he was diagnosed with treatment failure and treated with a combination of antibiotics and directly observed treatment.

instruction: What named entities related to COVID-19 infections can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: February 2021
Discharge Date: April 2021
Reason for Admission: Persistent fever and non-resolving pneumonia

Brief Hospital course:
The patient, a 35-year-old gentleman, was admitted to our institution in February 2021 due to persistent fever and non-resolving pneumonia caused by probable Organizing Pneumonia. The patient had a history of PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in October 2020. A bronchoscopic transbronchial lung biopsy was done, and the patient was started on high-dose steroids, with which he improved. He was discharged home.
The patient was readmitted in April 2021 due to a persistent fever. Since the patient was on high-dose steroids, the fever was attributed to a probable secondary infection or organizing pneumonia itself. Sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and an antibiotic, piperacillin, was commenced. Computed tomography thorax showed resolution of the previously seen left lower lobe consolidation but had new-onset bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGOs). Nasal swab for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR was positive (Cepheid assay, April 2021), with a Ct value of Envelope gene (E gene) 23.2 and nucleoprotein gene (N) 24.1. A diagnosis of COVID-19 re-infection was made. 
The patient received remdesivir injection and other symptomatic medications. He became afebrile within 2 days and was discharged from the hospital. During routine follow-up in June 2021, he was asymptomatic, and his anti-N and anti-S-RBD antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 proved to be positive (Table).
output: The following named entities related to COVID-19 infections can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary: SARS-CoV-2, PCR, COVID-19, remdesivir, anti-N, and anti-S-RBD antibodies. instruction: What type of tumor was identified on the MRI of the brain for a patient with a past medical history of Hodgkin lymphoma and presenting symptoms of occipital headaches, dizziness, dysarthria, and imbalance, who was subsequently taken for a suboccipital craniotomy?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]

Admission Date: [Date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Occipital headaches, dizziness, dysarthria, and imbalance.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 38-year-old female with a past medical history of Hodgkin lymphoma, presented to [Hospital's Name], Mexico with the chief complaint of occipital headaches, dizziness, dysarthria, and imbalance. A CT scan showed a midline superior cerebellar mass with surrounding edema, early hydrocephalus, and a small tentorial subdural hematoma. The patient was transferred to our service for further workup and treatment.

Diagnostic studies were performed, and given the presence of a non-MRI-compatible pacemaker, the MRI of the brain was not feasible. The lesion seen on the CT scan was favored to represent metastatic disease with lymphoma high on the differential diagnosis. However, replacing the pacemaker with a DDD Medtronic Advisa SureScan MRI-compatible pacemaker allowed for an MRI of the brain to be performed, which revealed an enhancing, likely extra-axial mass that was favored to represent a meningioma. The patient was taken to the operating room for a suboccipital craniotomy, and a gross total resection was achieved. Pathology returned as a high-grade peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

Postoperatively, the patient unfortunately developed a postoperative hematoma in her surgical cavity, which required emergent evacuation and the placement of an external ventricular drain and ultimately a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. However, the patient made a full recovery.

Discharge Condition:

The patient's condition has improved, and the patient has met all the discharge criteria.

Discharge Diagnoses:

1. High-grade peripheral nerve sheath tumor

2. Meningioma (likely extra-axial)

Discharge Instructions:

1. The patient is advised to continue to take the prescribed medication as directed by their primary care physician.

2. The patient is advised to schedule a follow-up visit with their primary care physician for additional care and monitoring.

3. The patient is advised to engage in appropriate physical activity and avoid any activities strenuous enough to cause discomfort.

4. The patient is advised to inform their primary care physician of any worrisome symptoms.

5. The patient is advised to follow all precautions and measures after discharge from the hospital. 

6. The patient is advised to avoid smoking, alcohol consumption, caffeine, and other stimulants that may interfere with the healing process.

7. The patient is advised to follow a balanced and nutritious diet.

8. If the patient has any questions, they are instructed to contact their primary care physician. 

Follow-Up Appointments:

Instructions have been given to the patient to schedule a follow-up visit with their primary care physician. The patient was instructed to call/visit the clinic for appointment scheduling.
output: The MRI of the brain revealed an enhancing, likely extra-axial mass that was favored to represent a meningioma for the patient with a past medical history of Hodgkin lymphoma and presenting symptoms of occipital headaches, dizziness, dysarthria, and imbalance, who was subsequently taken for a suboccipital craniotomy. Pathology returned as a high-grade peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

instruction: What was the genetic study result and its relation to the patient's diagnosis of ADTKD-MUC1 in this case of CKD? (related to relation extraction)
input:
Electronic Health Record Discharge Summary

Patient Information

Name: [Patient Name]
Age: 57 years old
Sex: Female
Medical record number: [Medical Record Number]

Hospital Course Summary

[Patient Name], a 56-year-old female, was referred to the nephrologist due to the diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (CKD) on a routine laboratory check-up. The patient was asymptomatic and had no history of alcohol intake, tobacco consumption, drug abuse, or medication exposure. Physical examination was unremarkable, and abnormal blood tests showed low haematocrit and haemoglobin levels, high urea and serum creatinine values, and proteinuria. A kidney biopsy revealed focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis with moderate interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. The patient was started on enalapril 5 mg twice a day and simvastatin 10 mg/day and received appropriate dietary advice. Sixteen months later, the patient returned to the nephrologist due to asthenia, fatigue, and cramps, and further blood tests showed worsened renal function. The patient was prescribed erythropoietin, enalapril, calcium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, and polystyrene calcium sulfonate. Six months later, the patient started hemodialysis and underwent a genetic study, which disclosed a mutation of the mucin-1 gene consistent with the diagnosis of ADTKD-MUC1 (Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstial Kidney Disease-Mucin-1). The laboratory results of the patient's daughter revealed mild proteinuria and normal kidney function. She was started on enalapril and received genetic counseling.

Hospital Course

This was a complicated case of CKD that progressed to end-stage renal disease requiring hemodialysis. The patient initially received conservative treatment with enalapril and simvastatin, as well as dietary advice. Later, the patient required erythropoietin, calcium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, and polystyrene calcium sulfonate. Genetic testing revealed that the patient had ADTKD-MUC1, which requires a long-term nephroprotection plan. The patient's daughter was found to have mild proteinuria and normal kidney function and was started on enalapril and received genetic counseling.

Diagnosis

ADTKD-MUC1 (Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstial Kidney Disease-Mucin-1)

Treatment/Plan

The patient requires long-term hemodialysis and regular follow-up with the nephrologist. The patient's daughter requires regular monitoring and genetic counseling due to her family history of CKD.

Consultations

The patient received consultations with the nephrologist and underwent a genetic study.

Discharge Instructions

The patient has not been discharged and requires long-term hemodialysis and regular follow-up with the nephrologist.
output: The genetic study revealed a mutation of the mucin-1 gene consistent with the diagnosis of ADTKD-MUC1, which is an autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease.

Pseudoaneurysm of a posterior right common femoral branch artery.

The patient was treated with coiling of the feeding artery by interventional radiology.

instruction: What is the diagnosis and treatment plan for the patient's diabetic myonecrosis as mentioned in the hospital discharge summary?
input:

The patient is a 41-year-old female with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis, hypertension, and congestive heart failure who presented to the ED with right leg pain. Imaging studies, including X-rays, venous Doppler, and CT, were normal, and she was discharged home with analgesics and follow-up with orthopedics. One month later, she returned to the ED with excruciating right thigh pain, leukocytosis, elevated creatinine kinase, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. MRI of the right leg revealed diffuse subcutaneous edema and intramuscular fascial edema around the proximal hamstring muscles without abscess or osteomyelitis. Patient was discharged home after physical therapy evaluation and was readmitted one week later after a fall with persistent leukocytosis, elevated CRP, ESR, and CK. Repeat lower extremity MRI showed diffuse swelling and edema-like signal involving the right thigh musculature with fluid-like signal at the fascial planes without any focal fluid collection, consistent with ischemic changes in the right thigh musculature. The diagnosis of diabetic myonecrosis was made, and patient was prescribed aspirin 81 mg daily, analgesics including acetaminophen and oxycodone as needed, and lidocaine patch. Patient's blood glucose was targeted from 140 to 180 mg/dL with adjustments of insulin glargine and lispro. She was evaluated by physical therapy and discharged home shortly with endocrine follow-up.

instruction: What was the diagnosis for the patient and what treatment was administered for their acquired hemophilia A, immune thrombocytopenia, and blood-loss anemia?
input:
Discharge Summary:

1. Patient Details:
- Name: Anonymous
- Age: 40 years
- Gender: Female
- Occupation: Bank Clerk

2. Reason for Admission:
- Oral cavity and nose mucosal bleeding
- Muscle hematoma on both legs
- Homolateral painful knees

3. Hospital Course:
- Coagulation test showed a severely prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with normal prothrombin time (PT) and thrombin time (TT).
- Laboratory investigations revealed severe anemia and thrombocytopenia.
- Plasma bilirubin levels were normal and reticulocyte percentage was 1.4%.
- Additional tests revealed that FVIII:C was 1%, FIX:C was 130%, and FVIII inhibitor (FVIII:I) was 210 BU/ml.
- The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test was negative, platelet associated antibody IgG is positive, and Lupus anticoagulants (LAC) were negative. 
- Complement levels were reduced.
- Autoimmune screen for CTD was normal. Virology tests for HIV, HPVB19, EBV, CMV, and hepatitis virus were all negative. A pectoral-abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan did not detect infection or tumor.
- The patient was diagnosed with acquired hemophilia A (AHA) along with immune thrombocytopenia and blood-loss anemia.
- Treatment included transfusion with packed red-blood cells, fresh frozen plasma (FFP), and human prothrombin complex concentrate (hPCC) to complement clotting factors.
- Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was administered at a total dose of 2 g/kg over 5 days and started with oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg/day.
- Intravenous cyclophosphamide and continued oral prednisone treatment were initiated when the aPTT did not shorten.
- Intravenous anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (Rituximab) treatment at 375 mg/m2 each week with tapering of the prednisone dose to 0.8 mg/kg/day was initiated.
- Shoulder joint bleeding gradually ceased after 4 weeks of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy.
- APTT and plasma FVIII were normalized and the FVIII:I titer became undetectable after 4 weeks of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy.
- Prednisolone was gradually reduced at 10 mg each week until it was discontinued.
- There was no relapse during the 3-year follow-up period.

4. Disposition:
- Stable condition upon discharge.
output: The patient was diagnosed with acquired hemophilia A along with immune thrombocytopenia and blood-loss anemia. The treatment included transfusion with packed red-blood cells, fresh frozen plasma (FFP), and human prothrombin complex concentrate (hPCC) to complement clotting factors. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was administered, followed by oral prednisone, intravenous cyclophosphamide, and anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (Rituximab) therapy. Prednisolone was gradually reduced, and the patient was stable upon discharge.

instruction: What is the relationship between the patient's B cell recovery and their relapses of nephrotic syndrome in the context of fibrillary glomerulonephritis, as revealed through relation extraction?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 55-year-old woman with a history of hypertension who presented with proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. She was referred to the nephrology department for further investigation.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent a percutaneous renal biopsy, which revealed diffuse mesangial expansion and focal thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. Immunofluorescence studies demonstrated intense mesangial and capillary loop smudgy staining for IgG, associated with glomerular deposition of complement component 3 (C3). Electron microscopy showed typical features of fibrillary glomerulonephritis (FGN).

Bone marrow examination and PET-CT did not detect any abnormalities, ruling out any malignant process. The patient was started on a higher dose of ACE inhibitor that resulted in a partial reduction of the proteinuria. She then received four doses of rituximab intravenously that resulted in significant reduction and temporary remission of proteinuria. However, the patient experienced relapses of nephrotic syndrome, and each relapse occurred in the context of B cell recovery.

Evaluation:
Circulating B cell subsets analysis revealed that the patient had a proportionally higher number of transitional (immature) B cells and a lower proportion of memory B cells among CD19+ cells compared to healthy blood donors. The patient had a higher proportion of switched memory B cells among memory CD19+CD27+ B cells.

Follow-Up:
The patient's renal function was stable at the 36-month follow-up. The patient was ultimately discharged with continuing treatment for FGN.

Diagnosis:
Fibrillary Glomerulonephritis

Disposition:
Discharged with continuation of treatment for FGN.
output: Based on the discharge summary, the patient experienced relapses of nephrotic syndrome in the context of B cell recovery. Circulating B cell subsets analysis revealed that the patient had a higher proportion of switched memory B cells among memory CD19+CD27+ B cells compared to healthy blood donors, which may suggest a potential role of B cells in the pathogenesis of fibrillary glomerulonephritis. However, the exact relationship between the patient's B cell recovery and relapses of nephrotic syndrome cannot be determined solely from the given information. Additional evidence and research are needed to fully understand this relationship.

The patient was initially seen in the general surgery outpatient department with intermittent right abdominal pain. Routine blood examination showed a white cell count of 14.71 × 109/L with 67.2% neutrophils and C-reactive protein of 59.65 mg/L. An abdominal CT scan depicted a retroperitoneal occupying lesion in the upper abdomen accompanied by an abdominal aorta dilatation. Laboratory tests showed a white cell count of 9400/μL with 62.8% neutrophils, CRP of 46 mg/L, and ESR of 23 mm/h. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the aorta showed an aortic pseudoaneurysm.

The patient will continue receiving oral antihypertensive medication and follow-up appointments with the department of rheumatism. No other specific discharge instructions are required.

The patient is stable and recovering well.

instruction: What was the treatment course for a 14-year-old female patient with severe and persistent lymphopenia during an episode of autoimmune hemolytic anemia, including the medications prescribed and any observed side effects?
input:
Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 14-year-old female patient who was brought to our attention due to severe and persistent lymphopenia during an episode of autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The patient's lab reports showed a marked reduction in lymphocyte count and a decrease in the number of CD4+ T cells. A bone marrow aspirate showed mild dyserythropoiesis, and genetic analysis revealed an ADA gene mutation. The patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulins and corticosteroids, and a gradual increase in lymphocyte count was observed.

Hospital Course:

The patient was diagnosed with severe and persistent lymphopenia during an episode of autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The patient's initial lab reports showed marked reduction in lymphocyte count and reduction in CD4+ T cells. The patient was treated with oral prednisone, but poor response to the treatment was observed. Therefore, she was switched to four intravenous pulses of methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulins. During the course of corticosteroid therapy, hemoglobin levels slowly increased and Coombs test became negative within 3 months. Prednisone was continued for 10 months with progressive tapering. However, this therapy was associated with multiple side effects, including alopecia, weight gain, moon face, stretch marks, and lymphopenia. Prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole and acyclovir was prescribed to reduce the risks related to lymphopenia. One year after stopping corticosteroid therapy, lymphocyte count was restored to normal levels and the patient discontinued prophylactic therapy with acyclovir and cotrimoxazole.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with severe and persistent lymphopenia during an episode of autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Genetic analysis revealed an ADA gene mutation.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with oral prednisone, but poor response to the treatment was observed. Therefore, she was switched to four intravenous pulses of methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulins. During the course of corticosteroid therapy, lymphopenia was observed, and prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole and acyclovir was prescribed. After corticosteroid tapering, the patient's total numbers of lymphocytes gradually increased and reached normal levels.

Follow-up:

The patient's lymphocyte count has been restored to normal levels and the patient discontinued prophylactic therapy with acyclovir and cotrimoxazole. Follow-up with the patient's physician is recommended to monitor for recurrence of autoimmune hemolytic anemia and progressive lymphopenia. Further genetic testing and counseling may be necessary for the patient and her family.
output: The patient was initially treated with oral prednisone but had a poor response, so they were switched to four intravenous pulses of methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulins. During corticosteroid therapy, lymphopenia and several side effects were observed, including alopecia, weight gain, moon face, stretch marks, and lymphopenia. Prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole and acyclovir was prescribed to reduce the risks related to lymphopenia. Outcome:
The postoperative examination four months later revealed that the bone contours had returned to normal, the asymmetry of the face had disappeared, and the cortical bone thickness had decreased and been remodeled to the previous normal appearance.

No follow-up treatment was advised.

instruction: What was the surgical management plan for the patient's high-grade biliary obstruction following a right hemicolectomy and PD due to a gunshot wound to the abdomen?

instruction: What was the suspected cause and confirmed diagnosis of the patient's cognitive impairment, and what was the treatment provided for it? (related to Relation Extraction)
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: 
Name: Patient 9 
Age: 71 
Gender: Female 
Admission Date: November 2010 

Reason for Admission: 
Patient 9 was admitted to the psychiatric department of our hospital in November 2010 with the initial diagnosis of rapidly progressing dementia or delirium.

Medical History:
A history of mild forgetfulness which was noticed half a year prior to the beginning of rapid deterioration and a slight mesiotemporal atrophy in the MRI together with a pathological score in the Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) test and in the Intercategorical Delayed Selective Reminding Test (IDSR) supported the initial diagnosis of primary dementia. 

Hospital Course:
Short periods of altered consciousness on admission were compatible with a delirious state. Later, the patient’s daughter reported a tick bite followed by a widespread rash. Thus, Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB) was suspected and confirmed by CSF investigations. The patient’s cognitive impairment remitted within the 2 weeks of antibiotic treatment with 2 g ceftriaxone/day. When discharged from the hospital the patient was still on galantamine and mirtazapine.

Follow-up Information:
At the first follow-up investigation after 1 month the patient scored 29/30 (z −0.375) in the MMSE and treatment with galantamine was stopped. At the second follow-up 1 year after treatment of LNB cognition was normal with MMSE 29/30, and mirtazapine could be stopped. At another follow-up 5 years and 5 months after treatment of LNB, cognition was stable, and testing of episodic memory by the IDSR 7 now showed a z-score of +0.734, i.e. above the mean for females of the same age, which strongly argued against any dementing process. 

Disposition:
Patient 9 was discharged in stable condition. 

Principal Diagnosis: Rapidly progressing dementia.

Other Diagnoses: Delirium, mild forgetfulness, mesiotemporal atrophy, LNB 

Procedures and Interventions: Antibiotic treatment with 2g ceftriaxone/day.

Condition on Discharge: Stable.

Follow-up Instructions: Schedule regular follow-up appointments with the physician to monitor cognitive function.
output: The suspected cause and confirmed diagnosis of the patient's cognitive impairment was Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB). The patient was treated with antibiotic therapy using 2g ceftriaxone/day, which resulted in remission of cognitive impairment within 2 weeks of treatment.

Twelve years after the primary operation, periodic computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography did not uncover any new local recurrences or metastases. The clinical course did not include severe adverse events, although low-grade adverse events included transient headache, nausea, fatigue, and a persistent red flare with induration at the injection site.

Invasive ductal carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, nodular and well-moderately differentiated type with lymph node metastasis.

The 4-year-old female child was admitted to the clinic with a chief complaint of thumb sucking habit. The mother tried to stop the habit by applying a bitter neem oil substance, which did not yield any significant result.

The patient's extraoral examination showed good facial symmetry and convex profile. The intraoral examination revealed an anterior open bite, average-sized tongue, and proclination of maxillary anterior teeth with grade III mobility in the maxillary central incisors. Additionally, while swallowing, the tongue was placed between maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth (tongue thrusting habit). The intraoral periapical radiograph also revealed root resorption along the lateral and apical aspects of maxillary central incisors.

Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, the patient was diagnosed with ARR (Anterior Reversed Occlusion) accompanied by thumb sucking and a compensated tongue thrusting habit.

The treatment plan was formulated and explained to the patient's mother after obtaining her consent. Local anesthesia was administered before the extraction of maxillary central incisors. The extracted teeth were cleaned and preserved in saline, and the patient was scheduled for further treatment after a week.

During the second appointment, treatment of thumb sucking and tongue thrusting was initiated by counseling the parent and the child. The adverse effects of the habits on the developing dentition were discussed. A habit reminder therapy using a customized bluegrass appliance with natural tooth pontics was planned based on the parental esthetic concern. The appliance was designed both for parental esthetic concern and habit reminder therapy.

The patient showed good progress, and there were no significant complications during the hospital course.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Anterior Reversed Occlusion (ARR)
2. Thumb Sucking Habit
3. Compensated Tongue Thrusting Habit

3. The patient should be encouraged to developing good oral hygiene habits, such as regularly brushing and flossing.
4. The parents should be reminded of the harm associated with thumb-sucking and tongue thrusting habits, and constant supervision should be provided to discourage these habits.

instruction: What imaging findings and symptoms led to the suspicion of malignancy in the 55-year-old female patient?
input:
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 55-year-old woman with no significant medical history, presented to the emergency room with a 1-day history of abdominal pain and a thick turbid discharge from the left inguinal area. Examination revealed leukocytosis, anemia, and hypoalbuminemia. Imaging studies revealed a microperforation of the sigmoid colon, abscess in the left lower quadrant, hepatic lesion, and bilateral hydronephrosis. Ultrasound demonstrated an intra-uterine device. There was a large, infiltrating heterogenous hyperattenuating mass invading the urinary bladder, left adnexa, sigmoid, left inguinal canal, and left pelvic wall area, which raised suspicion for malignancy. Due to suspected colon perforation and the enclosed mass in the small bowel, conservative treatment was initiated with parenteral antibiotics and fasting with total parental nutrition, while the imaging-guided percutaneous abscess drainage was performed.

After 10 days of conservative treatment, a repeat CT of the abdomen-pelvis showed improved abdominal abscess and liver lesion; however, no significant changes were detected in the conglomerated mass invading the pelvis. The patient developed mechanical small bowel obstruction requiring exploratory laparotomy, which revealed perforated colon, obstructive small bowel, and organs involved. Severe adhesion between the mass and pelvic organs, including the uterus, small and large bowels, and bladder was identified. Infection with Actinomyces species was confirmed on permanent histology.

Treatment:

En-bloc excision of the mass was performed using Hartmann’s procedure, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, small bowel resection, and appendectomy. The double J catheter was inserted into both the ureters without resection. The parenteral antibiotic regimen was changed to tigecycline, amikacin, metronidazole, and Penicillin G. The patient made an uneventful recovery and was started on a 6-month course of penicillin.

Follow-Up:

At 1-year follow-up, the patient was in good health and free of disease.
output: The suspicion of malignancy in the 55-year-old female patient was raised due to the presence of a large, infiltrating heterogenous hyperattenuating mass invading the urinary bladder, left adnexa, sigmoid, left inguinal canal, and left pelvic wall area, as seen on imaging studies.

instruction: What was the relation between the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma in this patient, and what procedures were performed to manage these conditions?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Gender: Male, Age: 32
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the hospital with intermittent abdominal pain and profuse episodic axillary hyperhidrosis. During surgical exploration for an acute appendicitis, what appeared to be a liver mass was detected. Diagnostic tests revealed abnormal levels of 24-hr urine metanephrine, normetanephrine, and total metanephrines. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the abdomen showed a mass centered in the right adrenal gland and another mass in the region of the porta hepatis. Consequently, the patient underwent a total right adrenalectomy. The pathology report confirmed the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma with a GAPP score of 9, which indicates a poorly differentiated tumor with the presence of necrosis, irregular cell nest form, high cellularity, minimal capsular invasion, and adrenergic features. Ki67 index 5% and S100 were negative. 

Following surgery, the patient exhibited normalized levels of plasma free metanephrines. However, the levels of plasma free normetanephrine remained elevated, raising the suspicion of paraganglioma. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen revealed a soft tissue mass in the region of the porta hepatis, which slightly increased in size compared to the MRI. In addition, a positron emission tomographic (PET) scan identified a thyroid mass. Further analysis indicated that the patient had papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Subsequently, the patient underwent resection of the porta hepatis mass and total thyroidectomy, with subsequent confirmation of paraganglioma and PTC, respectively. On surgical pathology, the paraganglioma was S100 positive. After the resection, the level of plasma free normetanephrine decreased significantly, while the level of plasma free metanephrine remained normal.

Genetic studies were negative for any sequence changes and deletion/duplications of EGLN1, FH, KIF1B, MAX, MEN1, NF1, RET, SDHAF2, SDHC, SDHB, SDHD, TMEM127, VHL, and SDHA.

The patient was discharged in a stable condition with close outpatient follow-up with endocrinology and surgery.

Diagnoses:

1. Pheochromocytoma
2. Paraganglioma
3. Papillary thyroid carcinoma

Procedures:

1. Total right adrenalectomy
2. Resection of the porta hepatis mass
3. Total thyroidectomy

Follow-up:

The patient requires close outpatient follow-up with endocrinology and surgery.

1. Follow all post-operative care instructions as provided by your healthcare provider. 
2. Attend all follow-up appointments with your healthcare provider. 
3. Keep track of any unusual symptoms or changes in your condition and report them immediately to your healthcare provider. 
4. Take all prescribed medications as instructed and complete the full course of treatment. 
5. Maintain a healthy diet and lifestyle. 
6. Avoid any strenuous activity or heavy lifting for a minimum of 2-4 weeks post-surgery, or until advised by your healthcare provider to resume normal activities. 
7. Ensure that any medication or prescription changes are coordinated with your primary care doctor and specialists. 

This discharge summary serves as a record of the patient's hospitalization course and condition at the time of discharge.

However, elevated levels of plasma free normetanephrine suggested the presence of paraganglioma, which was confirmed with a resection of the porta hepatis mass. The patient also had papillary thyroid carcinoma, which was managed with a total thyroidectomy. instruction: What Named Entities related to cytopenia and pancytopenia can be extracted through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
A 36-year-old female with sarcoidosis presented with fever, weight loss, enlarged right axillary lymph node, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. After axillary lymph node biopsy confirmed the presence of sarcoidosis, the patient was started on steroids, but exhibited mild improvement in symptoms. Over the next few months, the patient developed gradually increasing leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. A bone marrow biopsy confirmed the presence of noncaseating sarcoid granulomas, and the patient was maintained on steroids but showed no improvement in cytopenia. One year after diagnosis, the patient presented with fever, fatigue, and hepatosplenomegaly. Blood workup revealed worsening pancytopenia and high ferritin and liver dysfunction. Despite a trial of IVIG and methylprednisolone, the patient did not respond, developed encephalopathy and status epilepticus and was transferred to another facility for escalated care, where she died shortly thereafter. 

Summary:
This 36-year-old female patient with sarcoidosis initially presented with fever, weight loss, enlarged right axillary lymph node, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. After a biopsy confirmed the diagnosis, she was treated with steroids, but exhibited only mild improvement in symptoms. Over the course of the next year, the patient developed cytopenia and was maintained on steroids, with no improvement noted. Blood work and bone marrow biopsy indicated the presence of noncaseating sarcoid granulomas that persisted despite treatment. Later, the patient presented with fever, fatigue, and hepatosplenomegaly, and despite treatment with IVIG and methylprednisolone, further evaluations revealed diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement. Unfortunately, the patient did not survive and was transferred and later died at another facility.
output: The named entities related to cytopenia and pancytopenia that can be extracted through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary are leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia.

Hospital Course:

This 31-year-old gravida 3 para 1 patient was admitted to our facility at 19 weeks and 3 days' gestation to discuss the results of a morphology scan. The scan showed a grade 4 placenta previa covering the cervical os. She had a medical history significant for Arnold Chiari malformation, requiring craniotomy, and correction of a Syringomyelia in 2005. She also suffers from irritable bowel syndrome and has a BMI of 23. 

The patient had routine antenatal care which was unremarkable until the scan. Unfortunately, a repeat ultrasound the following day confirmed IUFD with an abnormally invasive placenta. 

Options were discussed with the patient, and it was decided for conservative management in order to preserve fertility. A plan was made for serial ultrasounds as an outpatient, to be followed by induction of labor when placental blood flow was no longer detectable. At day 33, the patient suffered a 300mL APH, and a dose of 80mg methotrexate was administered to accelerate placental devitalization. 

During the subsequent two days, the patient experienced moderate bleeds and increasingly significant contractions. She spontaneously delivered a male fetus with minimal bleeding during delivery on day 35. A brisk 2 L PPH followed the delivery, and the patient was immediately taken to the operating theater for examination under anesthesia and attempted manual removal. 

Due to only partial removal of the placenta manually, the case quickly progressed to laparotomy. Intraoperative findings revealed a full-thickness increta, and hysterotomy was performed to remove the remaining placenta manually. A Foley's catheter was inserted vaginally, and the placental bed was oversewn to establish haemostasis. 

The patient lost a total of 4 liters of blood and received multiple blood transfusions. She recovered without significant complication over the following days and was discharged one week later on oral antibiotics and aperients. At her six-week postnatal follow-up clinic, she experienced minimal lochia and was feeling generally well.

Diagnosis:

Grade 4 placenta previa covering the cervical os with IUFD and morbidly adherent placenta.

Procedures:

Hysterotomy performed with a transverse incision made above the prior caesarean incision and manual removal of the remaining placenta.

Conditions on Discharge:

Patient is discharged in a stable condition with no further complications.

instruction: What was the cause of respiratory distress in the infant according to the discharge summary and what diagnostic procedures were performed to identify it?
input:
Hospital Course:
This Caucasian infant was born by vaginal delivery at 37+2 weeks gestation, with a birth weight of 2045 g and length of 51 cm. He presented with respiratory distress, including suprasternal tugging and stridor, which required nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and subsequently mechanical ventilation. Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy (FFL) on day 2 following birth revealed bilateral vocal cord paralysis (BVCP) with severe airway obstruction. The patient was transferred to a medical and surgical neonatal intensive care unit on day 3. Rigid laryngotracheal endoscopy on day 4 showed no malformation or obstruction below the glottis. Neuroimaging investigations revealed deformation of the bulbo-medullary junction and a unilateral cavitated lesion with hypoplasia of vertebral arches and exo-occipital bone on CT at the cervico-occipital hinge. MR angiography showed the absence of the distal right vertebral artery, and MRI with fibre tracking confirmed hemisection of the right lateral and median sensorimotor fascicles. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials and fundus examination were normal. Despite left unilateral endoscopic laser cordotomy on day 7, the procedure was unsuccessful, and the infant was reintubated after 3 hours due to the reappearance of stridor and major signs of respiratory distress. Mechanical ventilation was maintained until the end of the stay, and as the patient's prognosis was deemed very poor, a multidisciplinary ethics consultation was sought, and the decision was made to limit care to the infant's comfort. The infant died at the age of 4 weeks. An autopsy was not performed. Array comparative genomic hybridization revealed no abnormality.
output: The cause of respiratory distress in the infant was bilateral vocal cord paralysis, which was identified through flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy. Additional diagnostic procedures, including rigid laryngotracheal endoscopy, neuroimaging investigations, and MR angiography were performed to assess the severity and underlying cause of the paralysis. However, no malformations or obstructions were found below the glottis, and the neuroimaging investigations revealed deformation of the bulbo-medullary junction and a unilateral cavitated lesion with hypoplasia of vertebral arches and exo-occipital bone instead. Despite left unilateral endoscopic laser cordotomy, this did not cure the airway obstruction.

instruction: What was the relation between the treatment administered for abomasal bloat and choke, the recurrence of bloating, and the subsequent surgical intervention in the 10-day-old male crossbred calf, based on relation extraction from the discharge summary?

Hospital Course:
A 10-day-old male crossbred calf was admitted with a severely distended abdomen, rapid and shallow breathing, visibly congested mucus membranes, and an abnormal gait. The patient had difficulty with urination and defecation, and was reluctant to feed from the dam. The distended abdomen was found to be due to abomasal bloat and choke, and a flexible stomach tube coated with mineral oil was inserted to release trapped gases and check the patency of the esophagus. The patient was administered antibiotic Pen Aqueous orally for 3 days and an isotonic solution containing Sodium Chloride, Sodium Bicarbonate, and Dextrose intravenously at a rate of 100 ml/kg over 3-5 hours for 2 days.

After 3 days of treatment the patient experienced a recurrence of bloating, and treatment was initiated a second time with antibiotic Pen & Strep and supportive therapy of glucose and multivitamin. Despite the current treatment, the patient again experienced bloat 5 hours after consuming milk from the dam.

To prevent recurrence, ruminal fistulation (rumenostomy) was conducted. The patient was separated from the herd for 10 days for close observation while taking penstrep and dexamethasone injections, as well as Deltamethrin 1% to prevent insect infestation and miyiasis. The surgical wound was cleaned daily and the patient was allowed to suckle milk from its dam twice a day during the follow-up period.

The calf showed improvements throughout the 6-month follow-up period after surgery, and the owner was recommended to reintroduce the calf to the existing herd. The owner sold the calf at 9 months of age to a beef farmer in another area of the country.

Summary:
The 10-day-old male crossbred calf was admitted with abomasal bloat and choke, and underwent treatment including a flexible stomach tube coated with mineral oil, antibiotic Pen Aqueous, and an isotonic solution containing Sodium Chloride, Sodium Bicarbonate, and Dextrose intravenously. After experiencing a recurrence of bloating, ruminal fistulation (rumenostomy) was conducted. The calf was separated from the herd for 10 days while receiving treatment and was allowed to suckle milk from its dam twice a day during the follow-up period. After a 6-month follow-up period, the owner was recommended to reintroduce the calf to the existing herd.
output: The treatment with antibiotics and intravenous solution was not successful in preventing a recurrence of bloating in the calf. As a result, ruminal fistulation was performed to prevent further bloat. After the surgical intervention, the calf showed improvements during the 6-month follow-up period and was recommended for reintroduction into the existing herd.

instruction: What is the connection between the patient's symptoms of muscle pain, dry skin, and facial puffiness and the diagnosed condition of severe hypothyroidism with raised levels of anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

Patient was admitted with symptoms of generalized muscle pain, dry skin, and mild facial puffiness. Laboratory investigations revealed severe hypothyroidism along with raised levels of anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, suggesting Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Elevated levels of serum creatine kinase and myoglobin levels were indicative of rhabdomyolysis. Transthoracic echocardiography detected minimal circumferential pericardial effusion, and flexible laryngoscopy was normal. 

The patient's symptoms improved with intravenous fluids and oral levothyroxine, and the levels of CK and myoglobin showed a decreasing trend. He was discharged on Day 4 and advised to continue taking the prescribed medication. The patient was instructed to follow up with his primary care physician and endocrinologist for further management of his thyroid condition. 

The patient's hospital course was unremarkable after initiation of treatment, and he was discharged in stable condition.
output: The patient's symptoms of generalized muscle pain, dry skin, and mild facial puffiness are consistent with the diagnosis of severe hypothyroidism and raised levels of anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, indicating autoimmune Hashimoto's thyroiditis as the underlying cause. Thyroid hormones play a crucial role in regulating cellular metabolism, and their deficiency can result in a range of symptoms, including muscle weakness, fatigue, and dry skin. Increased serum levels of muscle enzymes, such as CK and myoglobin, suggest muscle damage due to rhabdomyolysis, a rare complication of severe hypothyroidism. However, the minimal pericardial effusion detected on transthoracic echocardiography is likely unrelated to the thyroid condition and may require further evaluation by a cardiologist.

The patient then developed progressively worsening subcutaneous emphysema after the catheter was removed, and the diagnosis of tension pneumothorax was made. The thoracostomy tube was safely removed after the Rocket® PSU flow readings showed no air leak.

None prescribed at this time.

The patient is advised to monitor the thoracostomy wound and report any signs of infection or worsening symptoms. Follow-up appointments with the primary care physician and pulmonology are recommended to ensure proper healing and to monitor for any recurrence of symptoms.

The patient is advised to refrain from heavy lifting or strenuous activity until cleared by their primary care physician or pulmonologist.

No specific dietary restrictions were recommended.

The patient is advised to keep the wound clean and dry, and to monitor for any signs of infection, such as redness, swelling, or drainage.

instruction: What was the surgeon's diagnosis and treatment plan for the patient's condition of pilonidal sinus with secondary abscess formation in their third finger? (related to Relation Extraction)

Gender: Female

Diagnosis: Pilonidal sinus with secondary abscess formation

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 67-year-old right-handed female hairdresser, presented to a plastic surgeon with a three-month history of a swollen, painful, and intermittently discharging lesion in the pulp of her third finger. She denied any history of trauma but did report a long-standing history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, Raynaud's syndrome, and frequent small ulcers at her fingertips. A swab grew coliform bacteria after taking repeated courses of antibiotics which failed to resolve her symptoms. Regular medication included ramipril and vitamin D.

On physical examination, a swollen, tender, erythematous finger pulp with a small, crusty papule that did not produce discharge was noted without evidence of lymphangitis. Plain radiographs suggested a foreign body, without osteomyelitis. A calcinosis nodule was also noted in the pulp of her right fourth finger. The surgeon diagnosed pilonidal sinus with secondary abscess formation due to the patient's occupation as a hairdresser.

The surgeon recommended surgery and performed a fish mouth incision under local anaesthesia, incorporating an ellipse around the sinus, and excising the sinus cavity. The surgeon washed and sutured the wound. After showing signs of infection three days post-operatively, the patient received a one-week course of oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. Sutures were removed on the twelfth post-operative day. However, due to renewed signs of infection, the patient took a further two-week course of oral flucloxacillin. The wound healed, and the patient returned to work one month after surgery. Three months postoperatively, she remains asymptomatic but has chosen not to use gloves.

Treatment:
- Fish mouth incision under local anaesthesia incorporating an ellipse around the sinus and excising the sinus cavity
- One-week course of oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid for post-operative infection
- Two-week course of oral flucloxacillin for renewed signs of infection

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient is advised to continue monitoring the treated areas and seek medical attention if similar symptoms persist or return.

instruction: What diagnosis was confirmed for the one-year-old Thai boy after being admitted to the hospital, and what treatment option was recommended as curative? (related to the task of Relation Extraction)
input:
Hospital Course: 
This one-year-old Thai boy was admitted to Phramongkutklao Hospital due to subacute fever, abdominal distension, mucous diarrhea, and failure to thrive. The patient was evaluated based on his medical history, physical examination, and test results. The cause of vitamin K deficiency was presumed to stem from malabsorption, which later resulted in fat malabsorption and the detection of steatorrhea. Additionally, perianal abscess and lymphadenopathy of 3 cm in size at the left groin were also detected. The patient was diagnosed with BCG lymphadenitis and bilateral pneumonia with evidence of hepatosplenomegaly. A diagnosis of disseminated BCG infection and XL-CGD was later confirmed.

Hospital Course: Immunocompromised State and Infection: 
The patient was diagnosed with disseminated BCG infection and XL-CGD. The IgG level was slightly elevated, while IgM and IgA levels were normal. Lymphocyte subset analyses revealed normal T-cell and B-cell counts. The neutrophil DHR test revealed no fluorescence detection after granulocyte stimulation, which was compatible with XL-CGD.

Hospital Course: Treatment: 
Treatment was started with antituberculosis including isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and amikacin. Itraconazole and co-trimoxazole were given as the prophylactic treatment. The clinical of ascites and steatorrhea improved after 2 weeks of treatment. Subsequently, the patient will undergo allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT) as a curative treatment.

Hospital Course: Prognosis: 
A potential curative treatment option for XL-CGD is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The mother, who is six months pregnant, was evaluated for carrier status, and the neutrophil DHR assay revealed bimodal distribution compatible with the XL-CGD carrier. Therefore, genetic counseling and prenatal testing are recommended for the family.

Summary: 
This one-year-old Thai boy was diagnosed with disseminated BCG infection and XL-CGD, which was the root cause of fat malabsorption leading to vitamin K deficiency. The patient responded well to antituberculosis therapy and prophylactic medication. As a curative treatment, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT) was recommended. Genetic counseling and prenatal testing are advised for the family and those who may carry the XL-CGD gene.
output: The one-year-old Thai boy was diagnosed with disseminated BCG infection and XL-CGD, and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT) was recommended as a curative treatment. Genetic counseling and prenatal testing are advised for the family and those who may carry the XL-CGD gene.
