instruction: What Named Entities can be identified through Named Entity Recognition related to the patient's acute heart failure, AECOPD, and ulcers on the right leg in this discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED] 
Gender: Male 
Age: 76 

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to acute heart failure, Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (AECOPD) and ulcers on the right leg. Physical examination revealed wheezing, moist rale in both lungs, and purulent discharge from multifocal ulcers on the right leg. The ulcers developed over a span of two months, and the patient denied any history of trauma or plant cultivation. Routine laboratory tests revealed elevated WBC, N%, CRP, and acute decompensated metabolic acidosis. Gram stain examination from the ulcers showed large amounts of leukocytes and a moderate amount of Gram-negative bacteria. Chest X-ray confirmed the presence of pulmonary infection.

After initiating the appropriate treatment for heart failure and purulent spots, antibiotic therapy was initiated with cefoperazone/sulbactam. The patient showed significant improvement three days after the treatment with dyspnea and moist rale disappearance in the lungs. Subsequently, antibiotic treatment was discontinued, and dressing change was assured.

On the seventh day of hospitalization, the patient's body temperature rose to 38.5°C, and the surface of the ulcers was dry with no evidence of wound healing. Smear examination of the pus obtained from the deep part of the ulcer showed the presence of fungal hyphae. MRI of the right leg confirmed skin damage with inflammatory changes. Voriconazole and piperacillin/tazobactam were administered intravenously for suspected infection, resulting in significant improvement. Weeks later, the patient was discharged with oral voriconazole continuation.

Two months after the discharge, all the ulcers healed completely.

Diagnosis: 

Acute heart failure, AECOPD, ulcers on the right leg.

Treatment: 

The patient received treatment for heart failure and incision and drainage of purulent spots. Anti-infection therapy was initiated with cefoperazone/sulbactam. Voriconazole and piperacillin/tazobactam were administered intravenously for suspected infection.

Follow-up Care: 

At the two-month follow-up, all lesions had healed completely. The patient was advised to wash the lesions with potassium permanganate (1:5000) once every day.

A radiopaque mineralized outline of the canal was present through radiolucency of the external resorptive defect. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) was performed to determine the extent and depth of the lesion area in three spatial levels. Based on dental radiography and CBCT findings, tooth 36 was diagnosed as Heithersay Class 3 invasive cervical resorption (ICR) and classified as 3Bp.

Treatment:
The patient underwent debridement, perforation repair of the resorptive area with mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA), and root canal treatment, which was performed with the patient's informed consent. The tooth had been asymptomatic, and the root canals were copiously irrigated with sodium hypochlorite and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid before filling with gutta-percha and sealers.

Follow-up:
After one month, a free gingival graft (FGG) was performed to increase the width of attached gingiva surrounding the tooth because thin attached gingiva and plaque accumulation on the cervical contour were observed in tooth 36 with the temporary crown. The 3-year follow-up demonstrated that there were no clinical symptoms, such as pain, swelling, or mobility, with a periodontal pocket depth <3 mm, and adequate width of attached gingival was maintained compared with before FGG. In radiographs, the affected tooth and its surrounding tissues demonstrated no pathological changes.
output: The patient was diagnosed with Heithersay Class 3 invasive cervical resorption (ICR) in tooth 36, which was treated with debridement, perforation repair with mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA), and root canal treatment followed by a free gingival graft (FGG) after one month to increase the width of attached gingiva. The 3-year follow-up demonstrated no clinical symptoms and radiographs showed no pathological changes.

instruction: What was the result of the relation extraction task between the patient's pleuropulmonary blastoma and the identified pathogenic variant in the DICER1 gene?
input:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Admitting Diagnosis: Pleuresia and Pleural Drainage

Hospital Course: 
A 3-year-old girl was admitted to the hospital with fever and cough. She was diagnosed with pleuresia, and pleural drainage was performed. Antibiotics were prescribed, but the patient did not show any improvement. A CT scan was performed, which revealed a tissular lesion of the left lower pulmonary lobe and a tumor of the right kidney. Lung biopsy showed blastema, without being able to distinguish whether its origin was WT or PPB despite multiple analyses by various pathological experts. Following the recommendations of the national panel of expert of both tumors, the patient was treated for metastatic WT following the International Society of Paediatric Oncology protocol. A nephrectomy was performed after 6 weeks of chemotherapy with vincristine and actinomycin, with a good response in both sites. The histologic analysis confirmed the diagnosis of WT with an intermediate risk (epithelial type) which was classified as a stage IV. Lung surgery was scheduled several weeks later. During this period, a heterozygous pathogenic variant was identified in exon 23 of the DICER1 gene (LRG_492) using high-throughput sequencing of a panel of genes involved in endocrine tumor development. This variant c.4407_4410del, p.Ser1470Leufs*19, leading to loss of the RNase III active site, has been previously associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma. This led to a high suspicion of associated PPB. Pre-operative workup showed increase in tumor size, and chemotherapy was modified (by adding ifosfamide and doxorubicin) to try to reduce tumor volume and vascularization. After the first course of chemotherapy, the patient developed respiratory distress due to a massive increase in tumor size, leading to mediastinal compression. A left pleuro-pneumonectomy with intra-pericardic ligature of the vessels and without cardiac assistance was performed to remove the left lung. The patient's early postoperative course was uneventful. The pathologist confirmed the diagnosis, and it was a type 3 PPB with R0 resection. Postoperative chemotherapy consisted of eight courses (27 weeks) of vincristine, actinomycin, and doxorubicin. After 1-year follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic and was considered to be in remission.

Discharge Disposition: The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Condition at Discharge: The patient was stable and was doing well.

Follow-up: The patient was advised to follow-up with her Oncologist for long term care and regular check-ups.

Respectfully submitted, 
[Physician Name]
[Medical Center]
output: The identified pathogenic variant in the DICER1 gene (c.4407_4410del, p.Ser1470Leufs*19) led to a high suspicion of associated pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) in the patient, which was confirmed to be type 3 PPB with R0 resection after left pleuro-pneumonectomy. The relation extraction task between the patient's PPB and the identified pathogenic variant in the DICER1 gene suggests an association between the two.

instruction: What medical management did an 8-year-old child diagnosed with Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) with alimentary tract hemorrhage require after an unsuccessful treatment with methylprednisolone, infusion of blood products, and somatostatin?
input:
Hospital Course:
An 8-year-old child was admitted with complaints of purpura, hematemesis, bloody stools, and abdominal pain. He had an erythematous pinpoint rash on his arms that had spread to his legs. The patient was diagnosed with Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) with alimentary tract hemorrhage and was treated with methylprednisolone, infusion of blood products, and somatostatin. However, the treatment was not successful as the patient still had massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage, poor circulation, a reduced level of consciousness, and unstable vital signs.

Diagnostic Studies:
Abdominal ultrasonography and plain abdominal radiography gave negative results for enterobrosis. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed liquid samples and gas shadows on the left and front of the stomach.

Medical Management:
The patient underwent an emergency laparotomy. The surgery discovered that the anterior wall of the descending duodenum was thinner with a 1 cm × 1 cm diameter perforation, and the posterior wall had a 3 cm × 1 cm ulcer, which had penetrated into the peritoneum of the pancreas and experienced active bleeding from the broken end of the vessel. He was administered postoperative care such as nasal continuous positive airway pressure-assisted ventilation, anti-infection treatment, albumin transfusion, platelet transfusion, abdominal drainage, methylprednisolone, fluconazole antifungal treatment, and wound dressing.

Follow-up:
The patient's general symptoms gradually improved, vital signs were stable, and abdominal pain was relieved. The drainage tube was removed after discharge, and the abdominal CT was repeated after 1 month. The duodenostomy tube was removed 50 days after the surgery. During the 2-month follow-up assessment, there was no evidence of rebleeding.
output: After an unsuccessful treatment with methylprednisolone, infusion of blood products, and somatostatin for Henoch-Schönlein purpura with alimentary tract hemorrhage, an emergency laparotomy was performed. The patient was administered postoperative care such as nasal continuous positive airway pressure-assisted ventilation, anti-infection treatment, albumin transfusion, platelet transfusion, abdominal drainage, methylprednisolone, fluconazole antifungal treatment, and wound dressing.

The patient was stabilized and transferred to an outside hospital on post op day 3 for further recovery.

The patient was discharged to another medical facility on post op day 3. Arrangements were made for further medical care and recovery.

instruction: What was the cause of the patient's advanced atrioventricular block and subsequent cardiorespiratory arrest, and what intervention was necessary to reverse the condition?
input:
Patient: A 70-year-old male with a history of dyslipidaemia and smoking habits.
Admission: The patient was admitted due to an inferior ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
Treatment: The patient received thrombolysis due to the impossibility of achieving a timely percutaneous coronary artery intervention.
Complications: Advanced atrioventricular block requiring a transcutaneous pacemaker occurred soon after, followed by cardiorespiratory arrest in ventricular fibrillation, which was reversed after one cycle of advanced life support.
Transfer: The patient was transported by airplane to a PCI-capable centre.
Intervention: A 50-60% stenosis in the proximal segment of the right coronary artery was treated with a bare metal stent.
Discharge: The patient underwent urgent mitral valve replacement with a biological prosthetic valve (St. Jude #29), with preservation of anterior and posterior leaflets. The patient experienced a favourable post-operative recovery and was discharged 12 days after surgery with anticoagulant therapy for three months, in addition to dual antiplatelet therapy.
Follow-up: The patient initiated progressive heart failure symptoms (NYHA class III) on the fourth month after surgery.
Complications: Additional transthoracic and transoesophageal evaluations were performed and revealed a significant restriction of the prosthetic mitral valve leaflets mobility due to thrombotic material deposition, leading to severe obstruction.
Intervention: Urgent surgery, within twenty-four hours after diagnosis, was performed involving mitral bioprosthesis replacement with another biologic prosthesis with significant improvement in clinical status. Pathology examination of the excised prosthetic material confirmed prosthetic thrombosis, with no signs of endocarditis.
output: The advanced atrioventricular block and subsequent cardiorespiratory arrest were likely due to the inferior ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and the patient's history of dyslipidaemia and smoking habits. The intervention necessary to reverse the condition was a transcutaneous pacemaker followed by one cycle of advanced life support.

instruction: What Named Entities related to the diagnosis and treatment of lipoid pneumonia can be identified through Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Discharge Date: N/A

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was admitted to our pulmonology outpatient clinic with a four-week history of cough with mucous-purulent sputum and dyspnea. Physical examination revealed bibasal lung crackles. Chest X-ray showed bilateral infiltrates. A high resolution computed tomography (HRCT) was conducted, which revealed areas of ground glass appearance significantly in the lower lobes of both lungs and airspace consolidations were seen as well. The shadows improved 2 years later.

DIAGNOSIS:

The patient was diagnosed with lipoid pneumonia based on the bronchial wash and bronchoalveolar lavage (BALF) that was collected for immunological studies. The evaluation of BALF with specific staining and coloration showed the presence of fat-laden macrophages (oil red O stain). Extracellular oily droplets were found on a sputum cytology examination.

TREATMENT:

The patient's chronic use of amiodarone (200 mg OD) was considered the most likely cause of lipoid pneumonia. It was therefore discontinued and replaced with digoxin (0.25 mg OD) for the treatment of atrial fibrillation. She was also started on oral prednisolone (20 mg OD) which was gradually tapered over a period of six months.

FOLLOW-UP:

The patient is recommended to follow up with her primary care physician for further evaluation and management of her chronic conditions.

SUMMARY:

The patient was admitted with a history of cough with mucous-purulent sputum and dyspnea. Lipoid pneumonia was diagnosed based on the bronchial wash and bronchoalveolar lavage (BALF) that was collected for immunological studies. The patient's chronic use of amiodarone (200 mg OD) was considered the most likely cause and it was discontinued. instruction: What was the cause of the patient's recurrent transient ischemic attacks involving the posterior circulation, and what was the treatment plan after the acute posterior upper cervical cord infarction?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 70-year-old male with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and stroke

Hospital Course:
The patient initially presented to the Neurology clinic with transient episodes of gait disturbance, left-sided dysmetria, intermittent diplopia, and vertigo. Symptoms were attributed to recurrent transient ischemic attacks involving the posterior circulation. Follow-up CTA showed moderate left vertebral artery V4 and origin stenoses, which progressed over time despite treatment with aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin. The patient underwent elective cerebral angiogram with left VA angioplasty, which initially showed improvement; however, the patient developed new onset left upper extremity dysmetria and paresthesia a few hours postoperatively. He was discharged after 2 days but re-presented to the emergency room on the following day with left hemibody paresthesia and gait unsteadiness. MRI brain and dedicated MRI cervical spine confirmed acute posterior upper cervical cord infarction. CTA neck showed no restenosis of the left VA origin and patent V4 segment with resolution of previously seen thrombus. The patient was discharged home with the plan to continue aspirin and clopidogrel and outpatient physiotherapy. 

Follow-up:
Three months later, the patient reported resolution of left hemibody paresthesia, with mild residual left-hand coordination difficulties and gait imbalance. 

Impressions:
The patient presented with recurrent transient ischemic attacks involving the posterior circulation attributed to moderate left vertebral artery stenoses. Despite treatment with aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin, his symptoms persisted and worsened. He underwent elective cerebral angiogram with left VA angioplasty, which initially showed improvement but was complicated by acute posterior upper cervical cord infarction. Follow-up imaging showed no restenosis of the left VA origin and patent V4 segment with resolution of the previously seen thrombus. The patient was discharged home with mild residual left-hand coordination difficulties and gait imbalance.
output: The patient's recurrent transient ischemic attacks involving the posterior circulation were attributed to moderate left vertebral artery stenoses. Despite treatment with aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin, his symptoms persisted and worsened. The treatment plan after the acute posterior upper cervical cord infarction was to continue aspirin and clopidogrel and receive outpatient physiotherapy.

instruction: What is the relationship between the patient's diagnosis of SSC-CIP and their course of disease, as described in the discharge summary?

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to a different hospital due to a productive cough and required invasive assisted ventilation shortly after admission. She was later transferred to a tertiary care hospital for kinetic therapy and continuous renal replacement therapy due to oliguric acute kidney injury. Venovenous ECMO therapy was initiated due to progressive hypoxemia. The patient's nasopharyngeal swabs and tracheal aspirates tested negative for SARS-CoV-2. After tracheotomy and weaning, ECMO therapy and invasive assisted ventilation were no longer required, but the patient still needed intermittent renal replacement therapy.

During the course of the disease, the patient developed laboratory signs of liver injury during ECMO therapy before the clinical appearance of jaundice with elevated bilirubin levels, but sustained synthetic liver function reflected by international normalized ratio (INR) and serum albumin measurements. A diagnosis of SSC-CIP was confirmed by ERCP, showing intraductal filling defects in the intrahepatic bile ducts due to biliary casts. In addition, the patient received drugs that have previously been associated with SSC. Plasma levels of bilirubin and ammonia gradually increased after that, with stable liver synthesis reflected by normal values of the INR without substituting coagulation factors.

The patient developed progressive nausea, vomiting, weakness, and exhaustion as the disease progressed. Hepatic encephalopathy was treated but clinical symptoms worsened. Hemadsorption using the CytoSorb hemoperfusion device was used in combination with IRRT to eliminate bilirubin, ammonia, and CRP levels while serum albumin levels remained stable. Direct comparison revealed that bilirubin was less efficiently eliminated by hemadsorption compared to ammonia. During the successful elimination of bilirubin and ammonia, clinical symptoms of nausea, vomiting, weakness, and exhaustion improved. Following a continuation of IRRT but termination of hemadsorption therapy, bilirubin and ammonia levels increased again, worsening clinical symptoms within 20 days. The patient suddenly died due to cardiac arrhythmia before liver transplantation evaluation was initiated. 

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient passed away due to cardiac arrhythmia. 

Discharge Condition:

Deceased. 

Follow-up:

The patient requires no further follow-up. 

Attending Physician:

The attending physician was not named in the case report.

During the course of the disease, the patient developed laboratory signs of liver injury during ECMO therapy before the clinical appearance of jaundice with elevated bilirubin levels, but sustained synthetic liver function reflected by international normalized ratio (INR) and serum albumin measurements. The patient later received drugs that have previously been associated with SSC. Hemadsorption using the CytoSorb hemoperfusion device was used to eliminate bilirubin, ammonia, and CRP levels while serum albumin levels remained stable. While bilirubin was less efficiently eliminated by hemadsorption compared to ammonia, hemadsorption was successful in improving clinical symptoms of nausea, vomiting, weakness, and exhaustion. instruction: What was the relationship between the patient's microperforation and subsequent diagnosis of ischemic colitis, with reference to the Spigelian hernia and site of prior LVAD placement, as revealed by relation extraction?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 66-year-old male with a history of heart transplant and coronary artery disease, who presented with diarrhea, blood in stools, and a sub-epithelial lesion identified during a colonoscopy.

Hospital Course:

During the colonoscopy, the patient developed subjective fevers, chills, non-bloody emesis, and diarrhea. He was diagnosed with microperforation, and a CT was performed to assess for free air. The CT did not show any signs of perforation but revealed colonic extension through a Spigelian hernia at the site of the prior LVAD, with mild fat stranding. The small abdominal hernia was found to be easily reducible, and the patient was started on antibiotics and closely monitored for any changes. 

Over the next 24 hours, the patient's condition worsened, and he experienced abdominal pain, tachycardia, chills, and hypoxia. He required intubation, pressor support, and a repeat CT which demonstrated persistent colonic wall thickening over a 10 cm segment of the transverse colon consistent with ischemic colitis. The patient underwent an open procedure which included resection of the thickened segment and creation of an end colostomy. The pathology report confirmed ischemic colitis with mucosal ulceration and submucosal gangrenous necrosis.

The patient had a prolonged post-operative hospital course, eventually recovered, and was discharged with plans for a laparoscopic takedown of the end colostomy to return to rectal function.

Final Diagnosis:

Ischemic colitis with mucosal ulceration and submucosal gangrenous necrosis, likely secondary to colonic extension through a Spigelian hernia in the site of prior LVAD placement.

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to follow up with his gastroenterologist and surgeons for further evaluation and management. He is also encouraged to maintain a healthy lifestyle and continue his current medications under the guidance of his healthcare provider.

Summary:

This discharge summary outlines the hospital course of a 66-year-old male with a history of heart transplant and coronary artery disease who presented with diarrhea and blood in the stools. A diagnosis of microperforation was considered post colonoscopy, and a CT was performed, demonstrating colonic extension through a Spigelian hernia. The patient underwent surgery for ischemic colitis and eventually had an end colostomy. He had a prolonged post-operative hospital course, was eventually discharged and advised to follow up with his healthcare providers for further management.
output: The microperforation in the patient may have allowed the colon to extend through a Spigelian hernia located at the site of prior LVAD placement. This likely caused the subsequent diagnosis of ischemic colitis, which required surgical intervention. The pathology report confirmed mucosal ulceration and submucosal gangrenous necrosis.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and treatment plan for the patient's Goodpasture syndrome with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, as described in the discharge summary?
input:

Gender: Female
Age: 61 years
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Admitting Physician: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with shortness of breath on exertion, lower extremity edema, vomiting, subjective fever, and watery diarrhea. Upon admission, the patient was hemodynamically stable. The patient was diagnosed with acute kidney injury (AKI) secondary to acute tubular necrosis, which was presumably caused by volume depletion. Despite medical management of the AKI, the patient developed oliguria and worsening acidosis, which required hemodialysis.

Further diagnostic studies revealed the presence of serum myeloperoxidase-anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (MPO-ANCA), serum anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and red blood cells in the urine. A renal biopsy identified MPO-ANCA mediated with concurrent anti-GBM disease, crescentic necrotizing and focal sclerosing glomerulonephritis, which confirmed the diagnosis of Goodpasture syndrome with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

The patient received intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg for three days and four cycles of rituximab, followed by prednisone 60 mg daily. Patient's hospital course was complicated by a Clostridium difficile infection, hospital-acquired pneumonia, and a respiratory distress episode due to fluid overload and Goodpasture syndrome.

During patient's hospitalization, a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) was conducted, which revealed an ST and T wave abnormality compatible with anterolateral ischemia. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) identified an ejection fraction (EF) of 20% to 25%, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, systolic right atrial pressure (RAP) of 15 mmHg, and right ventricle systolic pressure (RVSP) of 59 mmHg. The left ventricle was normal in size, but there were regional wall motion abnormalities. Apical and basal segments contracted normally, but the mid-anteroseptal, inferolateral, and anteroapical walls were hypokinetic. The anteroapical wall appeared to be dyskinetic.

The patient was started on carvedilol and lisinopril and had a follow-up TTE three weeks later, which revealed an improved EF of 50%, grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, systolic RAP of 3 mmHg, RVSP of 33 mmHg, and an improvement in the previously described wall motion abnormalities, suggestive of resolving the mid-ventricular variant of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. 

The patient required intermittent dialysis during admission and was successfully discharged. The patient was asymptomatic, cardiovascular-wise, at the 18-month follow-up office visit; however, a kidney transplant was required due to chronic kidney disease.

Diagnoses:

1. Goodpasture syndrome with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
2. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
3. Hypertension
4. Hypothyroidism
5. Hyperlipidemia
6. Bronchiectasis
7. Polymyalgia rheumatica

Plan:

The patient was discharged with follow-up appointments with the rheumatology and nephrology departments. The patient was informed to follow up with post-transplant care. No other specific plans were indicated.

The patient also developed Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and was started on carvedilol and lisinopril, which resulted in an improvement in the patient's EF and wall motion abnormalities. No specific plans were indicated at discharge, and the patient was instructed to follow up with post-transplant care due to chronic kidney disease.

instruction: What was the diagnosis, diagnostic procedures, and treatment for the patient diagnosed with ALCAPA syndrome, mitral annular dilatation, and left-to-right shunt as outlined in the discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient, a 79-year-old woman, was admitted for evaluation of abnormal murmur. She presented with a 3-months history of worsening shortness of breath and orthopnea. Physical examination revealed a soft continuous murmur at the left upper chest with basal crackles in both lungs. Chest radiography showed mild cardiomegaly with mild pulmonary congestion. The ECG showed regular sinus rhythm without evidence of ischemia or prior myocardial infarction.
Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mildly dilated LV with markedly dilated left atrium. The LV ejection fraction was 60% with no wall motion abnormality. Transthoracic echocardiography also showed an unusual, tubular-like structure inside the interventricular septum with a turbulent, predominantly diastolic flow on color Doppler. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a markedly dilated RCA arising from the right aortic sinus, while the origin of the left coronary artery (LCA) could not be demonstrated. There was a tortuous, abnormal vessel located adjacent to the main pulmonary artery (MPA) emptying into the posteromedial aspect of the MPA. There was an accelerated, continuous flow across the stenotic ostium. Moreover, there was severe MR from a restricted posterior leaflet of the mitral valve (MV) associated with ventricular remodeling in combination with mitral annular dilatation.
Coronary angiography with a single RCA injection revealed a markedly dilated RCA providing multiple intercoronary collaterals of various sizes communicating with the left coronary system. The LCA later opacified the MPA through a stenotic ostium, establishing the diagnostic hallmark of ALCAPA syndrome. The calculated ratio of pulmonary-systemic blood flow was 1.4, confirming a significant left-to-right shunt. Coronary computed tomography angiography clearly identified the ALCAPA with a retropulmonary ostium. Volume-rendered image depicted the course of the anomalous coronary arteries and its inter-coronary collateral pathways along the epicardial surface and where the LCA connected to the MPA. Stress cardiovascular magnetic resonance perfusion imaging demonstrated no myocardial ischemia, suggesting adequate collateral circulation to the LV.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with ALCAPA syndrome, a congenital heart defect, resulting in a left-to-right shunt, and severe MR. No myocardial ischemia was detected through stress cardiovascular magnetic resonance perfusion imaging. The patient's LV and LCA were dilated while also experiencing mitral annular dilatation. The disease was diagnosed and monitored through various tests and imaging, such as Transthoracic echocardiography, Transesophageal echocardiography, coronary angiography, and coronary computed tomography angiography. The patient was referred for appropriate follow-up care and treatment.
output: The patient was diagnosed with ALCAPA syndrome, mitral annular dilatation, and left-to-right shunt. The diagnostic procedures included Transthoracic echocardiography, Transesophageal echocardiography, coronary angiography, and coronary computed tomography angiography. No myocardial ischemia was detected through stress cardiovascular magnetic resonance perfusion imaging. The patient was referred for appropriate follow-up care and treatment. However, specific details regarding the treatment were not provided in the given discharge summary.

instruction: What was the diagnosis of the patient and what was the course of treatment for their endocarditis, based on the Duke criteria, as described in the discharge summary?
input:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of chills, fever, malaise, fatigue, and recurrent tumbling despite antibiotic therapy. The patient had previously undergone abdominal surgery due to gastric carcinoma three months prior to admission. On admission, three independent sets of peripheral blood cultures were obtained, which depicted Lactobacillus species. Transesophageal echocardiogram showed degenerative changes of the mitral valve with moderate regurgitation as well as small endocarditis vegetation. Susceptibility testing revealed that the isolate was resistant to vancomycin. Based on the Duke criteria, the diagnosis of endocarditis was confirmed. Intravenous antibiotic therapy with ampicillin and gentamicin was initiated for six weeks. During antibiotic therapy, a PET/CT scan was performed, which showed florid inflammatory processes within the spleen due to peripheral embolization. The patient underwent abdominal surgery with splenectomy, and the other blood cultures during the antibiotic therapy were negative. There was no mitral valve replacement needed for cure.

The patient had undergone abdominal surgery due to gastric carcinoma three months prior to admission. Blood cultures revealed Lactobacillus species, and echocardiogram showed degenerative changes of the mitral valve with moderate regurgitation as well as small endocarditis vegetation. The diagnosis of endocarditis was confirmed based on the Duke criteria. During a six-week course of intravenous antibiotic therapy with ampicillin and gentamicin, a PET/CT scan showed inflammatory processes within the spleen due to peripheral embolization. The patient underwent abdominal surgery with splenectomy, and the other blood cultures during antibiotic therapy were negative. There was no mitral valve replacement needed for cure.

instruction: What developmental delays and physical impairments were identified in the patient with Cockayne syndrome during their hospital stay?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: July 2018
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to the Pediatric Orthopedic Clinic, Imam Khomeini Hospital, Tehran, Iran on July 2018 with the diagnosis of Cockayne syndrome.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, the patient presented with severe developmental delays and cognitive impairments, including the inability to walk or stand. Physical examination revealed flexion contractures in elbows, wrists, knees, and hips. Additionally, the patient displayed bilateral equinovarus deformity of feet and increased popliteal angle. Plantar reflexes showed extension response and DTRs were exaggerated. Spastic response of muscles was recorded after continuous stretching. Sitting balance was extremely unstable. 

Medical History:
The patient was born as the only child of otherwise healthy parents and was the result of a consanguine marriage. He had a normal pregnancy and a birth weight of 2950 grams. In the few first months of his life, he showed normal weight gain and development. However, the pediatrician noticed a decreased head circumference growth at 5 months age during a routine screening. Further investigation showed that the head circumference reached a plateau in its growth around 12 months age. Since then, the patient's general and developmental condition seemed to experience a sudden pause with progressive delay in growth and development. He lost his ability to rolling over and never gained any gross motor milestones. His face became expressionless and his eyes started to sink into the orbits. 

Diagnosis:
Although the physical examination had similarities to a patient with cerebral palsy, the patient's history was inconsistent with the diagnosis of CP in almost all aspects. After a thorough history-taking and further investigation, the diagnosis of Cockayne syndrome was established. The patient was homozygous for ECCR6 gene (genotype: c.2551 T>A /p.W851R- c.2551 T>A /p.W851R), and the parents were heterozygous for the same gene.

Outcome:
The patient was discharged with recommendations for continued occupational therapy to improve his quality of life. Additionally, his family was advised to provide support and comfort to the patient, as there is no cure for the condition.

Follow-up:
The patient's family was given a referral to a genetic counselor for genetic testing and counseling. Furthermore, the family was instructed to follow up with the pediatrician to monitor the patient's growth and development as well as the progression of the condition.

N/A

Cockayne syndrome

instruction: What chemotherapy regimen was initiated for the patient with Stage IIID moderately differentiated urachal adenocarcinoma, as mentioned in the discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

The 54-year-old male with a history of alcohol abuse was admitted to the emergency with acute-onset, diffuse, cramping abdominal pain, worst in the epigastrium and lasting one day. He had no prior abdominal surgeries. Upon examination, he had moderate guarding and generalized tenderness with hypoactive bowel sounds. The laboratory evaluation showed microcytic anemia and thrombocytopenia on complete blood count, hypokalemia on basic metabolic profile, and a normal lipase level. Abdominal X-ray showed an evolving small bowel obstruction, which was confirmed by a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast. On the same CT scan series, a urachal remnant with a superimposed mass lesion was depicted.

An emergent surgery was performed to release the small bowel obstruction after receiving a platelet transfusion. During the surgery, an extensive mass was found concerning for a malignancy. A frozen section was intraoperatively sent and read as adenocarcinoma. An incisional biopsy of the urachal mass was also sent, which resulted in a final pathology specimen of a moderately differentiated urachal adenocarcinoma.

The patient was staged at Stage IIID (Sheldon staging) due to the spread to local viscera other than the bladder. Due to the involvement of multiple loops of the small bowel and the mesentery of the small and large bowels, the tumor was deemed unresectable. Systemic chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), folinic acid, and oxaliplatin (modified FOLFOX-6) was initiated. The patient completed six cycles of chemotherapy and tolerated it well.

The patient is still awaiting additional imaging to evaluate the response to therapy. Further follow-up and management are recommended.
output: The initiated chemotherapy regimen for the patient with Stage IIID moderately differentiated urachal adenocarcinoma mentioned in the discharge summary was a systemic chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), folinic acid, and oxaliplatin (modified FOLFOX-6).

Discharge Summary

ADMISSION DATE: [REDACTED]           DISCHARGE DATE: [REDACTED]          

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was admitted with a complaint of patchy hair loss on the scalp, which was subsequently diagnosed as alopecia areata and treated with topical steroids. Four months posttreatment, the patient presented with intermittent fever, cough, and weight loss over the past 45 days. On examination, the patient was pale and cachexic with hepatosplenomegaly (16cm and 16.4cm, respectively). There was no cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or pedal edema. Alopecia over the scalp was regressing. Investigations showed anemia, elevated acute-phase reactants, serum LDH levels, and hypoalbuminemia. Subsequent imaging tests identified enlarged abdominal and thoracic lymph nodes, leading to a preliminary diagnosis of lymphoma. Bone marrow study showed no evidence of infiltration, and a laparoscopic biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of classical Hodgkin's lymphoma.

On the sixth post-laparoscopic day, the patient had two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures followed by altered sensorium. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was suggestive of pontine demyelination; however, there was no evidence of tumor deposits in the brain. Vitamin supplementation was initiated due to the patient's malnourished state. The neurologist suggested that the demyelination was a paraneoplastic manifestation of Hodgkin's lymphoma, and the patient was started on high-dose Methylprednisolone. Later, the patient was diagnosed with HSV-2 infection through CSF analysis after presenting with a high-grade fever with seizures. He received IV Acyclovir and continued on antiepileptics (Levetiracetam & Phenobarbitone) with controlled seizures. The patient sustained neurological deficits (spasticity & dystonia) and was started on chemotherapy (ABVD) once his general condition improved. Abdominal lymph nodes and hepatosplenomegaly regressed following chemotherapy, and his functional ability improved over time.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

Classical Hodgkin's Lymphoma (Lymphocyte-rich), Pontine Demyelination, HSV-2 Infection.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient should continue with the prescribed medication, and a follow-up appointment with the hematologist and a neurologist should be scheduled. The patient should also be advised regarding the importance of good nutrition and a healthy lifestyle. In case of any emergency, the patient should go directly to the emergency department of the hospital.
output: The preliminary diagnosis based on imaging tests was lymphoma, and a laparoscopic biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis of classical Hodgkin's lymphoma.

instruction: What was the relationship between the intraluminal migration of the gastric band into the distal jejunum and the small bowel obstruction found on plain abdominal radiography and CT scanning in the given discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: <redacted>
Date of Admission: <redacted>
Date of Discharge: <redacted>

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to our outpatient clinic with worsening abdominal pain in her left upper quadrant, loss of appetite, nausea, and having a "feculent" taste in her mouth. She had a previous medical history of laparoscopic adjustable gastric band (LAGB) implantation with weight loss of 30 kg after the procedure. However, she developed a partial perforation of the band into her stomach 3 years later, which required serial endoscopic follow-ups. From 2005 onwards, there were no further endoscopic follow-ups, and the patient regained weight up to a BMI of 36.3 kg/m2 until her current presentation. A clinical examination documented left-sided abdominal tenderness. Plain abdominal radiograph showed signs of small bowel obstruction. Computed tomography (CT) scanning revealed intraluminal migration of the gastric band into the distal jejunum – still connected to the subcutaneous reservoir – folding the intestine on the catheter like a hand organ instrument.

The patient underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which showed that the gastric band was impacted in the distal jejunum causing obstruction. An enterotomy was performed via umbilical mini-laparotomy, and the partially digested silicon band was retrieved. The involved jejunal segment was resected due to its conglomerate formation with possible stenosis, followed by end-to-end anastomosis. The operation was completed by removal of the port with the remaining catheter through the original port-site incision, and the catheter entrance into the stomach was left untouched. 

The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged from the hospital in a stable condition in good general health. She explicitly did not want a conversion about an alternative bariatric surgery and refused further follow-ups.

Diagnostic Findings:

- Left-sided abdominal tenderness without signs of abdominal guarding
- White blood cells (WBC) count of 11.3 G/l
- Small bowel obstruction on plain abdominal radiography
- Intraluminal migration of the gastric band into the distal jejunum on CT scanning.

Interventions:

- Diagnostic laparoscopy
- Enterotomy
- Resection of involved jejunal segment
- End-to-end anastomosis
- Removal of port with the remaining catheter through the original port-site incision

Medical Condition on Discharge:

The patient was discharged in good general health and stable condition with no active medical issues.

Follow-up:

The patient explicitly refused further follow-ups.
output: The intraluminal migration of the gastric band into the distal jejunum caused a small bowel obstruction, as seen on the plain abdominal radiography and CT scanning. The gastric band was impacted in the distal jejunum, folding the intestine on the catheter like a hand organ instrument, leading to obstruction.

Final Diagnosis: IgA Nephropathy with associated Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis

Hospital Course: The patient presented with nephrotic range proteinuria and occasional ankle oedema over the past year but otherwise felt well. On examination, he exhibited bipedal oedema up to the bottom third of his shins and mild arteriolar hyalinosis. Initial laboratory investigation found haemoglobin, white cell count and platelets to be within normal range but blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine were elevated. Subsequent urinalysis did not demonstrate any haematuria, leukocyturia or casts, but protein creatinine ratio was severely elevated. Electron microscopy showed extensive epithelial foot process effacement with microvillous change. Renal biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of IgA Nephropathy with associated Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis. 

The patient then began 6 cycles of chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, rituximab and prednisolone. At the end of chemotherapy, the patient was in complete remission haematologically and urine protein creatinine ratio had decreased substantially. Over the next 14 months, his urine protein creatinine ratio continued to fall. His serum creatinine, serum albumin and urine protein excretion remained stable at his most recent follow-up, 26 months post-chemotherapy.

Follow-up: Patient remains stable 26 months post-chemotherapy with regards to renal function and albuminuria. No further tests or interventions are currently required.

Initial investigation revealed elevated blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine, protein creatinine ratio and mild arteriolar hyalinosis. Renal biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of IgA Nephropathy with associated Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis. Patient was treated with 6 cycles of chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, rituximab and prednisolone resulting in complete remission haematologically and substantial decrease in urine protein creatinine ratio. Patient remains stable with regards to renal function and albuminuria 26 months post-chemotherapy.

instruction: What anticoagulant therapy was initiated for the patient's Trousseau syndrome, and what was the subsequent treatment for cerebral infarctions?
input:
Discharge Summary:

 
Hospital Course:

The patient is a 53-year-old male with a medical history of adenocarcinoma of the lung (T1bN3M1c, cStage IVb) positive for an EGFR gene deletion and cancer-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation. The patient was admitted to the hospital after experiencing a disturbance of consciousness and malaise. Upon admission, the patient had a decreased platelet count, an increased prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (PT-INR), and an increased fibrin degradation product level. Anticoagulant therapy with thrombomodulin alfa was initiated.

After two days of treatment with gefitinib, the patient showed signs of cerebral infarctions. Intravenous unfractionated heparin was administered, and the patient was treated with warfarin. The patient's coagulant profile improved, and he was switched to osimertinib after disease progression during gefitinib treatment. The patient stayed under observation with stable symptoms.

At the end of 11 days of treatment with gefitinib, the patient showed an improvement in the platelet count, and the brain test showed no further cerebral infarction. The patient continued to have leptomeningeal disease progression and eventually expired one month after discontinuation of osimertinib.

Summary of Care:

The patient presented to the hospital with back pain, and the contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 21-mm-diameter nodule in the lower lung with multiple liver and bone metastases. The patient received several tests, and it was determined that the patient's adenocarcinoma of the lung was positive for an EGFR gene deletion. The patient developed Trousseau syndrome, which resulted in cerebral infarctions. The patient was given anticoagulant therapy with thrombomodulin alfa and heparin, and eventually treated with osimertinib. Unfortunately, the patient showed disease progression, and further chemotherapy was not administered. The patient died one month after discontinuation of osimertinib.
output: The anticoagulant therapy initiated for the patient's Trousseau syndrome was thrombomodulin alfa. Subsequently, the patient was treated with intravenous unfractionated heparin.

The patient was discharged in stable condition without any significant medical issues.

Progressively worsening neck pain and numbness of the left upper extremity and the left face for the past 2 weeks.

The patient was experiencing progressively worsening neck pain and numbness of the left upper extremity and the left face for the past 2 weeks. He did not report any recent head or neck injuries. The patient's past medical history was not significant.

The neurological examination revealed a mildly spastic gait and exaggerated deep tendon reflexes in the bilateral upper and lower extremities. He also had mild dysuria and constipation. Muscle strength and vibration sense were normal, and no Babinski sign was present.

Peripheral blood examination revealed no significant abnormality. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was within normal limits except for slightly elevated protein. Unenhanced CT of the cervicothoracic spine showed diffuse dorsal epidural calcification at C3-T6. The lesion presented as a crescent shape along the spinal dura mater and had a well-defined border along the vertebral arch. Head CT and MR imaging revealed no significant abnormality.

C5/6 laminectomy was performed to biopsy for confirmation. Perioperative findings revealed an intact ligamentum flavum. A solid, grayish-white lesion was found just beneath the ligamentum flavum. Grocott, periodic acid-Schiff and Ziehl-Neelsen stains showed no obvious source of infection (e.g. fungal or tubercular), and there was no evidence of malignancy. The patient’s neurological symptoms during the postoperative course were uneventful, and follow-up CT performed 4 months later revealed no regrowth of the calcified lesion.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with CPPD crystal deposition disease along the spinal dura mater.

Summary:
A 54-year-old male presented with progressively worsening neck pain and numbness of the left upper extremity and the left face. Diagnostic tests revealed CPPD crystal deposition disease along the spinal dura mater. The patient underwent C5/6 laminectomy and biopsy for confirmation. instruction: What was the patient's initial working diagnosis and how did it progress during hospitalization, as mentioned in the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 71-year-old Caucasian man who was admitted to our hospital with the chief complaints of abrupt-onset blurry vision, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and ataxia.

History and Hospital course:
The patient had no prior history of stroke and had been taking prophylactic aspirin for years for a patent foramen ovale. On admission, the initial working diagnosis was of a cerebellar stroke, and the patient was transferred to the acute inpatient stroke rehabilitation service. Despite participation in rehabilitation therapies, his symptoms progressively worsened. He underwent a noncontrast head CT, which demonstrated indistinct, masslike lesions in the cerebellum necessitating transfer to the neurosurgery service. Steroids were administered, which produced rapid improvement in his symptoms. Contrast-enhanced CT performed later that day revealed three intensely enhancing masses in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The patient underwent right suboccipital craniotomy with partial resection of the visible tumor in the right cerebellum. Histopathology revealed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, non-germinal center type. 

Workup:
Carotid Doppler ultrasound showed no stenosis. Subsequent CT angiography showed no vascular compromise. CT with contrast enhancement and whole-body positron emission tomography failed to demonstrate a primary tumor of origin outside the central nervous system. The result of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) testing was negative. Bone marrow biopsy and testicular ultrasound demonstrated no evidence of lymphoma in these sites.

Management and Treatment:
The patient elected to pursue induction chemotherapy. He was started on the MATRix regimen (methotrexate, cytarabine, and rituximab), which the patient has tolerated well thus far, with no residual disease seen on contrast-enhanced head CT scans. Because of his age, the radiation oncology service recommended against whole-body irradiation to minimize neurotoxicity. 

Outcomes:
The patient has experienced marked improvement in his symptoms with treatment and is able to ambulate with a walker, but he still reports balance problems and blurry vision. 

Follow-up:
The patient will continue to follow up with the oncology service for further management and treatment. An ophthalmologic evaluation is also recommended to monitor the patient’s vision.
output: The patient's initial working diagnosis was cerebellar stroke, but it progressed to the diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, non-germinal center type. This was revealed through histopathology after the patient underwent right suboccipital craniotomy with partial resection of the visible tumor in the right cerebellum.

instruction: What is the relation between the patient's Dsg1 antibody levels and the effectiveness of rituximab infusions in treating pemphigus foliaceus?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted]
Age: 55 years
Gender: Male
Medical Record Number: [redacted]

Hospital Course Summary:
This 55-year-old male presenting with multiple erythematous papules and plaques with crusts on his back, chest, face, and scalp was found to have pemphigus foliaceus, with no mucosal involvement. The patient's blood tests, including differential blood count, liver enzymes, creatinine, and Dsg3 antibody level, were within the normal range. However, the patient's Dsg1 antibody level was highly elevated (130 U/ml; normal range <20 U/ml), and a slightly elevated γ-glutamyltransferase level was observed. Histological examination of a skin biopsy revealed an inflammatory infiltrate, eosinophilic spongiosis, and superficial epidermal blister formation, consistent with the diagnosis.

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated with prednisolone (10 mg/day) and azathioprine (100 mg/day), along with topical therapy with clobetasol propionate and chlorhexidine. Methylprednisolone infusions (750 mg) were also administered once a month for three months but did not result in complete remission. Dexamethasone (300 mg) and cyclophosphamide infusions (500 mg) were administered once a month, but azathioprine had to be discontinued due to increasing liver enzymes. This treatment was discontinued after five months as complete remission could not be achieved.

Subsequently, the patient was treated with rituximab, and two infusions (1 g each) were administered 2 weeks apart which led to a near-complete B-cell depletion in peripheral blood. This was accompanied by a decrease in Dsg1 antibody levels (below the detection range) and an almost complete remission of the skin lesions within the following year. Prednisolone (10 mg/day) and topical mometasone furoate were continued for the following 2 years. The prednisolone dose was reduced to 5 mg/day. The patient remained in remission for 7 years with this therapy, and Dsg1 antibody levels continued to remain within the normal range. 

However, in autumn 2017, skin lesions reappeared, which was accompanied by an increase in the Dsg1 antibody levels (75 U/ml). The prednisolone dosage was increased (temporarily up to 60 mg/day), but it was not sufficient to control the disease. Therefore, rituximab infusions (2 × 1 g within 14 days) were readministered, which led to slow continuous healing of the skin lesions.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's current condition is stable and under control, with almost complete remission of skin lesions, indicating a positive prognosis. The patient will be monitored regularly to prevent recurrence.

Recommendations:
It is recommended that the patient should maintain regular follow-up with a dermatologist to ensure long-term management of the medical condition for a complete recovery. The patient should also take appropriate precautions to avoid exposure to unnecessary physical and chemical stressors. 

Discharge medications include: None.

Follow-up: Follow-up appointment with a dermatologist in six months recommended.
output: The patient's highly elevated Dsg1 antibody levels were decreased to below the detection range after two infusions of rituximab, which led to near-complete B-cell depletion in peripheral blood, and almost complete remission of the skin lesions within the following year. The patient's gradual relapse in 2017 with an increase in the Dsg1 antibody levels suggests the effectiveness of rituximab may be related to the patient's Dsg1 antibody levels. However, the discharge summary does not provide information regarding the specific relation between the Dsg1 antibody levels and the effectiveness of rituximab.

The patient, a 78-year-old female with a history of CREST syndrome, presented to the emergency room with hematemesis and mild abdominal pain. She was diagnosed with acute-on-chronic anemia from gastrointestinal bleeding. During her hospital stay, she underwent urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy but no actively bleeding lesion was identified. She was discharged after tolerating liquid food; however, she was brought back to the emergency room for severe lower abdominal pain hours after discharge. The patient was diagnosed with bowel perforation and underwent exploratory laparotomy. Despite the surgery, the patient experienced complications and her family members decided to initiate comfort care.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient presented to the emergency room with hematemesis and mild abdominal pain. Laboratory studies revealed a WBC count of 29X10 ∧3/μl and a hemoglobin of 4.7 g/L. Elevated venous lactate level was noted. She received intravenous fluid resuscitation and empirical piperacillin/tazobactam as well as 2 units of red blood cells transfusion in the emergency room. A subsequent CT scan of the abdomen that showed significantly dilated colon and pneumatosis intestinalis. No surgical intervention was needed. Patient was then admitted to ICU for close monitoring and management of her condition. She underwent urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy, which revealed Barrett's-type esophageal mucosa and erosive gastritis without actively bleeding lesion; due to this, the patient was discharged home on the 4th day of hospitalization after tolerating liquid food. She was brought back to the emergency room a few hours after discharge due to severe lower abdominal pain and was diagnosed with bowel perforation, for which she underwent exploratory laparotomy. Patchy necrosis throughout the large intestine and a perforated lesion in the ascending colon were identified during the operation. Subtotal colectomy, omentectomy, and end ileostomy were performed. Pathological findings were consistent with colonic perforation with transmural ischemic necrosis and fibrosis. CT angiography and conventional angiogram were performed to determine the culprit artery for bowel ischemia and identified a noncritical stenosis in superior mesenteric artery. The patient was then transferred to ICU for postoperative care. However, her recovery was complicated with ventilation dependent respiratory failure and another episode of bowel perforation, which led to the initiation of comfort care due to her advanced age, comorbidities, and poor prognosis.

2. Gastrointestinal perforation with transmural ischemic necrosis and fibrosis.

Mitral valvuloplasty was performed first, followed by CABG with left internal mammary artery anastomosed to proximal LAD. Direct inspection through aortotomy confirmed the diagnosis of left main coronary atresia. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged after seven days. At the three-month follow-up, her condition remained stable and echocardiography showed normal heart function. A patent LIMA-LAD graft was observed on coronary angiography, with a small LAD.

instruction: What was the diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up plan for a 70-year-old male patient who presented with classic symptoms of hyperthyroidism, had a 4 cm thyroid nodule, received a total thyroidectomy, and was found to have FVPTC testing with regular monitoring on follow-up visit?
input:
Hospital Course:

This 70-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital presenting with increased appetite, palpitations, weight loss, and heat intolerance. Physical examination revealed the presence of a 4 cm thyroid nodule in the left lobe. The patient had a known history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and coronary artery disease.

The patient's thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level was suppressed 0.29 uIU/mL, while free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) were elevated. A radioiodine uptake scan detected an abnormal focus of hot uptake in the left lobe, which was suggestive of a hyperfunctioning toxic thyroid nodule. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) was performed, and the cytology report indicated thyroid carcinoma. 

Treatment:

The patient underwent total thyroidectomy, and the pathological report confirmed FVPTC findings. The lesion was limited to the solitary tumor, measuring a diameter of 3.5 cm. Ablative radioiodine therapy was not recommended due to the small size of the tumor. Post-surgery, the patient received levothyroxine medication to prevent hypothyroidism and to stop TSH stimulation. 

Follow-Up:

Serum TSH and serum thyroglobulin were regularly monitored. On follow-up visit, radioactive iodine whole-body scan showed no distant metastasis. 

Summary:

This 70-year-old male patient presented classic symptoms of hyperthyroidism which were investigated by FNA revealing FVPTC arising within a toxic nodule. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with no distant metastasis on follow-up visit. The patient received post-operative treatment and follow-up monitoring to manage the thyroid status.
output: The diagnosis for the 70-year-old male patient was hyperthyroidism caused by a hyperfunctioning toxic thyroid nodule that was confirmed to have FVPTC after undergoing total thyroidectomy. Ablative radioiodine therapy was not recommended due to the small size of the tumor. The patient received levothyroxine medication post-surgery to prevent hypothyroidism and underwent regular monitoring of serum TSH and thyroglobulin levels. On follow-up, there was no distant metastasis detected on the radioactive iodine whole-body scan.

Principal Diagnosis: Retroperitoneal hematoma with pseudoaneurysm

Hospital Course Summary

The 71-year-old male patient, an ex-smoker, was admitted to our facility with acute kidney injury secondary to suspected vasculitis. His peripheral anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (P-ANCA) levels confirmed crescentic glomerulonephritis as the root cause. Upon undergoing a right-sided renal biopsy, the patient experienced hemodynamic instability within the first 24 hours, accompanied by a hemoglobin drop of 3 grams, which indicated post-procedure hemorrhage. An initial contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiogram (CTA) showed a large retroperitoneal hematoma in the right posterior lumbar and iliac fossa region, which allowed us to identify a saccular pseudoaneurysm measuring 3 mm arising from the right second lumbar artery.

To treat the hematoma, the patient was transferred to our vascular center where we performed conventional angiography. Selective catheterization of the branch with the pseudoaneurysm was done with a microcatheter, and coil embolization was performed, followed by Gelfoam pledget embolization. The final angiogram demonstrated the exclusion of the pseudoaneurysm with preserved functionality in the main trunk of the lumbar artery. A selective renal angiogram was performed that showed no evidence of renal vascular injury. Post-embolization, the patient did not experience any further episodes of bleeding and was discharged in a stable condition.

During the patient's hospitalization, he was treated with antibiotics to prevent any potential bacterial infections and received multiple transfusions of packed red blood cells to address the post-procedure hemorrhage. His hemoglobin levels were monitored closely through regular laboratory testing, which demonstrated a progressive improvement. The patient received proper nursing care to manage pain, promote mobility, and facilitate early ambulation to prevent any thrombotic events. The patient was also advised to follow up with his primary care physician and our facility's vascular center for any future concerns.

In summary, the patient was admitted with acute kidney injury secondary to suspected vasculitis, which led to a post-procedure hemorrhage resulting in a large retroperitoneal hematoma with a saccular pseudoaneurysm. Interventional radiology performed the coil embolization and Gelfoam pledget embolization, thereby effectively treating the hematoma. The patient's hospitalization was uneventful post-procedure, and he was discharged in a stable condition with follow-up recommendations.

Its surface was almost entirely smooth, and some erosions and ulcerations were seen. It was elastic and hard and showed no tenderness on palpation. There was no palpable regional lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral ossifying fibroma with squamous cell carcinoma (pT1N0M0)

Tumorectomy was performed under general anesthesia to remove the tumor, including the surrounding tissue. One week after surgery, the wound was covered with an oral appliance for protection.

instruction: What was the diagnosis and treatment process for a patient with a spermatocele and indirect hernia with cord, testicle, and omentum as its contents according to the given discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
MR#: [Medical Record Number]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Medical History:
The patient, a 61-year-old male, presented with painless swelling in the right scrotum for 10 years.

Hospital Course:
On examination, a large soft and non-tender swelling was observed with free overlying skin that reached the base of the scrotum. A positive transillumination test indicated a fluid-filled unilocular cyst suggestive of spermatocele. A scrotal ultrasound revealed a unilocular cyst that measured 371 ml. The patient underwent scrotal exploration, which exposed a large unilocular cyst originating from the rete testis and partially covered by a membranous sheath. After dissection from the testicle, the giant spermatocele underwent sac release. The testicle and spermatic cord were enclosed in a thin sac-like structure, tracing it to the deep ring that entered the peritoneal cavity. The index finger palpation with omentum at the deep ring revealed a diagnosis of an indirect hernia of the complete type with spermatocele, cord, testicle, and omentum as its contents was made.

The sac was dissected up to the deep ring, incised laterally, and cord with testicle kept out of the sac (extrasacal). The twisting of the incised sac with sac-high ligation was performed, releasing it into the peritoneal cavity. The histopathology procedure confirmed the diagnosis of spermatocele and revealed that the hernia's sac type was fibrous.

Follow-up Period:
The patient underwent an uneventful follow-up period with no further complications.

Conclusion:
The patient received proper medical care and treatment and was discharged from the hospital in a stable condition on [Date].
output: According to the provided discharge summary, the patient was diagnosed with a spermatocele and an indirect hernia of complete type with cord, testicle, and omentum as its contents. The patient underwent scrotal exploration and sac release, with extrasacal cord and testicle, and twisting of the incised sac with sac-high ligation to release it into the peritoneal cavity. The histopathology procedure confirmed the diagnosis of spermatocele, and the follow-up period was uneventful with no further complications.

The 65-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital due to low back pain and left posterior thigh and calf pain caused by a vertebral tumor in the lumbar spine. The patient had undergone resection of retroperitoneal diffuse liposarcoma (DDL) five years previously, repeated resection for recurrence three years previously, and recurrence occurred one year previously. The revised Tokuhashi score was 11/15, and the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score was 10/18.

The patient underwent tumor curettage and L1 laminectomy followed by percutaneous pedicle screw fixation from the Th11 to L3 using intraoperative 3-D CT computer navigation. Positive staining for MDM2 and CDK4 by immunohistochemistry and negativity of DDIT3 or FUS by FISH confirmed dedifferentiated liposarcoma.

Discharge Status:

The patient's symptoms were improved after surgery for symptomatic relief, and she was discharged from the hospital. However, the retroperitoneal mass subsequently increased, and the patient passed away 1.5 years after surgery.

The patient underwent coil embolization under general anesthesia. The Right femoral artery puncture was made after left subclavian angiography, in which the left vertebral artery was not visible. Additional coil deployment took place after accidentally migrating some of the coil masses to the VA origin. The procedure was completed after the confirmation of PICA occlusion.

Outcome:
The patient recovered fully with supportive care in the ICU after the coil embolization, and follow-up MRI results showed no acute cerebral infarction in the PICA territory. The patient underwent a follow-up angiography a year after the procedure, which revealed no aneurysmal sacs in the distal PICA, and the recanalized VA was located medial to the deployed coil mass.

instruction: What clinical Named Entities related to the patient's endocrine system can be extracted using Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 49-year-old male, was admitted with symptoms of acromegaly and hypogonadism secondary to a suspected pituitary adenoma. Physical examination demonstrated minimal physical signs of acromegaly and normal testicular size. MRI showed a 9 x 9 mm mass lesion in the left inferior-posterior aspect of the sella turcica abutting the left carotid artery. The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery achieving gross total resection. Histopathology revealed a pituitary adenoma staining strongly on immunohistochemistry for prolactin and weakly for growth hormone (GH).

After surgery, lab tests showed elevated serum IGF-I and decreased serum testosterone levels. The patient was treated with oral CC, 25 mg/day, for six months. Lab evaluations showed improvement in total and free testosterone levels, normalization of serum IGF-I, and controlled GH and prolactin levels (). The patient reported resolution of fatigue and improved libido.

After discontinuing CC treatment for four months, the patient had recurrence of hypogonadal symptoms, and the lab tests showed return to near pretreatment values. Resuming CC therapy, the lab evaluations showed improvement in total and free testosterone levels and an IGF-I level returned to target, fulfilling “Koch's postulate” providing evidence of effectiveness of therapy.

The patient's joint aches, snoring, and swelling of hands improved after surgery, but the patient experienced persistent fatigue and sexual dysfunction. Overall, the patient responded well to treatment with oral clomiphene citrate and was advised to continue with this therapy.

Summary:

The 49-year-old male patient was admitted with symptoms of acromegaly and hypogonadism secondary to a pituitary adenoma. The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery, achieving gross total resection. Postoperatively, he developed hypogonadism and received oral CC. The patient showed an improvement in testosterone levels and normalization of serum IGF-I with CC treatment. The patient reported resolution of fatigue and improved libido, yet had some persistent symptoms. Overall, the patient responded well to treatment with oral clomiphene citrate and was advised to continue with this therapy.
output: The clinical Named Entities related to the patient's endocrine system that can be extracted from this discharge summary are acromegaly, hypogonadism, pituitary adenoma, prolactin, growth hormone, testosterone, IGF-I, and clomiphene citrate.

instruction: What was the initial suspected diagnosis of the hypodense mass found in the second/third portion of the duodenum on CT scan and what diagnosis was confirmed after biopsy and surgery?
input:
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 49-year-old Caucasian woman, presented to the emergency room with palpitations, shortness of breath, pallor, and black tarry stools. She was evaluated and diagnosed with anemia with a hemoglobin level of 4.4 g/dL. The patient was transfused and underwent a gastrointestinal bleeding workup, which included a CT scan of the abdomen. The CT scan revealed a possible hypodense mass in the second/third portion of the duodenum that was intraluminal with an extraluminal component abutting the uncinate process of the pancreas. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy were performed, which revealed an ulcerated mass in the second/third portion of the duodenum that was suspected to be a duodenal adenocarcinoma. Biopsy of the mass was obtained but showed cellular debris. The patient stabilized and stopped bleeding and was discharged home. 

The patient was seen at the hepatobiliary surgery clinic where additional testing was performed to stage the mass. Tumor markers were negative, and the patient's personal and family history were unremarkable. The patient underwent a pancreaticoduodenectomy based on the suspicion for a duodenal adenocarcinoma. She had an uneventful hospital stay and was discharged home on postoperative day five. 

Summary:

The patient, a 49-year-old Caucasian woman, was admitted to the emergency room with palpitations, shortness of breath, pallor, and black tarry stools. She was found to be anemic and was transfused. A gastrointestinal bleeding workup, including a CT scan of the abdomen, was initiated. The CT scan revealed a possible hypodense mass in the second/third portion of the duodenum that was suspected to be a duodenal adenocarcinoma. The patient underwent a biopsy, which was inconclusive, and was eventually scheduled for a pancreaticoduodenectomy. The surgery was successful, and the final pathology revealed a duodenal gangliocytic paraganglioma eroding into the pancreas. At her follow-up appointment eight months postoperatively, the patient was still free of disease.
output: The initial suspected diagnosis of the hypodense mass found in the second/third portion of the duodenum on CT scan was duodenal adenocarcinoma, but the final pathology revealed a duodenal gangliocytic paraganglioma eroding into the pancreas.

instruction: What was the diagnosis of the 70-year-old male patient, and what chemotherapy treatments were administered, leading to the relapse of the hemophagocytic syndrome and persistence of Hodgkin lymphoma?
input:
Hospital Course:
The 70-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital due to general debility, fever, and sweats lasting for two weeks. The initial diagnosis suspected prostatitis, however, after two different antibiotic treatments were provided without any improvement, a hematology malignancy was suspected. Blood count, smear, and abdominal CT scan have led to the suspicion of hemophagocytic syndrome and DLBCL. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy performed, and the diagnosis was confirmed to be Richter syndrome transforming a marginal zone lymphoma into a DLBCL associated with a stage IV lymphocyte-depleted classic Hodgkin lymphoma. The patient was treated by COP and ABVD chemotherapy before the diagnosis of HL was firmly established. After the diagnosis was firm, the patient was treated by three cycles of R-CHOEP chemotherapy. The initial response to this therapy was satisfactory until a urinary infection occurred and led to the relapse of the hemophagocytic syndrome and a persistence of the Hodgkin lymphoma. Despite antibiotic treatment and chemotherapy, multiple organ failure led to the patient’s decease.

A bone marrow biopsy revealed Richter syndrome transforming a marginal zone lymphoma into a DLBCL associated with a stage IV lymphocyte-depleted classic Hodgkin lymphoma. The patient received COP and ABVD chemotherapy before the diagnosis of HL was firmly established. After the diagnosis was firm, the patient was treated by three cycles of R-CHOEP chemotherapy, which provided an initial satisfactory response. However, the patient was readmitted due to a urinary infection, which led to a relapse of the hemophagocytic syndrome and a persistence of the Hodgkin lymphoma. Hospital course:

49-year-old male admitted to the urology clinic after incidental detection of a renal mass. He was asymptomatic during admission without any urological history. His physical examination was remarkable for morbid obesity, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, asthma, osteoarthritis, and gastro-esophageal reflux disease. He weighed 400 lbs. Hemoglobin was 131 g/L, creatinine was 96 umol/L, and eGFR was 80 ml/min/1.73m2.

A CT scan of the abdomen was done and revealed a large exophytic heterogeneous mass measuring 9.1 × 9.1 × 10.5 cm in the lower pole of the left kidney. A pre-operative CT scan of the chest and bone scan showed no metastatic disease. A renogram showed that the left renal mass was poorly functioning and that there was significant tubular dysfunction affecting both kidneys symmetrically. The function was estimated as 43% on the left and 57% on the right.

Surgical Procedure:

Patient underwent an uncomplicated open left partial nephrectomy after four months from the presentation. The tumor was confined to the kidney with negative surgical margins, and the pathological stage was pT2a, Nx, Mx.

Post-operative follow-up involved a CT image after six months to check for any local recurrence. The patient remained without evidence of any local or distant tumor recurrence.

Gross examination revealed a firm-to-rubbery 10cm tumor located in the lower pole of the left kidney. The microscopic examination showed a solid renal tumor with characteristic intermediate to large size cells with partially vacuolated eosinophilic cytoplasms. SDHB-deficient RCC was diagnosed from the biopsy.

Surveillance and genetic counseling:

Since the patient had an increased risk of paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas, annual or biennial biochemical and radiographic surveillance for PC and PGL was carried out. Additionally, genetic testing was offered to family members, who are at risk of inheriting the SDHB mutation.

Discharge condition:

The patient was discharged in a stable condition. Further follow-up was recommended to monitor for any signs of recurrence or complications.

SDHB-deficient RCC.

Recommendations:

The patient was recommended to continue annual or biennial biochemical and radiographic surveillance to monitor for recurrence of paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas, respectively. Genetic testing was offered to family members, who may be at risk of inheriting the SDHB mutation.

instruction: What was the suspected cause of type B lactic acidosis in the patient, and how was it managed during their hospital stay? (related to the task of Relation Extraction)
