input:
Discharge Summary:
 
Hospital Course:

The patient is a 35-year-old male with interventricular communication who presented to the emergency room with vomiting, fever and progressive dyspnea. On admission, he exhibited tachycardia, and a systo-diastolic murmur was heard. A chest X-ray revealed bilateral nodular infiltrates, and laboratory tests showed the increase of nitrogenous compounds and metabolic acidosis. A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed left ventricular enlargement and aortic insufficiency, while transesophageal echocardiogram showed aortic valve vegetation, ascending aorta dilatation, aortic regurgitation, and interventricular communication.

The patient was diagnosed with systemic embolization with findings of hypodense cortico-subcortical areas at the left parieto-occipital and right occipital regions on cranial tomography, and peripheral hypodense areas in the spleen and a subcapsular hypodense area at the inferior pole of the right kidney on abdominal tomography. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed cuneiform consolidation areas consistent with septic embolism. Blood cultures were drawn and turned out positive for oxacillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.

The patient underwent cardiac surgery and, during the procedure, a vegetation at the ventricular side of the aortic valve and an abscess along the aortic ring were found. Extracorporeal circulation was used for 3 hours and 10 minutes, and multiple blood transfusions were taken. The patient arrived at the intensive care unit hemodynamically unstable under high doses of noradrenalin and dobutamine. Unfortunately, the patient died on the fifth post-operatory day due to refractory shock.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with systemic embolization secondary to infective endocarditis, with culture-proven oxacillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. The patient underwent cardiac surgery, but unfortunately, he passed away due to refractory shock.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with progressive dyspnea for one month, which was accompanied by vomiting and fever for the past five days. He was admitted to the emergency department, where he was treated for infective endocarditis with Meropenem and Linezolid, which resulted in a positive blood culture result for Staphylococcus aureus. The patient developed signs of peripheral embolization, and imaging revealed systemic involvement with embolic infarctions in the lungs, brain, and spleen. instruction: What was the reason for the switch from cefazolin to vancomycin in the patient's treatment and what was the result of the aspirate cultures? (related to Relation Extraction)

Gender: Female

Diagnosis: Bilateral Lower Extremity Edema and a Left Lateral Leg Ulceration

The patient presented with painful bilateral lower extremity edema and a left lateral leg ulceration, she was admitted to the hospital and started on cefazolin for left lower extremity cellulitis on hospital day one. On hospital day three, the patient's CRP began to uptrend and she became febrile. At this point, her antibiotics were switched from cefazolin to vancomycin to cover MRSA. On hospital day five, the patient was noted to have a new erythematous area over the anterior left knee, inferior to the patella. Ultrasound revealed a small fluid collection superficial to the patellar tendon. The infrapatellar bursa was aspirated and sent for culture. 
An MRI was performed on hospital day seven but did not reveal any evidence of osteomyelitis. On hospital day eight, aspirate cultures returned with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The patient was clinically improved after starting piperacillin-tazobactam, and vancomycin was discontinued on hospital day seven. She was stable for discharge on hospital day eight and was sent out with a ten-day course of levofloxacin. Close follow-up with infectious disease was also recommended.

The patient's hospital stay was marked by a switch in antibiotics from cefazolin to vancomycin as a reaction to the uptrending CRP levels and feverish symptoms. This was done to cover MRSA. An MRI was delayed due to the patient's pacemaker. On hospital day eight, the patient was discharged with a ten-day course of levofloxacin after the aspirate cultures returned with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. 

Follow-Up:

The patient was advised to follow up with the infectious disease department after being discharged. A ten-day course of levofloxacin was prescribed to the patient to ensure a full recovery. 

Summary:

The patient presented with bilateral lower extremity edema and a left lateral leg ulceration. The patient was admitted, had imaging done, and was treated with a switch in antibiotics after experiencing uptrending CRP levels and feverish symptoms. Hospital Course:
The patient is a 33-year-old Chinese female who presented with sudden onset of a para-central large scotoma in her left eye seven days after receiving the third intramuscular administration of the rabies vaccine. The patient's symptoms and results from the investigations were consistent with the diagnosis of Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome (MEWDS). Other differential diagnoses included but were not limited to choroiditis, Acute Posterior Multifocal Placoid Pigment Epitheliopathy (APMPPE), and acute macular neuroretinopathy.

Treatment:
As the patient refused to take oral steroid, she received local steroid injection (retrobulbar injection of triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg).

Follow-up:
At the follow-up examination 2 months after the initial evaluation, symptoms, OCT, Fundus AF, and the visual field were partially resolved. Three years later, the patient was examined again, the fundus was completely restored to normal both on fundus photograph and OCT and the BCVA was 20/20 and all symptoms disappeared.

The patient underwent excision of the skin lesion, and the pathology report was not performed. The patient then developed a painful red lump on her right axilla and was referred to our hospital. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma was made. The patient received cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and dexamethasone and achieved complete remission. The patient received maintenance therapy and remains in complete remission at three years after treatment.

The patient was a 69-year-old male with a chronic complicated type B aortic dissection who underwent endovascular repair. The patient presented early postoperatively with left flank pain and hemodynamic instability. Despite intravenous bolus administration and a massive blood transfusion, the patient's vital signs could not be stabilized. Bedside ultrasonography revealed a giant left retroperitoneal hematoma, and the patient was suspected to have left retroperitoneal hemorrhage. The patient was immediately taken to the operating room for emergency transcatheter embolization.

Procedure:
The patient underwent an abdominal angiography that revealed two active bleeding sites located in the left renal artery's distal branches. The doctors performed a super-selective embolization of two renal arterial branches with metallic microcoils and histoacryl glue.

Outcome:
Completion angiography showed effective occlusion of the feeding vessel and termination of the left renal bleeding. However, postoperatively, the patient developed abdominal compartment syndrome, which led to multiple organ failure and ultimately, death two days after surgery.

However, the postoperative outcome was unfavorable, as the patient developed abdominal compartment syndrome, leading to multiple organ failure and ultimately death two days after surgery.

Further testing revealed bone metastases of the right rib and L2 vertebra, with a clinical stage of T2aN0M1. The patient was treated with radiation therapy and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), and his PSA level dropped to 0.053 ng/mL. At the age of 56 years, his PSA level was again elevated, and he was restarted on different hormonal treatments with flutamide, estramustine phosphate, enzalutamide, and abiraterone. At the age of 58 years, the patient developed a resistance to hormonal therapies.  
 
Using 11C-choline PET/CT imaging, multiple bone metastases without lymph node metastases or visceral metastases were confirmed. The patient then completed six cycles of Ra-223 therapy without any interruption and adverse effects. The third 11C-choline PET/CT after six cycles showed that existing lesions increased and new uptake spots were found in the thoracic spine, sacrum, right rib, and right ileum. During Ra-223 therapy, the patient’s serum ALP did not dramatically change, but PSA levels gradually increased. After the completion of Ra-223 therapy, a new chemotherapy with cabazitaxel was started.  

At the time of discharge, the patient’s symptoms and biochemical progression remained. Close monitoring, continuation of therapies, and further treatment are recommended. The patient should continue follow-ups with his primary care physician.
output: After developing a resistance to hormonal therapies, the patient received six cycles of Ra-223 therapy for bone metastases. However, the subsequent 11C-choline PET/CT showed increased lesions and new uptake spots. Cabazitaxel chemotherapy was then started. During Ra-223 therapy, the patient's serum ALP did not dramatically change, but PSA levels gradually increased. The discharge summary did not provide specific information regarding how cabazitaxel affected the patient's PSA levels and existing lesions.

instruction: What was the diagnosis of the patient with complaints of headache and fever for one week leading to the detection of osteolytic lesions in the skull, and what was the treatment given?
input:
Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [name]
Sex: Female
Age: 64
Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient was admitted to the emergency unit with complaints of headache and fever for one week. She reported pain over her whole skull without any specific trigger point. Cranial and peripheral neurologic function did not have any impairment. There was no nausea, vomiting, blurred vision, or nuchal stiffness.

MEDICAL HISTORY:
The patient denied drug or alcohol abuse.

FINDINGS:
Laboratory examination disclosed a normocytic anemia. Blood chemistry tests revealed abnormally elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase. Chest X-ray routine film showed no active lung lesions. A computerized tomography (CT) scan of the head was ordered to rule out intracranial abscess or other central nervous system problems.

DIAGNOSIS:
Multiple osteolytic lesions were detected in the skull, and subsequent immunofixation electrophoresis analysis of serum did not show any evidence of monoclonal gammopathy. Levels of serum tumor markers carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and cancer antigen 15-3 (CA 15-3) were meaningfully increased in concentration but levels of cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9) and cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) were within normal limits. A CT scan of chest and abdomen revealed osteosclerotic and osteolytic lesions similar to that of skull involving almost the whole skeleton but not a single clear-cut primary tumor site could be located. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed on the right side, posterior superior iliac crest, which revealed a metastatic adenocarcinoma.

TREATMENT:
Due to concern about the risk of fracture, the patient began to take tamoxifen, 20 mg twice daily. The effect seemed very satisfactory. After a period of probable “tamoxifen flare” with elevation of serum CA 15-3 and alkaline phosphatase levels for six weeks, both of them dropped gradually within four months (). Serum CA15-3 was within normal limits at the last follow-up. Positron emission tomography/CT (PET/CT) scans during the treatment course confirmed an impressive improvement of the bone marrow uptake. The mild activity remained in the lumbar spine could be either residual metastasis or, more favored by us, compensatory hyperactive hematopoiesis in its recovery phase (). 

SUMMARY:
The patient was diagnosed with metastatic adenocarcinoma due to the osteolytic lesions found on a CT scan of the skull. The patient was started on tamoxifen, 20 mg twice daily, which had a satisfactory effect. After a period of probable “tamoxifen flare” with elevation of serum CA 15-3 and alkaline phosphatase levels for six weeks, both of them dropped gradually within four months. Serum CA15-3 was within normal limits at the last follow-up. PET/CT scans during the treatment course confirmed an impressive improvement of the bone marrow uptake. The patient did not have headache or fever anymore and was discharged in stable condition.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient was advised to follow-up with her physician regularly for further assessment and treatment. Additionally, it is recommended that the patient continues taking tamoxifen as prescribed. The patient was advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle and exercise regularly to improve overall health. The patient was also advised to report any new symptoms that occur during the course of her treatment.
output: The patient was diagnosed with metastatic adenocarcinoma due to the osteolytic lesions found on a CT scan of the skull. The patient was started on tamoxifen, 20 mg twice daily, which had a satisfactory effect. After a period of probable “tamoxifen flare” with elevation of serum CA 15-3 and alkaline phosphatase levels for six weeks, both of them dropped gradually within four months. Serum CA15-3 was within normal limits at the last follow-up. Therefore, tamoxifen treatment was given for the patient.

instruction: What was the patient's final histopathological diagnosis and what was their pathological staging according to the information provided in the discharge summary?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 63-year-old Japanese man and a current smoker of more than 45 pack-years. A routine chest X-ray revealed an abnormal shadow in the left middle lung field. He underwent a chest computed tomography (CT) scan which showed a 3.6 × 2.8 cm pulmonary lesion in the left upper lobe with a clear boundary and heterogeneous contrast enhancement.
In the PET scan, the nodule showed an accumulation of 18F-fluorodexyglucose (FDG) with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUV max) of 4.95 in the early phase and 6.31 in the late phase. The trans-bronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) of the mass in the left upper lobe revealed non-small cell carcinoma.
A left upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection were performed. The resected tumor measured 3.8 × 2.8 × 2.8 cm in diameter. The resected specimen showed a well-established grayish lesion with areas of necrosis. The patient's final histopathological diagnosis was H-FLAC.
Both lymphatic and vascular invasion were detected. Microscopically, all margins were free, but mediastinal lymph nodes (#5) showed metastasis. The final pathological staging was Stage IIIA (pT2aN2M0). The patient received cisplatin plus vinorelbine as adjuvant chemotherapy, but it was canceled at two courses because of the dehydration and hyperglycemia induced by the chemotherapy. The patient had relapsed pleural dissemination at 25 months after the surgery. Postoperative serum CEA and AFP were 1.5 and 3.7 ng/mL, respectively. But, serum CEA at the time of relapse was 132.4 ng/mL, and AFP was unfortunately not searched.
output: The patient's final histopathological diagnosis was H-FLAC and their pathological staging was Stage IIIA (pT2aN2M0), as per the information provided in the discharge summary.

instruction: What is the identified relationship between autoimmune atrophic gastritis, the patient's decreased vitamin B12 levels, and the findings of gastric atrophy, cystic dilatation of gastric glands, and decreased parietal cells on esophagogastroduodenoscopy?
input:
Hospital Course:
The patient, a 66-year-old Japanese woman, was admitted to the Department of Neurology for investigation of aphasia. Upon laboratory testing, decreased levels of vitamin B12 were noted. Further evaluation with esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed gastric atrophy predominantly in the fornix and in the body, cystic dilatation of the gastric glands, and a significant decrease in parietal cells. Additionally, the patient had increased levels of rheumatoid factor, hemoglobin A1c, and gastrin. The patient was positive for anti-intrinsic factor antibody and antiparietal cell antibody. These findings led to a diagnosis of autoimmune atrophic gastritis. 

Discharge Summary:
The patient was safely discharged from the hospital after a comprehensive evaluation and treatment of autoimmune atrophic gastritis. Appropriate laboratory tests and endoscopy helped diagnose and treat the patient's condition. Recommendations for continued follow-up care were given to the patient upon discharge.
output: The identified relationship between autoimmune atrophic gastritis, the patient's decreased vitamin B12 levels, and the findings of gastric atrophy, cystic dilatation of gastric glands, and decreased parietal cells on esophagogastroduodenoscopy is that autoimmune atrophic gastritis leads to damage and destruction of the parietal cells in the stomach, which in turn results in a decrease in the production of intrinsic factor. As intrinsic factor production decreases, the patient's ability to absorb vitamin B12 from the diet is also reduced, leading to decreased vitamin B12 levels. This deficiency can cause the neurological symptom of aphasia, as well as megaloblastic anemia. Furthermore, the esophagogastroduodenoscopy findings, including gastric atrophy, cystic dilatation of gastric glands, and decreased parietal cells, are consistent with the diagnosis of autoimmune atrophic gastritis.

instruction: What evidence in the discharge summary supports the use of pulse methyl-prednisolone therapy and long-term azithromycin for management of the patient's bronchiolitis obliterans (BO)?
input:

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED] days

Diagnosis:

- Persistent rhinovirus and adenovirus infections

Hospital Course:
A 14-month-old male patient was admitted to the hospital with respiratory distress, wheeze, and hypoxia, preceded by 24 hours of coryza, fever, and reduced feeding. He was diagnosed with pneumonia and was intubated and ventilated for 4 days. After being extubated, he was transferred to the high dependency unit (HDU) on continuous positive airways pressure (CPAP) ventilation. He continued to have persistent work of breathing, expiratory wheeze, and symptoms and signs of air trapping. He achieved weight gain and oxygenation when started on Heated Humidified High Flow Nasal cannula therapy (HHHFNC).

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of nasopharyngeal aspirates (NPAs) revealed persistent rhinovirus and adenovirus infections. No biopsy or histopathological investigation was performed to confirm BO. He had two further intercurrent bacterial respiratory infections during his inpatient stay, treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Immunological investigations revealed IgG and IgM hypogammaglobulinemia but normal IgA. The patient received weekly supplemental immunoglobulins.

A CT chest was performed and showed a mosaic pattern attenuation of both lung fields with a combination of air trapping and oligaemia, consistent with BO, believed to be secondary to the persistent adenovirus infection.

After a multidisciplinary team discussion, it was decided to commence pulse methyl-prednisolone therapy and long-term azithromycin for management of BO. Cidofovir was administered to control the adenovirus replication.

An array comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) revealed mosaic tetrasomy of short arm of chromosome 9. The patient is currently being given weekly supplemental immunoglobulins.

Most recently, the child has now cleared the long-term rhinovirus and adenovirus infections and has been weaned off steroids and long-term oxygen therapy. Ongoing problems include recent Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection with a wet cough.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is discharged in stable condition. Close monitoring and follow-up appointments are crucial to assess any progression of his condition. Parents are advised to seek medical attention if the patient displays any signs of respiratory distress.

- Respiratory Clinic: [REDACTED]

instruction: What Named Entities can be recognized in the discharge summary with regards to the diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis and the treatment given for it?
input:
Hospital Course Summary:

This hospital course summary pertains to a 35-year-old male who presented to the Emergency Department with a 10-day history of high-grade fever, shortness of breath, palpitations, and joint pain. The patient was found to have a history of intravenous drug abuse but denied any other medical conditions or allergies. A review of other organ systems was unremarkable. The patient had a known ostium secundum with left-to-right shunt, which was previously diagnosed by transoesophageal echocardiography. Further tests were conducted, including complete blood cell count, malarial and dengue tests, and serology for HIV and hepatitis. The CBC showed a slightly low hemoglobin level and an elevated total leukocyte count. All other tests were insignificant.

Given the persistent high-grade fever, Infective Endocarditis (IE) was suspected, and echocardiography and blood culture were performed. Echocardiography showed no vegetation. However, blood samples were found to be positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and treated accordingly with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin for a period of six weeks. After the fever subsided, surgery for the closure of ASD was performed successfully. The patient was discharged from the hospital after good recovery and referred to a rehabilitation center for drug abuse. Continued monthly follow-up visits have since shown that the patient continues to do well.

instruction: What was the course of treatment for the 54-year-old female patient with renal cell carcinoma and multiple pulmonary metastasis, and what was the outcome?

A 54-year-old female patient presented with intermittent low-grade fever and mild dry cough for two months. Anorexia and weight loss were also reported. She had a recent history of being investigated for right renal calculus. The patient reported being treated with antibiotics by several doctors for possible infection.
 
Physical Examination:
The patient appeared ill and was mildly pale. No enlarged lymph nodes or hepatosplenomegaly were observed. Examination of the respiratory system revealed no pleural effusions or added sounds. Her pulse rate was regular and her blood pressure was within normal limits.

Diagnostic Results:
Initial diagnostic investigations included complete blood count which showed normochromic normocytic anemia. Inflammatory markers were significantly elevated with an elevated ESR of 130 in the first hour and CRP of 124 u/l. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures were negative repeatedly.  Chest radiograph showed multiple bilateral opacities with small nodular lesions over all three zones of both lungs. Ultrasound scan of the abdomen showed no significant abnormality. The CECT revealed a renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with multiple pulmonary metastasis.

Treatment:
The patient was empirically treated with antibiotics for two weeks but did not respond. She was then transferred to oncology care and treated with oral Sunitinib, a multitargeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor. The treatment led to a resolution of hepatic abnormalities.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged to continue treatment with oral Sunitinib. Close follow-up with the oncology team was recommended.
output: The 54-year-old female patient with renal cell carcinoma and multiple pulmonary metastasis was treated with oral Sunitinib, a multitargeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, after two weeks of unsuccessful antibiotic treatment. instruction: What were the patient's antenatal syphilis diagnosis and treatment, and how did they lead to the diagnosis of congenital syphilis?
input:
Discharge Summary

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Patient Name: Ms. [LAST NAME], [FIRST NAME]
Sex: Female
Age: 29 years
Race: Caucasian
Medical Record Number: [NUMBER]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our Fetal Medicine Centre at 19+5 weeks of gestation due to positive serology for syphilis in the first trimester. No clinical manifestations of the disease were found during the examination. The patient had a history of a feverish erythematosus maculopapular rash localized to trunk, limbs, palms, and soles two years before. The diagnosis of syphilis was performed only during antenatal screening in the first trimester by a positive venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) and a treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA) title of 1:2560. The HIV status of the patient was negative.

Antibiotic therapy was immediately started with benzathine penicillin G 7.2 million units total, administered as 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals according to the stage of syphilis, in line with CDC guidelines. Syphilis serology tests were stable with VDRL positive and a TPHA title of 1:2560 at the end of the treatment. The patient's husband also had positive VDRL (1:320) and TPHA titres, and he was treated with a recommended regimen.

The scan performed at 19+5 weeks of gestation revealed no abnormalities, and fetal growth parameters were normal. However, at 23+5 weeks of gestation, a follow-up scan showed a massive hydrocephalus, severe hydrothorax, ascites, and hepatomegaly. The measurement of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) showed an increased peak systolic velocity for gestational age. The patient's blood tests for cytomegalovirus, coxsackievirus, parvovirus, toxoplasma, and herpes virus types 1 and 2 were found negative while syphilis serologic tests were confirmed positive with RPR title 1:4 and TPHA title 1:640. Fetal karyotype was normal. After thorough counseling on the fetal anomaly, the patient decided to pursue the termination of pregnancy.

Fetal autopsy showed multiple abnormalities including a cutaneous erythematous papular disseminated rash, widespread edema, ascites, hydrothorax, internal obstructed hydrocephalus, ischemic-haemorrhagic brain injury with disseminated lesions, productive pachymeningitis with dystrophic calcification, hepatomegaly, acute hepatic and splenic hematopoiesis, productive bilateral peripyelitis, pronounced glomerulus-poiesis, and involution of the thymus. The research of Treponema Pallidum with coloring of Warthin-Starry identified images compatible with the morphological appearance of the germ. The diagnostic conclusion deposed for congenital syphilis.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged home in stable condition. Recommendations for follow-up care and management were given accordingly.
output: The patient was diagnosed with syphilis during antenatal screening in the first trimester through positive VDRL and TPHA tests. Antibiotic therapy with benzathine penicillin G was immediately started and serology tests were stable at the end of treatment. However, a follow-up ultrasound at 23+5 weeks of gestation revealed fetal abnormalities such as massive hydrocephalus, severe hydrothorax, and hepatomegaly. Blood tests confirmed positive syphilis serology with RPR and TPHA titres, and the fetal autopsy later diagnosed it as congenital syphilis. The initial antenatal syphilis diagnosis and prompt treatment did not prevent the progression of congenital syphilis in the fetus.

instruction: What were the procedures performed and complications encountered in the treatment of bilateral urolithiasis and Escherichia coli urinary tract infection in the given discharge summary?

Stable.

None.

1. Right proximal ureteral stone.

instruction: What was the cause of the patient's diarrhea and weight loss, and what was the treatment approach for the diagnosed condition according to the discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Chief Complaint: Diarrhea and weight loss

History of Present Illness:

The patient is a 30-year-old female with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and stage V lupus nephritis who underwent a deceased donor renal transplant 10 years prior. She presented with a chief complaint of diarrhea consisting of loose, watery bowel movements, mild nausea, anorexia, abdominal cramping, and an unintentional 15-pound weight loss. A detailed workup was performed, and a positive fecal lactoferrin, normal fecal fat content, and antitissue transglutaminase antibody, a negative Clostridium difficile stool toxin, and a positive stool infectious panel PCR for sapovirus were found.

Hospital Course:

During the hospital course, the patient was initially treated with intravenous fluids and antidiarrheal medications. Mycophenolate mofetil dose was decreased gradually and eventually discontinued. Azathioprine was started in place of mycophenolate mofetil, and the patient did have some improvement in the consistency of her stools but the overall large volume output persisted. Nitazoxanide 500 mg orally (PO) twice daily was initiated, and the patient's diarrhea improved within 3 days. She was treated with the medication for 7 days total, and a repeat stool infectious panel 1 month after therapy demonstrated a negative sapovirus PCR.

Summary of Treatment:

The patient's diarrhea and weight loss were likely due to sapovirus infection, a common cause of gastroenteritis. The patient was managed with intravenous fluids, decreased dosage of mycophenolate mofetil, and azathioprine. Nitazoxanide was initiated, leading to the improvement of symptoms. The patient was successfully treated and was discharged in stable condition.

Medications:

The patient was treated initially with intravenous fluids, antidiarrheal medications, and nitazoxanide. Her mycophenolate mofetil dose was gradually decreased and eventually discontinued, and azathioprine was started in place of mycophenolate mofetil.

Follow-up:

The patient's stool infectious panel was negative 1 month after therapy, indicating successful treatment. The patient was advised to follow up with her transplant nephrologist in the coming weeks to adjust her immunosuppression regimen.
output: The patient's diarrhea and weight loss were likely due to sapovirus infection, which was successfully treated with intravenous fluids, decreased dosage of mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, and a 7-day course of nitazoxanide. According to the discharge summary, the patient was advised to follow up with her transplant nephrologist in the coming weeks to adjust her immunosuppression regimen. Patient: 34-year-old male with a history of diminished vision in both eyes

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with a complaint of diminished vision in both eyes for the past 10 years. He also reported diminished night vision that was stationary and non-progressive. The patient had no significant medical history or family history of nyctalopia. Ocular examination revealed a visual acuity of 6/36 (OD) and FCCF (OS), and the pupillary reactions were sluggish in both eyes.

Diagnosis:

Initially, the patient was considered to be suffering from choroideremia, retinitis pigmentosa, and scarred posterior uveitis. Further evaluation revealed no evidence of uveitis, and the patient's siblings showed normal retina during examination. After reviewing the patient's past medical history, it was found that he had attempted suicide 10 years ago and consumed the chemical used in the iodination of salt. The patient's symptoms of deteriorated vision in both eyes began after the suicide attempt.

Medical Tests:

An OCT evaluation showed evidence of outer retinal atrophy with associated sub-foveal scarring, and a thinning of the choriocapillaris was noted on the OCT scans. An electroretinogram (ERG) showed a flat response in both eyes on scotopic stimulation. An old fundus fluorescein angiogram revealed noticeable areas of choroidal hyperfluorescence due to extensive window defects, indicating RPE damage.

Treatment and Follow-up:

The patient's condition is not treatable with current medical interventions, and his vision cannot be restored. Recommendations made by a multidisciplinary team suggest that the patient adapts to his current vision and participate in counseling for depression and suicidality. The patient was advised to seek medical care if there are any changes in vision or symptoms.
output: The patient's history of attempting suicide and consuming the iodination chemical is highly likely to have caused the patient's current diagnosis of outer retinal atrophy with associated sub-foveal scarring and choroidal hyperfluorescence due to extensive window defects, leading to RPE damage and deteriorated vision in both eyes.

instruction: What Named Entities related to the patient's condition of psychomotor developmental retardation can be identified using Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary?
input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 5-month-old boy 
Diagnosis: Psychomotor developmental retardation

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the pediatric neurodevelopmental unit of Bayi Children’s Hospital with psychomotor developmental retardation. The patient presented with an inability to control his head, hypsokinesis, inability to turn over or grasp, and high muscle tension.

Diagnostic Workup:

A urine sample was collected, pretreated with urease and derivatized with BSTFA + 1% trimethylchlorosilane. The metabolites in the urine were analyzed by GC-MS, revealing visibly increased excretion of 2-HG in the urine.

A genetic diagnosis was performed by sequencing the entire coding region sequences of L2HGDH. Two novel mutations were identified in exon 3 of the patient, a homozygous missense mutation (c.407 A > G, p.K136R) and a heterozygous deletion of one nucleotide (c.408delG, p.K136SfsX3).

Imaging:

A brain MRI revealed symmetrical, high-signal changes in the subcortical white matter, basal ganglia, and cerebellar dentate nuclei. The lateral ventricular wall showed multiple nodular gray matter heterotopia. The right side of the cerebellar hemisphere and vermis showed dysplasia.

Conclusion:

The patient's symptoms and diagnostic workup were consistent with a diagnosis of psychomotor developmental retardation. Further testing revealed two novel mutations in L2HGDH, confirming an autosomal recessive trait. The homozygous missense mutation (c.407 A > G, p.K136R) was predicted to be the pathogenic mutation of the patient. The patient was discharged with a plan for ongoing monitoring and support.
output: The Named Entities related to the patient's condition of psychomotor developmental retardation that can be identified using Named Entity Recognition in this discharge summary are the following: Bayi Children's Hospital, L2HGDH gene, 2-HG, homozygous missense mutation (c.407 A > G, p.K136R), heterozygous deletion of one nucleotide (c.408delG, p.K136SfsX3), subcortical white matter, basal ganglia, cerebellar dentate nuclei, lateral ventricular wall, gray matter heterotopia, cerebellar hemisphere, and vermis dysplasia. instruction: What is the relation between the patient's treatment with intratumoral VAE and the size and pain of the calvarian skull metastasis?

The patient was admitted to the hospital for treatment of deep rectal cancer with lung metastases. The primary tumor was excised via deep anterior rectum resection and classified as moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Following surgery, the patient underwent several rounds of chemotherapy and radiation therapy for metastatic lesions. Despite treatment, the patient's cancer lesions continued to progress over time, resulting in the development of multiple bone and head metastases.

The patient was treated with various chemotherapy regimens, radiation therapy, and bisphosphonate therapy over the course of several years. The patient received intratumoral VAE treatment for the calvarian skull metastasis, which led to a reduction in pain and tenderness and decreased the size of the metastasis significantly. The patient's other metastases remained stable during the VAE treatment, but later progressed, leading to the patient's death at the age of 74 years.

Medical History:

The patient had a medical history of appendectomy and hysterectomy, and hepatic cysts were present. The patient was also diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypertension and was treated with appropriate medications.

Conclusion:

The patient's treatment for deep rectal cancer with lung metastases involved several rounds of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and bisphosphonate therapy, along with intratumoral VAE treatment for the calvarian skull metastasis. Despite the patient's initial response to treatment, the cancer lesions eventually progressed, leading to the patient's death. The patient had a comprehensive medical history, and appropriate treatment was provided for concurrent medical conditions.
output: The patient's intratumoral VAE treatment led to a reduction in pain and tenderness and significantly decreased the size of the calvarian skull metastasis.

The patient underwent conservative management for several days, which was not effective, and eventually underwent a transsphenoidal endoscopic exploration, with septoplasty and packing of the sphenoid sinus with abdominal fat graft, and with the insertion of a lumbar drain. instruction: What is the patient's diagnosis and description of histopathological examination after undergoing laparoscopic cecectomy for evaluation of an enlarged and diffusely thickened appendix?

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated an enlarged and diffusely thickened appendix, and colonoscopy revealed that the appendiceal mucosa was benign. Laparoscopic cecectomy was performed, revealing a thick, enlarged and fibrotic appendiceal wall. Histopathological examination showed a single layer of atypical mucinous epithelial cells lining the appendix and multiple neurofibromas. Pathologically, the patient was diagnosed with appendiceal neurofibroma of NF1 with LAMNs. The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable, and he was discharged on post-operative day 3.
 
Summary of Hospitalization:
A 62-year-old man with NF1 was admitted for evaluation of an enlarged and diffusely thickened appendix. The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable, and he was discharged on post-operative day 3.
output: The patient's diagnosis after undergoing laparoscopic cecectomy for evaluation of an enlarged and diffusely thickened appendix was appendiceal neurofibroma of NF1 with LAMNs. Histopathological examination showed a single layer of atypical mucinous epithelial cells lining the appendix and multiple neurofibromas.
